World.title: Oil jumps to $105, pushing up chances of a US interest rate increase
World.content:
Share Oil jumps to $105, pushing up chances of a US interest rate increase on social media

Oil prices have increased by four percent, with benchmark Brent crude hitting $105 a barrel after the biggest rise in attacks on shipping since the Iran war began spurred trader concerns about further supply disruptions.

Brent crude futures were up $4.05, or four percent, at $105.26 a barrel by 1215 GMT on Thursday. United States oil topped $100 a barrel for the first time since May, as West Texas Intermediate crude futures CLc1 rose $3.99, or 4.15 percent, to $100.04.

Brent prices have surged by more than 30 percent from lows touched in early August, as a permanent agreement between the US and Iran to cease attacks never materialised and fighting resumed.

Iran-aligned Houthis seized control of Yemen’s port of Mocha on Thursday, further threatening Red Sea traffic, while Gulf traffic remains restricted through the Strait of Hormuz as tanker attacks in the region have intensified in recent days.

“The recent run-up in prices lays bare the market’s approach: this conflict will last longer than anticipated even a month ago, let alone at the beginning of the summer. If oil supply and exports are diminished, the oil balance remains tight and prices remain elevated,” PVM analyst John Evans said.

Iran said it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, after the US hit five Iranian oil tankers. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it would escalate its response to any further attacks.

While fears of prolonged and more severe supply disruptions in the Gulf have lifted Brent above $100, analysts say the durability of the rally will hinge on China.



Chinese demand

China, the world’s largest crude importer, has stepped up purchases in recent weeks after months of subdued demand, boosting physical crude markets, ING analysts said in a note.

If Chinese buying continues to recover, it could amplify the impact of any supply disruptions and drive prices higher, while a pullback in imports could temper market gains, ING said.

“For months, the bearish case rested on soft Chinese demand,” said David Jorbenaze, global oil market lead at commodities information provider, ICIS.

Rising oil prices have worsened worries about inflation and cranked up pressure within the bond market, helping to lower stocks again on Wall Street.

The S&P 500 fell 0.6 percent and is on track for a fourth straight loss.

The increase in oil prices has pushed the price for a gallon of regular petrol to an average of nearly $4.28 across the US, according to the American Automobile Association. That is not only costing more at the pump but also through higher prices for all kinds of products that move by truck to store shelves.

Following Thursday’s reports, traders are betting on a close to 70 percent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That’s up from the 61 percent probability seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That’s also despite President Donald Trump’s consistent lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher.

World.title: Yemen's Houthis reportedly seize strategic Red Sea port of Mokha
World.content:
On Tuesday, the Houthis launched dozens of drones and missiles at southern Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 civilians and causing fires at several oil facilities that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi authorities.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for dozens of Saudi air strikes on their territory in north-western Yemen in recent days, including one on a prison in the town of Hazm in Jawf province that local officials said killed at least 23 civilians.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The Red Sea has become crucial for Saudi Arabia's oil exports since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

World.title: Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?
World.content:
Under US federal law, it is illegal to give payments that are intended to influence the way a person is voting.

However, some experts have said the offer made by Trump in Texas on Wednesday could be seen as a pledge to cut taxes, which is legal.

Dr Joan Mahoney, lecturer in law at the University of Southampton, told the BBC she thought the offer would be legal as it would be similar to a campaign promise - though she said politicians "don't usually do it quite this explicitly".

"On the one hand it sounds a bit like a bribe, vote for the Republicans and you'll get money, which would be decidedly illegal," she said.

"But on the other hand it would go to everyone, regardless of how they voted so it isn't in that sense a bribe.

"I think it would be legal. It's the same kind of campaign pledge as saying 'if my party wins we'll reduce taxes'. Every party does that all the time... and that's obviously perfectly legal."

However, Laurel Rapp, director of the US and North America programme at Chatham House, told the BBC that Trump's offer seemed to be "a very different, very transactional agreement" from the kind of promise usually made by candidates in an election period.

World.title: Pilot warned Amazon cargo plane going too fast before deadly crash, data shows
World.content:
The flight data released by NTSB included the plane's speed, altitude, and other details like flap deployment as it approached the runway. The update also included the summary of conversation between the two pilots.

The summary noted the pilot's cautions about speed occurred "throughout the remainder of the recording" as did the inconsistent verbal response.

The update said there was an electronic "sink rate sink rate" callout during the final minutes - an automated safety warning about the speed of descent.

There was also an âelectronic "too low terrain" callout, another automated verbal warning that the plane was flying too close to the ground without being properly prepared for landing.

Aviation attorney Pablo Rojas told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that it was difficult to know without the actual recording what the NTSB was referring to when it noted the inconsistent verbal response.

"But, it really confirms that this was, in a way, a doomed approach," he said.

Rojas noted that flap deployment data included in NTSB's update also could be an area of concern. The flaps, located on the back of the wings, are "part of what helps the plane kind of slow down and gently approach a landing", he said.

"The flap deployment here happened much later in the accident sequence," Rojas said. "That's maybe because the pilots were responding to the fact that they were going too fast."

After it overshot the runway, the plane - Amazon Prime Air Flight 7598 - struck equipment on the ground, hit a white Ford van, then continued onward through a perimeter fence.

It then collided with a Toyota Corolla, before coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.

The five who died were part of a plane-cleaning crew in the van. Miami authorities on Tuesday identified them as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.

World.title: Israel's Netanyahu to sue newspaper over claim UAE warned him of 7 October attack
World.content:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has told lawyers to begin defamation proceedings against an Israeli newspaper over reports that the leader of the United Arab Emirates warned him that Hamas was planning an operation just days before the 7 October 2023 attacks.

According to book extracts published by Haaretz, UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan had a phone call with Netanyahu that September.

The report said Netanyahu was warned that the then-Hamas chief in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, was planning a major operation.

Netanyahu's office said "no warning was given to the prime minister from the United Arab Emirates before 7 October", calling the report part of a "sinister plot".

Haaretz, which has historically been a vocal critic of the prime minister, has stood by its reporting and rejected Netanyahu's defamation claim, saying its "sole purpose is to silence journalistic criticism".

The report - and Netanyahu's angry denials, accusing Haaretz of lies - comes as the general election campaign in Israel starts to heat up. The polls on 27 October are widely considered a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership.

On 7 October 2023, thousands of Hamas-led gunmen breached the Gaza border fence and attacked nearby Israeli communities, military bases and a large music festival. About 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken back to Gaza as hostages.

Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which at least 73,670 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Ever since 7 October, accusations have been laid against Netanyahu that he did not act quickly enough after the attack began. He has resisted an independent public inquiry into what happened and this latest report will only fuel critics' suspicions.

The report, published on Tuesday, cited three "foreign senior sources" and a Palestinian adviser to Sheikh Mohammed as saying that, in the final days of September 2023, a representative from the UAE embassy went to the Israeli prime minister's office with a special phone to ensure the conversation would remain confidential.

During that call, Haaretz reported, Netanyahu was given an explicit warning by Sheikh Mohammed - that Sinwar had told a former Palestinian official that Hamas was preparing a major operation that he described as an "earthquake".

"Bin Zayed expressed concern that the event in question would not only lead to bloodshed but also destabilise the entire region," Haaretz said, adding that the information contained in its report was a result of extensive research of dozens of sources, documents and correspondence, all carried out for a book, Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment, written by Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval.

"To his surprise however, the prime minister reacted with relative calm," Haaretz reported. "Netanyahu said that, in his assessment, Hamas intended to operate in the West Bank area, and he reassured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario."

The report went on to recount that the Emirati leader relayed the conversation he had with Netanyahu to the then CIA director William J Burns. It also said Netanyahu failed to brief the heads of Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency and Mossad intelligence agency, as well as the Israeli army's chief of staff about his conversation with the UAE president.

The report was published on the same day that the UK announced sanctions on illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank. The decision angered the Israeli government, which announced several countermeasures, including ordering the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.

But while that development made international headlines, it was the Haaretz story that led the news in a country getting ready for elections.

Netanyahu's Likud Party accused Haaretz of "blatant foreign interference in Israel's elections", while the prime minister said on X that the story had "clear political timing, as part of the left's election campaign".

Lawyers for Haaretz responded to Netanyahu's plans to begin legal proceedings, saying they would not be deterred by what they described as the prime minister's attempts to silence journalistic criticism.

The lawyers' letter stated that the report was "the product of an in-depth journalistic investigations and is based on sources pertaining to an issue of paramount public importance".

"In the absence of a full accountability to the public on behalf of your client, the press fulfils its role and exposes step by step the information to the public," it added.

While the UAE has not addressed the conversation specifically, it did not deny it either, issuing a statement emphasising that, since the attack by Hamas, it has worked towards de-escalation, regional stability and preventing violence.

"UAE and Israeli government entities have maintained open and direct lines of communication since the inception of the relationship more than five years ago," the UAE's ministry of foreign affairs said in a statement after the publication of Haaretz's report. "When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities."

Four of Israel's main opposition leaders issued a joint statement demanding an investigation into what happened.

"Netanyahu and his partners in the 7 October government are unfit to continue in office," said Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Lieberman and Yair Golan.

"We will work with the co-ordination and responsibility required to prevent them from leading to another disaster."

World.title: Twenty-five dead after fire on cargo ship in eastern China
World.content:
Twenty-five people have been killed in a fire on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked at a port in eastern China, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.

Of the 42 people on board, 17 were were evacuated of which five are in hospital in stable condition, CCTV reports.

The vessel was undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in the city of Qingdao when the blaze erupted at around 11:15 local time (03:15 GMT). It was put out just over three hours later, according to CCTV.

Photos released by state media showed the vessel to be the Ocean Melody, a 190m (623ft) long Liberia-flagged carrier which arrived in Qingdao on 31 August, according to tracking site MarineTraffic.

World.title: More than 20 children feared dead in DR Congo school fire
World.content:
At least 24 schoolchildren are feared dead in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, a senior official there has said.

Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.

Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain.

Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.

Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.

A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.

Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year.

Rebelâappointed authorities say they are assessing the situation and will release a provisional death toll this evening.

Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties.

"The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said.

"With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."

The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall.

In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

World.title: Royal family rift after popular TV news presenter chosen to succeed Ugandan king
World.content:
"My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday night of creating "confusion and turmoil" while the family was still grieving.

Meanwhile the late king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, has said royal guards have been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed, restricting the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing the situation as "house arrest".

She appealed to the army's leadership and President Yoweri Museveni to allow the family to mourn and bury Oyo in peace on Saturday.

"I appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."

Thousands of mourners are expected to attend the burial at the royal tombs near the palace in Fort Portal in western Uganda.

His body was returned to Uganda from the US on Friday, and preparations for the funeral are under way.

Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. Its monarch has no formal political authority but remains an important cultural figure in western Uganda.

Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967, but they were restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.

World.title: Apple's new boss starts with big gamble on £1,999 first folding iPhone
World.content:
Apple has launched its most expensive iPhone ever - a foldable handheld that costs at least Â£1,999 and marks the first major iPhone design change in almost 20 years.

The iPhone Duo is a gamble by new boss John Ternus, who took over from long-time chief executive Tim Cook this month.

Apple is entering the foldable phone market comparatively late, following the likes of South Korea's Samsung and China's Huawei.

Ternus told an audience at Apple's California headquarters: "Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together". Apple's model, he claimed "redefine[s] the experience of using a foldable phone".

In the US, prices start at $1,999, but can go up to $3,200. It has taken eight years to develop, something Ternus was directly involved in after spending many years as a top executive inside Apple's hardware division.

When unfolded, it looks like a small iPad and a wider iPhone when it is folded.

Ternus said: "It's entirely new and at the same time remarkably familiar. A similar size to your passport, it feels familiar to hold and comfortable to use with one hand."

But the product is facing established competitors. "The real fight is China, where Huawei owns nearly 80% of foldables," said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president for data and analytics, devices at IDC EMEA.

World.title: Shell faces trial over alleged misleading evidence in Nigeria oil spill case
World.content:
The UK High Court has ruled that allegations that witnesses who testified for Shell over oil spills in Nigeria sought to mislead the court can be examined ahead of the full trial of a long-running legal battle involving two Niger Delta communities.

The ruling followed a series of hearings in July 2026 concerning claims by the communities that their land in Bille, in Nigeria’s Niger Delta, was devastated by oil pollution allegedly caused by Shell.

In a statement issued by Leigh Day, a UK law firm representing the communities, and shared with PREMIUM TIMES on Thursday, the firm said the disputed witness evidence was given between 2016 and 2021 during jurisdiction proceedings before the High Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court.

Shell had sought to have the case dismissed from the English courts, arguing that the claims should be heard in Nigeria.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Its position was based partly on evidence that Shell Nigeria was wholly autonomous from its London-based parent company, Shell Plc.

However, the UK Supreme Court unanimously rejected Shell’s jurisdiction arguments in 2021, allowing the substantive claims to proceed.

The full trial is scheduled to begin at the High Court in May 2027, the statement noted.

Alleged misleading evidence

The Bille communities are seeking aggravated damages, alleging that Shell knowingly relied on false or misleading factual assertions by its witnesses in an attempt to prevent their claims from proceeding in the English courts.

Shell’s lawyers had argued that the allegations concerning the witness evidence should be dealt with separately after the main trial, if the claimants were successful.

According to the statement, the High Court rejected that approach, ruling that the issue should be considered before the substantive trial because it could affect the credibility of witnesses Shell intends to rely upon.

A separate hearing is also expected to determine whether Shell’s communications with its internal and external lawyers concerning the disputed evidence should remain protected by legal professional privilege, the law firm said.

The claimants argue that Shell has lost that privilege because of its alleged improper conduct.

Shell’s pipeline concerns

The case comes amid renewed scrutiny of Shell’s environmental record in Nigeria.

In June, PREMIUM TIMES reported that Shell continued operating one of its major oil pipelines in Nigeria for years despite internal warnings about environmental risks and infrastructure concerns, according to newly disclosed company documents.

The documents, obtained by the BBC through ongoing litigation in the UK, included emails, technical assessments and internal presentations showing that Shell executives repeatedly raised concerns about the safety and condition of the Nembe Creek Trunk Line (NCTL), a key pipeline transporting crude oil from inland oilfields to export facilities.

The revelations have added to scrutiny of decades of environmental pollution in the Niger Delta, where repeated oil spills have damaged wetlands, mangroves and fishing communities.

The documents were disclosed as part of legal proceedings brought by communities around the creeks and mangroves of the Niger Delta seeking to hold Shell liable for pollution linked to more than 100 oil leaks between 2011 and 2013.

A PREMIUM TIMES investigation published in June also found that the continuous eruption of toxic gases is threatening lives and livelihoods in Bille, amid decades of pollution and the improper decommissioning of abandoned oil facilities across the riverine community.

Ruling on Bille pollution claims

The High Court also rejected aspects of Shell’s challenge to the claimants’ updated pleadings, which set out the factual and legal basis for holding Shell responsible for pollution in Bille.

According to Leigh Day, the court confirmed that the communities can argue that Shell is responsible for pollution affecting the area even where residents cannot identify every individual spill that contributed to the contamination.

The court also clarified that the claims are not “all or nothing” or “global claims.”

READ ALSO: Ten oil spills recorded in Niger Delta in July

The decision could have wider implications for environmental litigation involving pollution caused by multiple incidents, particularly where affected communities may find it difficult to identify every individual polluting event and establish its precise contribution to the overall damage.

Matthew Renshaw, an international partner at Leigh Day, welcomed the ruling.

“Shell’s attempts to frustrate the progress of these claims has now reached a dead end and the case will now proceed to trial in full,” Mr Renshaw said.

He said the communities were pleased that the court had recognised the importance of determining whether Shell’s witnesses gave false or misleading evidence during the earlier proceedings.

According to Mr Renshaw, the ruling also establishes an important precedent for environmental cases involving multiple pollution events, allowing claimants to rely on a common-sense assessment of the harm caused without having to identify every individual incident and link it to a specific injury.

Shell’s position on the allegations will be tested as the proceedings continue, with the substantive trial expected to commence in May 2027.

World.title: Police investigate deaths of three siblings, 27 others in Ondo
World.content:
The Ondo State Police Command says it has commenced an investigation into the deaths of 27 people in Odigbo Local Government Area of the state.

The command disclosed this in a statement by its spokesperson, Jimoh Abayomi, on Wednesday in Akure, the state capital.

The victims, residents of Araromi-Obu, Odigbo and Orita New Town, died under circumstances suspected to be connected with poisoning.

Mr Abayomi said the police, in collaboration with the Ondo State Government and relevant health authorities, have commenced a comprehensive investigation into the incidents with a view to determining the actual cause of the reported deaths.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Police personnel, including Police Medical Services, are working closely with officials of the Ondo State Ministry of Health and the Odigbo Local Government health authorities in the collection of relevant information and evidence, while medical and toxicological examinations are being conducted to ascertain the substance, if any, responsible for the fatalities,” he said.

He cautioned members of the public against spreading unverified information on the matter, assuring that the actual number of casualties and the real cause of their deaths would be established through the ongoing investigation.

The police also advised residents of the affected communities to remain calm and cooperate with the authorities by providing useful information that may assist the investigation.

“At this stage, the Command wishes to caution members of the public against spreading unverified information or attributing the deaths to any particular substance, as the investigation and laboratory analyses are still ongoing. The actual number of casualties and the precise cause of the deaths will be established through the ongoing investigation.”

“Members of the public are also urged to refrain from consuming unregulated or suspicious alcoholic and herbal preparations pending the outcome of the investigation,” Mr Abayomi added.

“The Commissioner of Police, Ondo State Command, CP Felix Ohagwu, psc, mnips, mspsp, has assured members of the public that the Command is committed to unraveling the circumstances surrounding the unfortunate incidents and will take appropriate action against anyone found culpable.”

The command also shed light on the recent deaths of three siblings within the precincts of the Owena Barracks in Akure, the state capital.

The victims were identified as 11-year-old twins Joshua and Jacob Jonah, and their five-year-old sister, Blessing Jonah.

They reportedly accompanied their father, Samuel Jonah, to the farm on Friday, 4 September, but their lifeless bodies were found in the water the next day.

Mr Abayomi said the children left their father on the farm to return home but only discovered that they were missing after he arrived home.

A search operation was subsequently launched, leading to the discovery of the bodies of the three children on Saturday, 5 September, near the bank of a small river on the farm.

“The Command is diligently documenting all available facts and circumstances surrounding the unfortunate occurrence, with a view to establishing the exact circumstances leading to the children’s deaths,” he said.

The police spokesperson also urged parents and guardians to exercise greater vigilance over children, particularly when they are near rivers, streams, ponds and other bodies of water.

Ondo Govt speaks

Meanwhile, the Ondo State Commissioner for Health, Banji Ajaka, confirmed the deaths of 27 people in Odigbo and said the incident would be thoroughly investigated to establish the actual cause of the deaths.

The commissioner, however, did not disclose the specific substance suspected to have caused the fatalities, stressing that medical and health officials were expected to conduct further assessments in the affected communities.

Mr Ajaka said the government was taking the matter seriously and would provide more details after the ongoing investigation had established the circumstances surrounding the incident.

World.title: Akpabio petitions SSS over purported anti-North comment
World.content:
President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio, has petitioned the State Security Service (SSS) over a purported anti-North statement allegedly attributed to him.

The Special Assistant to the President of the Senate on Media, Jackson Udom, disclosed this in a statement issued on Wednesday in Abuja.

A viral statement allegedly quoted Mr Akpabio as threatening that Northerners would suffer if President Bola Tinubu lost the 2027 presidential election.

Mr Udom said the petition, signed by Akpabio’s Chief of Staff, Chinedu Akubueze, urged the SSS (also known as the Department of State Services) to urgently investigate the dissemination of the alleged false, inflammatory and divisive statement.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the graphic, bearing Mr Akpabio’s photograph and designation, attributed the following words to him: ‘Northerners you will be the ones to suffer the most if you allow Tinubu to lose the election.’

“Unequivocally, the President of the Senate did not make this statement.

“No date, venue, speech, interview, video, audio recordings, official statement or credible news report has been produced to authenticate it.

“The graphic carries no identifiable publisher’s mark or verifiable source,” he said.

Mr Udom said the statement appeared to have been deliberately manufactured and presented as an authentic quotation for the purpose of deceiving unsuspecting members of the public.

He said those behind the scheme intended to provoke regional resentment against Mr Akpabio and portray him as threatening people in the Northern part of the country.

According to him, preliminary examination of publicly accessible Facebook records identified some persons as among the earliest traceable amplifiers of the purported fabricated graphic.

He listed the persons as Abdullai Musa, who posted the graphic in a Facebook group styled ‘Sheik Muhammad bin Uthman Group 24.’

Others were Uzoma Chilaka, whose Facebook post allegedly reproduced the graphic commentary expressly credited to him, and Ibrahim Ammar, a verified Facebook account that subsequently reproduced the graphic and similar commentary.

“These persons should not be presumed guilty before investigation.

“Nevertheless, their early and substantial roles in circulating the material make them persons of interest, who may possess information capable of identifying the graphic designer, original uploader, sponsors, intermediaries and distribution network,” he said.

Mr Udom said their publication records, devices, communications and the provenance of the image should therefore be investigated in accordance with the law.

World.title: 2027: Peter Obi names Tinubu’s policy he’ll retain if elected
World.content:
Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, says he will retain President Bola Tinubu’s floating exchange-rate policy if elected in 2027, but will focus on increasing production to strengthen the naira.

Mr Obi said this in an interview with Arise TV on Thursday.

Asked to identify one policy of the Tinubu administration he would retain, the former Anambra State governor said the floating of the naira was one of them.

“There’s one: the floating of the naira. I’m not going to defend it. But I’m going to put productivity to work to make it more valuable to the people,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The former governor has previously said he would have floated the naira but in a more organised manner, arguing that currency devaluation or a float works better when supported by increased domestic production.

In a June 2025 interview, Mr Obi said there was “nothing wrong” with floating or devaluing the naira, but warned that doing so in an economy with low productivity could worsen economic pressures.

He said his administration would prioritise agriculture, manufacturing and other productive sectors to increase Nigeria’s output and make its exports more competitive.

The Central Bank of Nigeria introduced the foreign exchange reforms shortly after Mr Tinubu assumed office in 2023, allowing market forces to determine the value of the naira and ending the previous multiple exchange-rate regime.

The reform led to a sharp depreciation of the naira and has been blamed by critics for contributing to higher prices and worsening living costs. Supporters of the policy have argued that it removed distortions in the foreign exchange market and created a more transparent system.

Obi warns against ethnic politics

Mr Obi also warned against allowing ethnicity to determine the outcome of the 2027 presidential election.

“Our election should not be driven by tribalism,” he said.

The warning comes as political parties and their candidates intensify preparations for the 2027 election, with ethnic and regional considerations increasingly featuring in political debates.

Mr Obi, who contested the 2023 presidential election on the platform of the Labour Party, is now the NDC’s candidate.

His comments also come amid renewed discussions about opposition cooperation ahead of the election. He recently appeared at the launch of Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde’s presidential campaign office and described Mr Makinde as qualified to lead Nigeria.

In his Thursday interview, Mr Obi also argued that Nigeria’s problems could be addressed through purposeful leadership, institutional reforms and investment in critical sectors.

He identified national unity, security, justice and the rule of law among his priorities, while also promising to tackle corruption and improve healthcare, education and poverty reduction if elected.

Mr Obi’s latest position on the naira float is consistent with his earlier argument that the problem was not necessarily the decision to allow the currency to find its market value, but the absence of sufficient production to support the economy.

In his 2025 ARISE News interview, he said Nigeria needed to increase production in agriculture and manufacturing and implement economic reforms in an organised manner.

World.title: Man suspects foul play after his three missing children were found dead beside a stream in Ondo
World.content:
A security guard, Samuel Jonah, has appealed to the police and other security agencies to unravel the mystery behind the sudden deaths of his three children, whose bodies were found beside a stream within the precinct of the Owena Army Barracks in Akure, the Ondo State capital

The siblings were identified as 11-year-old twins Joshua and Jacob Jonah, and their five-year-old sister, Blessing Jonah.

Narrating the incident, Mr Jonah, who works as a security guard within the barracks, said he, his wife and the three children had gone to the farm on Friday, 4 September to do some work.

He said after some time he left the farm to go and collect his salary, while his wife also went to attend a ceremony somewhere in Akure.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He further stated that before they left, they instructed the children to return home at 6 p.m, but that by 8 p.m. they had not returned, prompting the search for them.

“I told them that their mother and I would be going home, and that they could continue playing around but should return home at 6 p.m. Their mother and I later went somewhere. By 6 p.m., we returned home, but I did not see my children,” he said.

Mr Jonah, who said he had routinely taken his children to the farm before the tragedy, said he became increasingly worried when the children had not returned home by 8 p.m.

“I began to think that something was wrong. I took my motorcycle and rushed to the farm,” he added.

He said that apart from alerting the military police at the barracks immediately, he also contacted friends and other acquaintances to help search for the children.

He said he also checked at their church, thinking the children could have gone there, but they were not found.

The grieving father, who has lived in Akure since 2003, said he was called the following day that the children had been found dead beside a river.

Foul play?

Although the initial suspicion was that they could have drowned in the water, Mr Jonah said the circumstances surrounding their deaths were too suspicious to be dismissed as drowning.

According to him, the children’s bodies were neither sufficiently wet nor did their stomachs contain water when they were found dead.

He also said he observed blood coming from their ears and from the body of his youngest daughter.

Mr Jonah maintained that the death of his children could be as a result of foul play, as his observation of their bodies shows, urging security agencies to help unravel the true circumstances of their death.

He said that though he has no direct proof, he wants authorities to investigate thoroughly.

The children’s uncle, Mazi Hassan, described the incident as shocking and called for justice.

“Three children from one family cannot just die like that. Government should investigate and bring those responsible to book,” Mr Hassan said.

Police, army speak

Meanwhile, the Ondo State Police Command said it has commenced an investigation into the deaths of the three children.

The police spokesperson in the state, Jimoh Abayomi, said the children were left on the farm and their father reportedly discovered that they were missing after he arrived home.

He said a search operation was subsequently launched, leading to the discovery of the bodies of the three children on Saturday, 5 September, near the bank of a small river on the farm.

“The Command is diligently documenting all available facts and circumstances surrounding the unfortunate occurrence, with a view to establishing the exact circumstances leading to the children’s deaths,” Mr Abayomi said.

The spokesperson said the Ondo State Commissioner of Police, Felix Ohagwu, had expressed condolences to the family over the loss of the siblings.

“Ohagwu expressed condolences to the bereaved family and assured them of the command’s commitment to uncovering the circumstances surrounding the tragedy,” he said.

Mr Abayomi urged parents and guardians to exercise greater vigilance over their children, particularly when they are near rivers, streams, ponds and other bodies of water,” he said.

Meanwhile, the remains of the three siblings have reportedly been released to the family for burial.

When contacted, the spokesperson for the 32 Artillery Brigade of the Nigerian Army, Akure, Innocent Omale, said he became aware of the incident through social media but confirmed that the police had taken over the case.

World.title: Pete Edochie’s Viral Interview: Seven remarks that got Nigerians talking
World.content:
Veteran Nollywood actor Pete Edochie has sparked conversations on social media following a wide-ranging interview in which he spoke about his career, marriage, culture, politics and his standing in the Nigerian film industry.

The actor, renowned for his commanding screen presence and proverbial expressions, was a guest on comedian Isbae U’s “Curiosity Made Me Ask”, where he fielded questions about subjects ranging from being described as a Nollywood legend to his views on marriage and cultural identity.

Several excerpts from the interview have since circulated on social media, generating debate over some of the 79-year-old actor’s views.

Several excerpts from the interview have since gone viral, with his remarks on marriage, cultural identity and his place in Nollywood history generating debate on social media.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Here are seven remarks from the interview that stood out.

‘I’ve never called myself a legend’

Addressing the description of him as a legend, the 79-year-old said, “As a matter of fact, people refer to me as a legend. I’ve never introduced myself as one. So, they assess me as one. I never do anything to impress anybody, no. This is an interview. I do my best to come across sensibly. I have never done anything; I am not in competition with anybody.

“I’ve never got them to say, “This is Pete Edochie; I’m a legend. So, if you say I’m a legend, I thank you very much. If you say, ‘Get away, I’m not a legend; it’s your business; I don’t give a damn.’ I saw myself as something of an actor, and I decided to experiment, and it worked.”

‘Whoever says we’re on the same plane, let him come out’ — his challenge to other veteran actors

Speaking about comparisons between him and other actors over who is older and who started their acting career first, he said, “When I did “The Merchant of Venice” in 1962, I was 15 years old. Then there was nothing like a film; it was all stage. Except you had Shakespeare in your head. You don’t qualify to be on stage. Call any of them you know who can handle “Shakespeare.” Let that person challenge me. MGM evaluated filming efforts across the African continent. And they said there are only two people we recognise as actors. Pete Edochie and John Carney of South Africa.

“Whoever says we’re on the same plane, let him come out. When I did “Things Fall Apart” in 1985, there was nothing like Nollywood. Nollywood came on board in 1992. When they did “Living in Bondage”, I was the only person in this country who did a film, and white people flew in to come and interview me. No other person has achieved it. Let the person come out. I am glad to be celebrated very much. Very good. People have been writing all sorts of nonsense, claiming they’re senior to Pete Edochie, I just allow them to. Anything goes on in Lagos, so I don’t mind.

“They are entitled to all those things. So I don’t bother. I don’t respond. But now that you have said it, I am now challenging you. Let the people come out. When the white man gives you credit for employing his language effectively to communicate, then you say, I think I have done well.

“I was given national honours before all of them. I got national honours under Olusegun Obasanjo. Others campaigned for theirs. I never campaigned for mine. I sit down in my house, and the honours come. I think last year, a university from Togo or something; I don’t remember now. They brought me two doctoral degrees to my house.”

Why men shouldn’t kneel to propose

On the practice of men getting down on one knee to propose marriage to women, Edochie said, “Do you (Isbae U) have any evidence that your father proposed to your mother kneeling? I am asking you a simple question. I’m not going the other way. I never do anything because I saw others doing it. I’m a Christian, and a Catholic. If I go into the church and I genuflect, then I make the sign of the cross. What does it mean? I have stepped into the abode of a high spirit. And I must acknowledge that. That is why I go down on my knees.

“If you kneel and offer a woman a ring, you are conceding the headship of the family to her. And that is what a lot of you who advocate for that don’t even understand. Have you ever asked yourself why marriages don’t last in Western countries? That’s the reason. So if your wife decides to divorce you, she’s entitled to maybe half or 75% of what you have. They are beginning to realise it now by opening service in the name of their mothers, not themselves anymore. So the women are beginning to lose.”

‘One wife is enough for any man’

Commenting on polygamy, the actor said, “I believe that one wife is okay for any man. If it works for you, come on, take 20. Or better still, go and ask the Ooni of Ife. He has a lot of them. Let him tell you how he copes with them. When you look at animals, you’ll see why we are referred to as animals. The average dog will not be satisfied with one female dog, just like a cockerel and all that. But you find out that at the end of the day, you keep hopping from one to another. I mean, it’s not that it’s a big deal or that there’s something that those have that these don’t have. Whatever gives you all the excitement originates from you, not the women.

“I had an uncle once. He’s dead now. He married his first wife. And he married the second one. Then, finally, he married the third one. I asked him why. He said there was no way they would all conspire against him at the same time. They went to conspire against him. The other one will come and tell me, tell him what they are saying. Then he said he’s not comfortable. He’s not balanced now. He’s fully wifed. Not long after, he left. I don’t expect you to take more than one wife, no.”

Why Igbo men should embrace traditional dressing

On the Igbo people’s preference for Western clothing over traditional attire, Edochie maintained that, “I have a lot of love and respect for the Yoruba man. He does not joke with his culture. No matter the situation, he comes across with his culture. And I love him for that. I want my people to do the same thing. Have you ever seen me put on a tie? It doesn’t make sense. If people sit around at a concourse, you look around, you can always pick the

“Yoruba people who are there because sartorially, they have to express themselves in their tradition. That’s what our people ought to do. What are we putting on a suit for? It’s not necessary. You go to the north, you see the Hausa man has the traditional gear. Then you go to Warri and all that. You see all these things. I think it’s some colonial mentality. It’s tragic. They should not at all. The time for that is gone.”

‘Don’t pray for your wife to feed you’

Edochie further advised men against allowing their wives to become the breadwinners, saying, “You want us to dwell in the future when we are not there yet. Wait until you get married. Then you see what that institution is like. You might marry somebody who will offer you hell and you’ll not be happy sitting down after all the insults to start washing her undies. If your mates come to your house and they see you washing the undies of your wife, they can desert you immediately.

“Don’t pray for your wife to feed you. If you get into such a situation, you’d like to take poison and die. This is wisdom from somebody who’s been in that institution for almost 60 years. I’ve been married for the past 57 years. If things change and your wife has to feed you for two or three days, you’d like to take poison. The kind of insult that will be heaped on you because your wife is feeding…”

Why Awolowo remains his favourite politician

On his favourite politician, he noted, “I’m not into politics but if you ask me who my favourite politician is, I will tell you it’s Awolowo. You people were not born when Awolowo was in active politics. Awolowo will tell you I’m going to build this thing. It will cost a certain amount, and this is where I’m going to get it. There has been no politician to achieve that. Outside Awolowo, then, Michael Okpara, in the East. Awolowo introduced a lot of things in Nigeria that were not there previously.

“Awolowo brought television into Nigeria. It did. Then you would hear, this is WNBC, first in Africa. That was Awolowo. That was in 1959. Then in 1960, we in the East established our own television, and we were saying this is EMBC, second to none. We were second to the West, but we didn’t want to accept it, so we were saying second to none. Awolowo introduced it. Awolowo introduced free primary education, and it surprised everybody who was born then in the West. No matter where you came from, you benefited from it.

“So on a couple of occasions, when I tell people that this man was my favourite, regrettably, he never became the president of the country. But he wasn’t somebody who would invest so much energy promising you heaven and earth without doing anything. He was not that. If Awolowo told you, I’m going to build these things here, he would build them. Even though I am not interested in politics, he was my favourite politician.”

World.title: When a black scholar becomes a symbol: The Jason Arday controversy, By Toyin Falola
World.content:
Occasionally, what a person achieves eclipses who they are. They may be allowed into an institution because of scholarship, research, intellectual contribution, or intellectual promise. But that credential can come to matter more than they do. Their appointment becomes a symbol of advancement. Their success becomes a testament to diversification. Their failure, if it ever occurs, can become something bigger than individual disappointment. It can become justification as to why people like them shouldn’t have been there to fail in the first place. This is just one of many tough questions raised during a panel discussion about Jason Arday. When Jason Arday was appointed Professor of Sociology at the University of Cambridge in 2023, he was thrust into the spotlight as the youngest black professor at Cambridge, and his research involves race, inequality, higher education and mental health. His ascent was symbolic of more than just individual achievement. It took place during hundreds of years of racial exclusion in UK academia and alongside universities’ modern attempts to brand themselves as inclusive.

But visibility also has a price often left out of conversations about diversity. The more visible a person’s presence becomes at an institution, the more unusual that presence is thought to be, the easier it is for that person to become symbolic of that institution. Jason Arday was no longer just Jason Arday the scholar, researcher, and teacher. His presence on that faculty was used as proof that Cambridge was changing. It can also be used as proof, by those against such changes, that Cambridge has reduced its standards or changed them. This is what I called the “representational burden”. Representational burden occurs when a scholar becomes more than just themselves in the eyes of an institution. Their success is now symbolic of a whole group of people. And if they fail, they also fail as that representative body. The burden starts when we value or deplore a scholar not only for their own actions and successes, but for what their presence means about the wider institution. Do universities praise that scholar’s success as a successful scholar or as proof of diversity? Do critics judge that scholar as an individual or as a “representational body”?

Which brings me to the issue of academic scrutiny. Scrutiny is not the problem. Universities require it. Scholarly activity requires criticism, evidence, and even questioning of claims. If a scholar comes from a historically oppressed minority, he or she cannot rightfully claim protection from legitimate criticism just because they claim marginalization. However, just because there are legitimate standards does not mean they are always applied with equal vigor, nor that they don’t harbor biases. The tough part, then, is not deciding if academic integrity should be protected. It’s deciding if it is protected fairly, without double standards, and by means that can differentiate an allegation from fact.

That mattered particularly in relation to discussion about Arday’s academic record and the subsequent investigation of his background. Professor Lester split the discussion about Arday’s academic conduct from the later scrutiny of his personal history. He confirmed errors had been made in Arday’s academic attributions but said claims relating to Arday’s PhD thesis had already been investigated by the awarding body. According to Prof. Lester’s account, that investigation identified citation errors but considered them excusable. Prof. Lester also argued that some of the extraordinary claims associated with Arday’s life story had subsequently acquired evidence, while others remained difficult to substantiate. His larger point was that questions surrounding a person’s biography should not automatically be transformed into evidence about the integrity of that person’s academic publications.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This distinction is more than a technical one. It invites us to consider what happens when the biography of a public figure becomes part of the process through which that person’s intellectual credibility is judged. A scholar may have an imperfect biography. The individual might distort the event in his mind, exaggerate the situation, misconstrue the occurrence, make statements that will not be easy to verify later, or recount his life story in accordance with the memoir format. In itself, none of this invalidates the individual’s scholarship. Academic claims and autobiographical claims belong to different categories and require different forms of evaluation. Once those categories are collapsed, however, suspicion begins to accumulate. A question about citation can become a question about biography; a question about biography can become a question about character; and a question about character can then be used to cast doubt upon professional achievement. Individual allegations begin to reinforce one another even when they do not possess the same evidentiary basis.

The media becomes particularly important at this point because public scrutiny does not remain within the university. According to Professor Lester’s account during the discussion, after Nathan Cofnas published a blog accusing Arday of plagiarism, 274 British press articles appeared within 22 days. Professor Lester further stated that 23 of these were connected in some way to the Free-Speech Union network associated with Toby Young, that 19 appeared after Arday’s resignation, and that 21 were published in The Spectator. He argued that the initial plagiarism allegations had not been proven and that the scrutiny subsequently expanded into Arday’s character and life story. These figures and interpretations are Professor Lester’s account of the media campaign and should therefore be understood as part of his argument about the controversy.

Yet the larger media question remains significant beyond the accuracy of any individual figure. When an allegation is being reiterated frequently to become the primary narrative associated with an individual, what does happen? Repetition has its own peculiar effect. When an allegation starts off as a claim that needs to be backed up with evidence, frequent iteration of that allegation in newspapers, on websites, on social media, and in analysis could transform it into a familiar piece of information; familiarity could then easily take the place of proof. It is more likely for the audience to recall the allegation rather than the qualification made in it. That does not mean that the act of scrutiny by the media is itself an illegitimate act. The media plays a crucial role in raising questions regarding powerful organisations. Yet, the frequency of scrutiny does become relevant when an identifiable individual is being scrutinised.

This raises another question that emerged from the discussion: who has the authority to judge an academic? A university has procedures for investigating misconduct. External examiners possess disciplinary expertise. Academic colleagues understand the conventions of their fields. Journalists may investigate matters of legitimate public interest, while the wider public has an interest in institutions that receive public legitimacy and resources. But these forms of authority are not interchangeable. A newspaper allegation is not a university finding. A social-media campaign is not a disciplinary investigation. Public suspicion is not the same thing as academic judgment. Once these distinctions disappear, the authority to judge becomes dispersed among actors who do not necessarily possess the same evidence, expertise, or responsibility.

Professor Shose Kessi pushed this question further by drawing attention to the way institutional processes operate. She did not argue against investigation. Instead, she emphasized the need to examine the process through which investigations are conducted: who sits on committees, what criteria are used, how complaints are handled and how conclusions are reached. A procedure can appear neutral while containing less visible practices that produce different outcomes for different groups. When multiple complaints repeatedly concern a particular demographic, the institution, she argued, has a responsibility to examine its own practices rather than treating every case as an isolated problem.

This changes the question from whether rules exist to how rules operate. Institutions can possess formally neutral procedures while applying those procedures unevenly. The existence of a rule does not by itself establish equality. What matters is how the rule is interpreted, who is subjected to it, who is protected by it, and whose circumstances are considered relevant when judgment is made. This is particularly important in academic institutions because universities do not simply judge scholarship. They also judge people. They determine who is appointed, promoted, funded, supported and recognized as authoritative. The procedures through which these decisions are made therefore become part of the production of academic legitimacy itself.

The distinction between critique and attack becomes important for the same reason. Sabelo McInziba argued that there is a difference between engaging critically with a scholar’s work and turning criticism into personal attack and slander. He suggested that the engagement with Arday had moved beyond ordinary scholarly criticism and involved deeper, organized interests. Yet his argument also returned to the importance of process. Different groups may contribute to testing allegations, but their participation must be grounded in the integrity of the process. The integrity of the process is as important as the outcome. The issue, therefore, is not whether criticism should be permitted. An academy without criticism would cease to be one. The issue is whether criticism remains connected to evidence and proportionality. Academic integrity cannot be defended by abandoning the procedures through which integrity is established. If the process becomes detached from evidence, consistency, and fairness, then academic integrity itself becomes vulnerable. What begins as an effort to protect standards can become an exercise in institutional power. The distinction between critique and attack is consequently not merely semantic. It is a distinction between challenging knowledge and discrediting a person.

There is another difficulty that becomes visible when a Black scholar achieves an extraordinary position. As the story grows more extraordinary, the easier it will be for the institution and society to turn that individual into an inspirational icon. The life of Arday had already been constructed in the discourse of human potential: an individual who has faced many difficulties in his early life, yet has managed to reach one of the most prestigious positions within British academia. There is something powerful about such a story. But there is also a danger in making the inspirational narrative the primary meaning of the person. Once a scholar becomes a symbol of possibility, the individual may be denied the ordinary human permission to be imperfect.

This is when the idea of Black excellence raises its complications. Excellent achievement is important, but the requirement of outstanding work hides an unpleasant truth. If Black academics have to prove their exceptional talent in order to be accepted in an institution, then the glorification of such exceptionalism might actually reinforce the obstacles they had to overcome. An exceptional individual becomes proof of how well the system works, while the structures that have made this success exceptional stay unnoticed. One succeeded, and the institution used that success to claim that it was open. The question of how many equally capable people were never given the opportunity to succeed remains unanswered.

To be clear, the story should not be reduced to a simple narrative of triumph over adversity because such a reading can obscure the structures that determine whose potential is recognised, cultivated, funded, and encouraged. The remarkable individual can become the centre of the story while the institutional conditions surrounding that individual disappear from view. The more useful question is therefore not simply how one person overcame barriers, but how many people with potential never received the opportunity to demonstrate what they could become.

Professor Christine Vogt-William approached the problem through the related ideas of invisibility and hyper-surveillance. For black and minority ethnic academics, there can exist an awkward balance whereby they are not being recognised enough as intellectual subjects but are seen very much indeed when things go awry. Good news may be seen as an exception and lucky coincidence, whereas bad news becomes inflated. The result is a paradoxical form of visibility: the scholar can be visible as a representative of diversity without necessarily being fully recognised as an intellectual individual. This helps explain why the Arday controversy cannot simply be collapsed into the question of whether racism existed or whether academic misconduct should be investigated. These questions must remain conceptually distinct while still allowing us to examine the conditions under which they interact.

Professor Vogt-William’s intervention also introduced the question of consistency. Her question revolved around how universities like Cambridge and Ghent can hire academics for whom she felt her views of race realism and scientific racism applied, whereas there is a great deal of focus on the hiring and research of Arday. She raised this question on the grounds of consistency within institutions: If academic legitimacy is argued so strongly in one case, then is it not reasonable to raise similar questions in another? Rather, it raises the larger issue of whether principles such as merit, academic integrity, and institutional standards retain the same meaning when applied to different people.

This is where the individual case begins to open into a structural question. Jason Arday’s story matters not only because of what happened to one scholar but because it forces us to examine the conditions under which certain people enter institutions of authority. Who is believed to possess intellectual potential? Who receives the resources necessary to develop that potential? Who is encouraged when they struggle? Who is scrutinized when they succeed? Who is permitted to make mistakes without those mistakes becoming evidence against an entire category of people? These questions move the discussion away from the individual and toward the institution that determines how individuals are recognised in the first place.

The academy requires standards and criticism. Accountability is also required here, although in a way that does not confuse the issue of fairness about whom the accountability applies to, what evidence is, who gets to judge, and how judgment is carried out. In the absence of such clarification, accountability turns into a form of performance, scrutiny becomes a form of punishment, and academic integrity turns into a language through which institutional power is exerted. The real question is, of course, not whether Jason Arday was perfect. He was human. The question is whether an academy committed to equality can allow its Black scholars to be human while still holding them to serious intellectual standards. An equal academy is not one in which Black scholars are protected from criticism. It is a criticism that is moderated by the same rules of evidence, balance, and proportion as criticism of anyone else. It is not an institution where Black intellectuals are celebrated because they are Black, or where their Blackness makes them even more subject to skepticism. It is an academy in which they are allowed to be scholars first.

The controversy surrounding Jason Arday therefore leaves us with a difficult proposition. And perhaps it is not only about who gets accepted in the academy, but about what happens to them after they join. Because inclusion cannot be measured in terms of how many Black scholars are occupying positions of power. One must take into account the nature of the kind of scrutiny they face, the kind of flaws they can commit, and the kind of support they receive, as well as whether they are allowed to lead their lives as individuals or as symbols. Once one asks the question in such a way, the issue becomes not only about the life story of a particular person. The issue becomes about what the academy does. How an institution recognises intelligence and makes opportunities available to certain individuals, and how it constructs notions of merit in response to people who were previously marginalised moving to the position of power.

The Arday question therefore does not end with the controversy surrounding Jason Arday. It begins there. His story forces us to look beyond the individual and examine the institutional environment into which he entered. The reason we have to ask ourselves why some academics come loaded with representation, why some need to be exceptional in order to be seen as ordinary, and how criteria for determining academic legitimacy might themselves become problematic in light of concerns around race and power. The second question is therefore inescapable: In that the Arday affair was not just about one person’s conduct but also about the processes through which academic authority is constructed, assessed and defended, then how are those processes determined? What constitutes the appearance of neutrality in a university that produces inequalities of recognition, scrutiny and opportunity?

Toyin Falola, a professor of History, University Distinguished Teaching Professor, and Jacob and Frances Sanger Mossiker Chair in the Humanities at The University of Texas at Austin, is the Bobapitan of Ibadanland.

PS: This is the first report on a panel on “Jason Arday and Race in the Academy,” held on 6 September. For the full recording, check HERE.

World.title: Police, ADC supporters clash in Kaduna as 2027 campaigns begin
World.content:
Tension erupted in Kaduna on Wednesday as security operatives and supporters of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) clashed during a solidarity walk for the party’s governorship candidate, Isa Ashiru, in the state capital.

The confrontation occurred at or around Murtala Square as ADC supporters gathered for a solidarity march to signal the beginning of the party’s campaign activities ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

The ADC accused the police and the state government of using security operatives and alleged political thugs to disrupt what it described as a peaceful gathering.

The party said tear gas was fired at its supporters, leaving some injured and forcing participants to disperse.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

But a government official, who spoke to PREMIUM TIMES, offered a different account, saying the police intervened to prevent a breakdown of law and order and to protect residents and property.

Efforts by PREMIUM TIMES to obtain the police’s version of the incident were unsuccessful as calls to the command’s spokesperson did not go through.

ADC accuses police of disrupting peaceful march

In a statement signed by Mr Ashiru, the ADC governorship candidate, the party described the gathering as a peaceful demonstration by “thousands” of its supporters.

The party said the protesters had gathered “not with weapons, not with stones, not with incitement” but to express support for the ADC and demand what it called a better Kaduna.

The ADC alleged that the APC-led government deployed security operatives and “hired thugs” to disrupt the walk.

It also accused the police of firing tear gas at unarmed supporters.

The party cited Sections 39 and 40 of the 1999 Constitution, which protect freedom of expression and peaceful assembly and association, arguing that the use of force against its supporters amounted to a violation of their constitutional rights.

“The people of Kaduna are not children to be scattered with canisters. They are not subjects to be cowed by hired muscle. They are citizens,” Mr Ashiru said in the statement.

The ADC also referred to a previous Kaduna High Court ruling which it said declared attempts by the police to suspend political gatherings unconstitutional.

The party vowed to continue its political activities despite the incident.

“We will continue to assemble. We will continue to speak. We will continue to organise. We will continue to walk,” Mr Ashiru said.

Government says police intervened to prevent breakdown of law and order

The government official, who doesn’t want his name to be mentioned because he was not authorised to speak on the matter, however, said the police intervened to prevent violence and protect members of the public.

The official said the security agencies acted because of concerns that hoodlums could take advantage of the gathering to destroy the property of innocent residents and disrupt normal activities in the city.

Some people who spoke to PREMIUM TIMES also said several supporters were injured during the confrontation and that tear gas was used to disperse the crowd.

The accounts could not immediately be independently verified.

The incident comes at a politically sensitive moment for Kaduna, with campaigns for the 2027 governorship and State House of Assembly elections officially beginning on 9 September.

Kaduna enters a heated 2027 contest

The confrontation comes as Kaduna enters what is expected to be one of the most competitive governorship contests in northern Nigeria.

Governor Uba Sani of the All Progressives Congress (APC) is seeking a second term, while Mr Ashiru is running again after unsuccessful bids in 2019 and 2023.

Mr Ashiru contested the 2023 election for the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and finished second to Mr Sani.

He later moved to the ADC and won its governorship primary in May 2026 with 86,113 votes.

The ADC has since moved to strengthen its campaign organisation.

Mr Ashiru appointed John Ayuba, a former Kaduna commissioner and university lecturer, as Director-General of his campaign council, alongside other officials responsible for operations and administration.

He has also selected former Kaduna State lawmaker, Irimiya Kantitok, as his running mate.

The party’s campaign is also drawing strength from the political realignment involving former Governor Nasir El-Rufai, who has left the APC and joined the ADC.

APC relies on incumbency

Mr Sani, meanwhile, enters the contest with the advantage of incumbency and the political structure of the ruling APC.

He secured the APC governorship ticket through an affirmation process in which he received 459,393 votes.

The governor’s camp has also attracted several politicians who were previously associated with opposition parties, strengthening the APC’s structure ahead of the election.

On Wednesday, the Kaduna APC announced the commencement of its governorship and State House of Assembly campaign, saying it would focus on the achievements of the Sani administration rather than personal attacks on opposition candidates.

World.title: Full list: Countries Nigerians can visit with no visa appointment
World.content:
Nigerian passport holders can travel to dozens of countries without going through the traditional visa application process or attending a visa appointment before departure.

The latest 2026 Henley Passport Index shows that Nigerian citizens have access to 44 destinations through a combination of visa-free entry, visa on arrival and electronic visa arrangements. Nigeria ranked 90th globally in the July 2026 index, while its visa-free access score remained at 44 destinations.

For travellers, this means they can avoid the traditional process of booking an embassy appointment, submitting documents in person and waiting for a visa decision before travelling to these destinations.

However, the requirements differ from country to country. Some destinations allow Nigerians to enter without a visa, while others issue visas on arrival or require an online application or travel authorisation.

Countries Nigerians can visit without a traditional visa appointment

Africa

Benin Burkina Faso Burundi – visa on arrival Cameroon Cape Verde Islands Chad Comoros Islands – visa on arrival Côte d’Ivoire Djibouti Ghana Guinea Guinea-Bissau Kenya Liberia Madagascar – visa on arrival Mali Mauritius Mozambique Niger Rwanda Senegal Seychelles Sierra Leone The Gambia Togo

These destinations make up a large part of the travel access available to Nigerian passport holders, particularly within West Africa, where ECOWAS free-movement arrangements provide visa-free access to several countries.

Caribbean

Barbados Dominica Haiti Montserrat St Kitts and Nevis

Asia and the Middle East

Cambodia – visa on arrival Iran – visa on arrival Lebanon Maldives – visa on arrival Timor-Leste – visa on arrival

Oceania and Pacific

Cook Islands Fiji Kiribati Micronesia Niue – visa on arrival Palau Islands – visa on arrival Samoa – visa on arrival Tuvalu Vanuatu

The list is based on the destinations included in the latest 2026 passport-access data, although individual entry conditions can change.

What “no visa appointment” means

Not all 44 destinations offer completely visa-free entry.

Visa-free means travellers can enter without obtaining a visa before departure, subject to the country’s normal border requirements.

Visa on arrival means the traveller does not need to obtain a visa at an embassy before travelling. Instead, the visa is issued at the destination’s airport or other approved entry point.

Some countries may also require an online application or electronic travel authorisation. This can be completed before departure without the traditional in-person embassy appointment.

For example, Kenya is included among the destinations accessible to Nigerians, but travellers still need to complete the country’s electronic travel requirements before travelling. Seychelles also requires travellers to obtain a travel authorisation.
