Bram Verelst, Senior Researcher, Conflict Prevention, Management and Peacebuilding in the Great Lakes Region, ISS

Nicodemus Minde, Researcher and adjunct faculty member at United States International University - Africa, Nairobi

World.title: Africa: US Repeatedly Votes Against Africa's Interests At the UN
World.content:
analysis

The US was the only country that voted against a recent Africa-sponsored resolution at the UN.

On Friday, the UN General Assembly voted to adopt a new world map that accurately depicts Africa's size. Togo introduced the resolution. It sought to replace the age-old Mercator map with the Equal Earth projection, which is considered more accurate.

The traditional Mercator map is inaccurate not only in its depictions of Africa and other regions close to the equator -- the imaginary line that circles the Earth halfway and divides the North and South poles -- but also in its exaggeration of the size of countries and regions farther from the equator.



As cartography Professor James Cheshire at University College London puts it, the Mercator projection was created in 1659 to help European sailors navigate the oceans. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well," he told the BBC.

But it carries a colonial legacy and reinforces a long-standing Eurocentric hierarchy of global importance.

Yet on Friday, the US voted against adopting the modern, more accurate equal-earth projector.

PREMIUM TIMES reports that the US was the only country that voted against the resolution. Even Israel, one of its closest allies and a country that has shared Washington's position in the General Assembly over the past year, voted in favour of the resolution. All 54 African countries voted in favour as well.

The US decision has drawn worldwide attention and sparked discussion about its rationale, which Nigerian international relations expert Owei Lakemfa described as "ridiculous."

Francesca Albanese, UN Special Rapporteur, mocked the US and argued that it voted against the resolution because it is uncomfortable with a representation of the world that doesn't centre the traditional Western perspective.

However, rather than viewing the US vote against Africa's interests as an isolated event, a review of major UN resolutions in the past year shows it as another instance of the US opposing Africa's interests on restorative justice.

Vote on slavery

Earlier in the year, the US stood against the request to recognise the transatlantic slave trade as the gravest crime against humanity.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that Ghana made the request to the assembly, backed by African states, in pursuit of healing and reparative justice.

Ghana introduced the resolution, which sought to declare the "trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity" in March.

A total of 123 member states voted in favour of the resolution, including 54 African member states. However, 52 countries abstained, mostly European countries. The abstentions include Britain, Portugal, and Spain, which were, arguably, the most guilty of the slave trade and colonialism.

The transatlantic slave trade represents one of the darkest chapters in human history, marked by the systematic exploitation, displacement, and dehumanisation of millions of Africans.

An estimated 15 million Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic between the 15th and 19th centuries. Many died during the Middle Passage, while survivors were subjected to forced labour and systemic abuse in the West.

Yet, the US was one of the three countries that voted against a resolution that described the slave trade as the gravest crime against humanity. The other two were Argentina and Israel.

The resolution also urged states to consider apologising for the slave trade and the creation of a reparations fund, which Ghana says will be used to repair the damage caused by the slave trade.

More resolutions

Aside from pan-African resolutions put forward by African countries, the US has also voted against several other resolutions of interest to African countries. This includes issues in which African states voted overwhelmingly in favour.

Last December, for instance, it voted against the resolution on South-South and Triangular Cooperation, which sought to help developing countries tackle challenges and achieve their goals.

The resolution sought to strengthen cooperation among developing countries. It also argued that financing and resource mobilisation are prerequisites for scaling up such cooperation.

A total of 182 countries voted in favour of the resolution, including Nigeria, Niger, Côte d'Ivoire, Senegal, South Sudan, and South Africa. Ten abstained, while the US was the only country to vote against it.

The US also voted against the demand for an end to US sanctions against Cuba in October.

PREMIUM TIMES reported the strong relations between Cuba and African states. Relations between the two sides date back to the post-colonial era.

Cuba has also made significant contributions in healthcare, education, and technical development across multiple African countries.

The resolution was an attempt to reaffirm the demand for an end to the US economic, commercial and financial embargo on Cuba, which it had declared multiple times.

At least 165 states, including African states, in the 184-member chamber voted in favour of the resolution, including Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa, Angola, and the 50 African member states of the UN.

The US was among the seven countries that voted against the resolution.

Also, when the UN General Assembly considered a high-level UN meeting to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action (DDPA) in July 2026, the US kicked against the time.

The DDPA is a UN framework, which seeks to address racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance."

US justification for dissenting

At the General Assembly on Friday, US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said the resolution mocked the work and purpose of the UN General Assembly.

She insisted the resolution was a "superfluous" agenda that distracted attention from genuine world problems.

"Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th Century, and their role in promoting reparations and 'cognitive justice'," Ms Ferencevych said.

The US official's argument becomes difficult to rationalise when compared to the actions of her principal, President Donald Trump, who has been unilaterally renaming transnational symbols without any basis.

Mr Trump recently announced that he has renamed Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes in North America, to Lake America.

Mr Trump took his trade war with Canada to the water in late August and, with a stroke of a pen, tried to erase over 400 years of cartographic history by renaming Lake Ontario.

Last year, Mr Trump also announced that he had renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

Further justifying the US's opposition to the redrawing of the world map, Ms Ferencevych said that although the initiative is presented as "an anodyne effort to update cartographic proportions", the US "clearly sees it cannot be separated from the much larger and more radical ideological project it belongs to."

"When the United Nations questions why it is losing legitimacy in the world and is not taken seriously time and again, we point to resolutions such as this," she said.

But Togo's Foreign Minister, Robert Dussey, argued that "a fair world begins with a fair map."

"A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood."

UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries are not mandated to implement them. However, the resolution could lead to updates in classroom curricula and everyday technology.

The US also announced that it rejected the resolution on the transatlantic slave trade, which asked states to acknowledge the depth of violence caused by the slave trade, because it did not believe countries should be obliged to pay reparations for actions not prohibited by international law when they happened.

The US ambassador to the UN, Dan Negrea, also accused African countries of using past suffering as leverage to secure funding from other countries.

Close 

He said, "The US objects to the cynical usage of historical wrongs as a leverage point to reallocate modern resources to people and nations who are distantly related to the historical victims."

While justifying its opposition to the resolution backed by African countries, calling for an end to the embargo on Cuba, the US accused Cuba of supporting "terrorist organisations around the globe," a claim virtually no one else believes.

What are analysts saying?

The President of the Society for International Relations Awareness (SIRA), Owei Lakemfa, attributed US actions to its mindset of global dominance and its imperialistic tendencies.

"The US sees itself as the commander of the world. It has a mentality of trying to enslave other people, so whenever you have other people moving towards progress, it does not."

"Although the issue of slavery was mainly a European thing, the US was a beneficiary. How do you justify reparations for the holocaust, but not for slavery? It's just not logical for a so-called freedom-loving, pro-human rights establishment," he said.

Mr Lakemfa called the US position on the world map "ridiculous," adding that adopting a more accurate global map will expand human knowledge and correct misdeeds.

"I don't see what the US will lose if the map of the world shows its true size."

"All this shows is that Africa must unite for its Pan-African vision. It is only then that the rest of the world will respect us," Mr Lakemfa said.

Babafemi Badejo, a professor of political science and foreign policy analyst, argued that the US votes only based on what it sees as its own interests.

He said the only lasting solution is for African countries to build their influence and relevance in the world.

"This way, they would be in a better position to influence the decisions of the US and other countries through persuasive negotiations," he said.

World.title: South Africa: Another Fuel Hike On the Cards for Mzansi Drivers in October
World.content:
Petrol 95 is showing an expected price jump of roughly 200 cents per litre based on early September 2026 data.

High global oil prices are also pushing local diesel and paraffin prices up by well over 160 cents per litre.

The latest daily fuel figures show that the price motorists pay at the pumps is lagging far behind what it actually costs to bring fuel into the country. This gap is officially called an "under recovery," and it means heavy price increases are on the way to make up the difference.

Between late August and 8 September 2026, the average shortfall for Petrol 95 grew to 200.54 cents per litre. For Petrol 93, the gap was 188.47 cents per litre.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Diesel drivers will also feel the pinch. The expected price hike for 0.05% diesel is 166.26 cents per litre, while 0.005% diesel is facing a 198.02 cents per litre increase. Illuminating paraffin is short by an average of 206.20 cents per litre.

The main reason for this pain at the pumps is the rising cost of fuel on global markets. These high international prices added 215.33 cents per litre to the cost of Petrol 95 and 203.01 cents per litre to Petrol 93. Global prices also drove up diesel costs by between 185.03 cents and 217.43 cents per litre.

A slightly stronger rand is the only thing softening the blow. The exchange rate helped shave a few cents off these increases, bringing between 14.53 cents and 19.41 cents per litre in relief across all fuel types. On 8 September 2026, the rand was trading at R16.06 to the US dollar.

Daily snapshots show the situation getting worse. On 8 September 2026 alone, the single-day shortfall reached 256.01 cents per litre for Petrol 95 and 243.05 cents per litre for Petrol 93.

Currently, Gauteng pump prices set on 2 September 2026 sit at R26.92 per litre for Petrol 95 and R26.76 for Petrol 93. Wholesale diesel costs are R29.11 per litre for 0.05% diesel and R29.56 per litre for 0.005% diesel.

World.title: Lesotho: Lesotho MP to Repay R6-Million in Tender Fraud Case
World.content:
Anti-corruption agency says Jane Lekunya and his wife were involved in a corrupt scheme that cost the government R109-million

Lesotho's anti-corruption agency, the DCEO, has announced that opposition MP Jane Lekunya has agreed to return M6-million which he benefited from agricultural tenders in an alleged M109-million fraud.

The DCEO said he had agreed to cooperate in the prosecution of his alleged accomplices.

Investigators say agriculture ministry officials bypassed competitive bidding and inflated tender prices for fertilisers, seeds and pesticides.

The DCEO is pursuing asset recovery alongside criminal proceedings, and says it could recover public funds more quickly this way.

A member of the Lesotho Parliament has agreed to repay M6-million (M1=R1) from an allegedly corrupt scheme involving the supply of fertilisers, seeds and pesticides to the Ministry of Agriculture, according to the country's Directorate on Corruption and Economic Offences (DCEO).

Jane Lekunya, from the opposition Democratic Congress, has agreed to cooperate with prosecutors in the M109-million case, involving private companies and ministry officials linked to the fraudulent award of the tenders.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

This comes after Lekunya challenged the DCEO's attempt in March 2025 to prosecute him for fraud, corruption and money laundering.

According to court documents, senior agriculture ministry officials bypassed competitive bidding procedures to award tenders to companies linked to local businessman Moeketsi Ntaote. The tender prices were inflated to create room for illicit payments.

The Lesotho government provides an 80% subsidy to farmers on fertilisers and a 70% subsidy on seeds, pesticides and herbicides to boost food production.

The DCEO said the corrupt scheme cost the government M109-million between 2021 and 2022, with suspicious transfers between the accounts of those involved continuing into 2023 after the government had fully paid the companies involved.

Court documents filed by the DCEO in September 2024 show that Ntaote's companies - Glorified Group of Companies, Advanced Agricultural Products, and Movement (Pty) Ltd - were awarded numerous tenders through limited or selective bidding.

The DCEO said Ntaote obtained several of the tenders through procurement manager Mapaseka Nkone, with the assistance of former principal secretary Nchakha Makara.

Makara's case was dealt with separately. He pleaded guilty and was fined M500,000 by the Maseru Magistrates' Court in June 2025.

After securing the tenders through Nkone, Ntaote transferred money to Lekunya, who then passed funds to Nkone and other alleged accomplices, the DCEO said.

Following the money

Financial records cited by the DCEO show several suspicious transactions involving Lekunya. On 23 December 2021, M5.5-million was transferred from Ntaote's FNB account to Lekunya's account. A further M3.5-million was transferred on 18 March 2022, followed by M123,000 on 12 April 2022.

The DCEO said Lekunya received more than M1.6-million from Ntaote and his companies in March and May 2021. And Lekunya's wife, Makhoase Lekunya, received M22.6-million into her investment account from Ntaote's companies.

The DCEO said Makhoase used some of the money to purchase agricultural products. It is pursuing a case against her.

According to the DCEO's court papers, Lekunya's company, Guardrisk Insurance Brokers (no relation to South Africa's Guardrisk Group), was used to move and conceal money linked to the tender scheme.

The DCEO further said that in October 2021, M2.1-million was transferred from Guardrisk to Advanced Agricultural's PostBank account as a loan to Ntaote.

Movement, one of Ntaote's companies, later repaid the M2.1-million to Guardrisk in January 2022, together with an additional M100,000.

In another transaction, M5.6-million was transferred through Guardrisk to finance the purchase of a property in Somerset West, South Africa, under Pavilion Properties. According to the DCEO, the property was bought on behalf of Ntaote using money generated from fraudulent tender payments.

The DCEO accused the Lekunyas of helping to launder payments to ministry officials who had corruptly awarded the tenders through Guardrisk Insurance Brokers.

In March 2025, the DCEO obtained an order freezing 22 bank accounts and assets of Lekunya, his businesses and other people and companies allegedly linked to the scheme. The frozen bank accounts included five belonging to Ntaote's companies, three belonging to Guardrisk, three belonging to Lekunya and six belonging to his wife. The order also covered three accounts belonging to Nkone and two belonging to Ntaote.

Lekunya then approached the Constitutional Court seeking to stop the DCEO from charging him with fraud, corruption and money laundering. He asked the court to stay the charges until his constitutional challenge had been heard to finality.

After hearing arguments from the Lekunyas and the DCEO, Chief Justice Sakoane ruled that the matter was not urgent and removed it from the urgent roll, allowing the DCEO to proceed with the case under the ordinary court rules.

Advocate Christopher Lephuthing, who represented the Lekunyas in the case, told GroundUp he had already informed the judges at that stage that Lekunya had turned state witness.

He said the Lekunyas "have never been formally charged in the criminal case".

Close 

DCEO turns to recovering funds

On Wednesday, DCEO spokesperson Matlhokomelo Senoko issued a statement saying the anti-corruption agency had decided to pursue an asset recovery case alongside the criminal proceedings to recover public funds more quickly.

The decision, she said, was informed by the length of time criminal cases can take to conclude.

Senoko said Lekunya appeared before the High Court of Lesotho on Monday.

The DCEO investigations found that Lekunya "received a financial benefit as a result of financing contracts that were obtained fraudulently".

Following discussions with the DCEO, Lekunya undertook to return the entire M6-million, which the DCEO says was obtained through fraud.

"He also agreed to cooperate with the prosecution in the case involving contracts awarded fraudulently [to his alleged accomplices]," said Senoko.

"The DCEO further informs the public that cases against the other accused persons, namely Mapaseka Nkone, Moeketsi Constantinus Ntaote, Glorified Group of Companies (Pty) Ltd and Movement (Pty) Ltd, will continue before the courts as investigations have been completed."

To date no action has been taken by Parliament or the Democratic Congress against Lekunya.

World.title: Kenya: Nairobi Water Announces 26-Hour Shutdown Affecting Large Parts of City
World.content:
The city centre of Nairobi, Kenya from the Kenyatta International Conference Centre in 2015.

Nairobi — Thousands of Nairobi residents are set to experience a water shortage from Friday morning after the Nairobi City Water and Sewerage Company announced a scheduled shutdown of the Sasumua Water Treatment Plant.

The shutdown will begin at 6am on Friday, and is expected to continue until 8am on Saturday, September 12, as the utility undertakes emergency repairs along the Sasumua-Kabete pipeline.

Nairobi Water said the works will affect water supply across large parts of Nairobi, including residential estates, hospitals, learning institutions, the Central Business District and parts of the airport corridor.

Among the affected areas are Westlands, Lavington, Kileleshwa, Kilimani, Hurlingham, Upper Hill, Dagoretti, Kawangware, Waithaka, Uthiru, Mutuini, Gatina, Jamhuri and Kibera.



Other areas listed in the notice include Langata, Nairobi West, Madaraka, Karen, South B, South C, the CBD, Industrial Area, Eastlands, Mathare, Huruma and parts of the Outer Ring corridor.

The shutdown will also affect key institutions and facilities, including the University of Nairobi Main Campus, Kenyatta National Hospital, KEMRI, Coptic Hospital, Daystar University, Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, the Standard Gauge Railway and the United Nations Environment Programme.

Nairobi Water said residents in the affected areas should make arrangements to have enough water before the shutdown begins.

The company urged customers to store adequate water in advance and use available supplies sparingly throughout the repair period.

The utility said the shutdown was necessary to facilitate emergency repair works on the Sasumua-Kabete pipeline, which supplies treated water to parts of the capital.

"Every effort will be made to restore water supply as quickly and safely as possible," Nairobi Water said.

The company apologised for the inconvenience and appealed to residents to cooperate as the repairs are undertaken.

The affected areas include:Westlands/Lavington: Riverside Drive, Chalbi Drive, Convent Drive, Gitanga Road, Kunde Road, Hedred, Mbaazi, Masanduku, Leloghi Gardens, Ole Ndume Road, King'ara Road and Riara Road.

Kileleshwa: Kandara Road, Gichugu Road, Mazeras Road, Mbooni Road, Othaya Road, Kaputei, Laikipia Road, Githunguri, DoD, St George's School and Tembere Road.

Kilimani/Hurlingham: Argwings Kodhek Road, Hurlingham Shopping Centre, Mtito Andei Road, Kindaruma Road, Rose Avenue, Lower George Padmore Road, Daystar University, Denis Pritt Road and Coptic Hospital.

Upper Hill: Matumbato, Kiambere, Masaba, Mawenzi Road, parts of Hospital Road, Kenya Road, Elgon Road and Kenyatta National Hospital.

Dagoretti/Kawangware/Waithaka: Lower Gitanga Road, parts of Kawangware, Sunset Estate, Sohill City Estates, Kagira, Kagondo, Muhuri Road, Upper Kabiria, Mithonge, Kamwanya, Kahuho Road, Ngina Road, Kikuyu Road, Waithaka, Ndwaru Road, Upper Waithaka, Dagoretti Market and surrounding areas.

Close 

CBD/South B and C/Airport corridor: The CBD, Mombasa Road, South B and South C, Mater Hospital, JKIA, SGR, Athi River EPZA, Mukuru, Imara Daima, Tassia Estate, Embakasi Village and parts of North Airport Road.

Eastlands: Eastleigh, Maringo, Buruburu Phases 3 and 4, Gikomba, Pumwani, Majengo, Shauri Moyo, Jericho, Jerusalem and Kimathi areas.

Mathare/Huruma/Outer Ring: Mathare North, GSU, Rafiki, Utalii College, KPLC Training School, Traffic Headquarters, Mathari Hospital, Mlango Kubwa, Juja Road, Huruma, Ngei, Kosovo, Racecourse, Ushirika, parts of Ngumba, Thome, Survey, Safari Park Hotel, Kenya Breweries and parts of Baba Dogo.

The whole of Industrial Area, including Masai Road and adjacent areas, will also be affected.

Nairobi Water said customers in Karen and surrounding areas, as well as Kibera, Kang'ethe, Togo Flats and other listed neighbourhoods, should similarly prepare for the interruption.

The company said it regretted the inconvenience caused by the shutdown and assured customers that it would work to restore normal supplies as soon as the emergency repairs are completed.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 10, 2026
World.content:
press review

Spain Warned of Ceuta Mass Crossing Before Surge

Newly declassified Spanish government documents show that intelligence services warned authorities a day before a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta that social media groups were encouraging thousands of migrants to enter Spanish territory. On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service reportedly alerted Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that WhatsApp and Facebook groups were promoting a crossing by swimming and over the border fence, with around 180,000 people receiving the messages. The warning comes amid political controversy over Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's claim that the scale of the 30 July influx could not have been predicted. At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta over two days, with at least 100 people reportedly dying, while thousands remained in makeshift camps. Opposition parties say the documents contradict the government's account. Officials maintain that the intelligence did not indicate the unprecedented scale of the crossing and was merely an exchange of information rather than a formal alert.

Tunisian Flotilla Activists Remain Jailed as Hunger Striker Deteriorates



Four Tunisian activists remain in pre-trial detention six months after authorities began arresting organisers linked to the pro-Palestinian Global Sumud Flotilla, with growing concern over the deteriorating health of activist Wael Naouar. Naouar has been on hunger strike since 16 August to protest his continued detention and is now in his fourth week without food. His lawyer said that he has lost 18 kilograms and is suffering from low blood pressure, low blood sugar, breathing and mobility difficulties, and severe pain. Seven activists were initially detained, with three later released. Naouar and three others remain under investigation over alleged suspicious financial flows linked to the flotilla. The detainees face allegations including money laundering, aggravated breach of trust and forgery, which supporters reject as an attempt to criminalise solidarity with Palestinians and peaceful activism. Human rights groups have raised concerns over Tunisia's shrinking civic space and use of criminal and financial investigations against activists. The four detainees are due back in court on 16 September.

Severe Funding Cuts Force Sudan Health Clinic Closures

Severe cuts to humanitarian funding are forcing health clinics across war-torn Sudan to close, leaving patients to travel further for treatment and pushing remaining hospitals towards breaking point, Médecins Sans Frontières warns. MSF said that admissions at its supported facilities in Central Darfur rose by 22.5% between January and April compared with the same period last year. 45 healthcare centres lost funding in May. In refugee and displacement camps, maternity and surgical services have closed, forcing pregnant women to travel for hours to access emergency care. The number of aid organisations operating around Um Rakuba camp has fallen from about 35 in 2021 to fewer than 10. Some clinics have seen patient numbers collapse because people can no longer afford transport. MSF said that the funding crisis was worsened by the closure of USAID programmes and reductions in international aid. Sudan's $2.87 billion humanitarian response plan is only about 41% funded. Around 37% of the country's health facilities are reportedly completely out of service as millions face hunger, displacement and severe malnutrition.

UN Welcomes Libya Election Deal

Libya's rival political factions have reached an agreement on election rules and the composition of the country's electoral commission, in what the UN Security Council has described as an important step towards holding national elections for the first time in more than a decade. The 30 August agreement, reached through a UN-backed negotiating process, provides for a reconstituted High National Elections Commission and changes to the legal framework for parliamentary and presidential elections, which are to be held within two years under a unified government. The UN Security Council has urged Libya's political leaders to implement the deal quickly and backed the UN mission led by Special Representative Hannah Tetteh. However, Tetteh has warned that trust remains fragile among political leaders and ordinary Libyans, with major challenges including unifying the country's divided military, security and economic institutions. She also highlighted online harassment and hate speech targeting women in public life. She said that stronger legal protections are needed to ensure women can participate in politics and civic affairs without intimidation.

Close 

Uganda Withdraws From Invictus Games

Uganda has withdrawn from the Invictus Games, just two months after announcing it would participate in next year's event for wounded military veterans. General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Uganda's chief of defence and the president's son, said the country was pulling out to avoid being seen as opposing King Charles III. His decision follows a letter from the King making clear that Prince Harry and Meghan are no longer working royals. Kainerugaba referred to the controversy surrounding the couple. He said Uganda would not take part in anything without the King's approval. However, royal sources said Charles supports projects assisting wounded service personnel. The Invictus Games organisers said they had not received official confirmation of Uganda's withdrawal and were seeking clarification. Uganda had become the 26th country to join the games, which are due to take place in Birmingham next year.

World.title: Nobody wants AI-generated sports commentators, but a pro golf tournament is introducing one anyway
World.content:
Golf fans who tune into this week's New Mexico Open broadcast will be introduced to a new commentator by the name of Duff Foreman. He'll join former PGA Tour winner Notah Begay III and well-known broadcaster Ryan Burr on the call, although Foreman won't technically be on site, seeing as how he's not an actual person.

Foreman is believed to be the first-ever AI-generated golf commentator that will be interacting live on-screen alongside human hosts. It is expected that Foreman will jump into unscripted conversations while providing insights and commentary about the play, the golf course, weather, conditions, and the rules of the game throughout nine hours of live coverage.

The very obvious question here is why? Why are we (humans) adding an AI character (not a human) to a golf broadcast? The New Mexico Open may only be a state tournament streamed on YouTube and televised locally, but it is still a professional event with a purse of $137,000 being contested by Sun Country PGA, a section of the PGA of America.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Begay, who will be pulling double duty and teeing it up in the tournament, tried to justify why an AI character is joining the broadcast.

"Golf fans are always looking for a better understanding of what players are thinking and why they make certain decisions," Begay said in a press release shared by tournament organizers. "If Duff Foreman delivers what we’re expecting, he’ll become another voice in the broadcast, helping us explain strategy, analyze swings, consider changing conditions like weather and course setup, and answer questions in real time. I think that kind of conversation could make the game more interesting and enjoyable for viewers."

Begay is right, golf fans are constantly looking for more insights involving the game and how players go about their business during competition. However, his claim that an AI-generated character that was built on a computer is going to deliver a better understanding of what a human is thinking and how said human comes to a decision may be one of the most disingenuous comments ever shared in an official press release, and in the year 2026, that is saying something.

The "conversation" Begay is hopeful to have with the AI commentator will not be "enjoyable for viewers;" it will be universally hated and mocked, just like the rollout of Foreman across social media in the buildup to the event has been.

Foreman has an X account that not only posts nothing but pointless AI slop, but also has a link in the bio section that directs viewers to a YouTube channel called X-Treme Golf. There, you'll find more AI content, such as Foreman playing golf from the summit of Mt. Everest.

Foreman and this 'content' are universally seen as being pointless and disturbingly dystopian, which brings us back to the original question: Why is an AI-generated commentator being added to a golf broadcast?

I think the answer is both wildly complicated and extremely straightforward.

We're living in incredibly bizarre times where everything you look at, it seems AI is grabbing hold of whatever that something is. Whether the impact of AI is having a positive or negative impact varies depending on the situation and the humans being impacted, but AI is here, and it is evolving by the day.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

All signs point to AI being a part of our new norm, and the complicated part is that nobody knows what's around the corner, but knows that something is.

This brings us to the straightforwardness of it all.

You – and that 'you' includes golf broadcasts now – can not afford to be the last one to peek around the corner to see what that something is when everyone seems to be fighting to have the first glimpse.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

There isn't a world – at least we should hope there isn't one – where the Duff Foremans of the world will start taking over sports broadcasting booths.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

The New Mexico Open and the PGA of America, however, can now say they were the first to fully integrate an AI commentator into a live golf broadcast.

In this current state of the world, where the words 'first' and 'artificial intelligence' hold real power, building something entirely unnecessary and unwanted can be viewed as a legitimate move on the never-ending chessboard that represents the AI rat race.

World.title: DAVID MARCUS: In Dallas, GOP seeks unity on 9/11, Kirk anniversaries
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A shadow conservative convention took place Wednesday just 15 miles west of President Donald Trump's big shindig in Dallas, with Republicans civilly discussing some of the issues causing fissures in the GOP, and seeking unity in the movement.

Both events occurred as the nation prepared to mark two solemn anniversaries, Sept. 10, the day we lost Charlie Kirk, and Sept. 11, the day that nearly 3,000 Americans were killed by Islamist terror.

Forum, as the shadow conference was called, featured speakers like the Claremont Institute's Michael Anton, an architect of President Trump’s immigration policies, and lively debates, such as one over the future of AI between Joe Lonsdale and Joe Allen.

REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG

The evening ended with a tribute to Kirk, reminding everyone on the right that they have too much in common to let petty differences divide them.

The biggest division in Dallas this week among Republicans is over the administration’s plan, led by Vice President JD Vance, to allow married stay-at-home moms to receive federal benefits. Traditionalists are calling it socialism, while populists are arguing it makes the most of a system already in place and accusing the other side of obstinance.

Party unity has been an undercurrent all week in Big D, according to Ross Hemminger, president of the Log Cabin Republicans.

"It’s critical, people need to keep their eye on the ball, they need to be completely and totally focused, the president needs a Republican Congress or things are going to go completely off the rails," Hemminger said.

A similar sentiment was sounded by Jack Posobiec, a close friend of Charlie Kirk.

"I know that Charlie held as his North Star the idea of building the coalition and of keeping the coalition together," Posobiec said. "What Charlie understood is, this is an umbrella. We’re all members of the coalition."

Texas Republicans can see firsthand the importance of coming together, after a bruising Senate primary saw state Attorney General Ken Paxton knock out longtime incumbent John Cornyn. Brian, a convention goer in his 40s who works in finance but spent a decade on Capitol Hill before that, said there's no time for bad blood within the party.

"I wish Cornyn had won, I think things would be easier, but he didn’t," Brian said. "The voters chose Ken Paxton and he is our nominee."

The crucial subplot to all the infighting in the GOP – that Republicans in Dallas are seeking to quell – is the battle for the future of the party once President Trump leaves office in January 2029, not just in terms of who the nominee might be, but what the heart and soul of the party will be.

Cara, in her 30s who works in political advertising, said the party has a plethora of potential 2028 candidates.

"I really love JD Vance and I think he is the future, but I like [Sen. Ted] Cruz and [Gov. Ron] DeSantis, too," she said. "Unlike Democrats, we have a lot of great options."

While the ideological divides in the GOP are real, they are nowhere near as polarizing as those facing the Democrats, who have a wing of their party that is literally embracing socialism and crazy ideas like abolishing the Senate.

In fact, the Democrat civil war has grown so vitriolic that, in a shocking move, Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. John Fetterman gave remarks, via video, to the assembled crowd at the Republican convention, spurring more speculation that a party switch could be in his future.

Meanwhile, in the Texas Senate race, Rep. Jasmine Crockett, who lost a bitter primary to James Talarico, still will not appear with, or even endorse, the candidate voters chose.

DEM SENATOR DELIVERS SURPRISE VIDEO AT REPUBLICAN CONVENTION BACKING MCCORMICK

All in all, despite some sniping and nasty remarks between the traditionalists and the New Right, Republicans are in much better shape regarding party unity.

The assassination of Charlie Kirk and 9/11, the former fresh in hearts and minds, and the latter somehow 25 years in past, need to be solid reminders to Republicans across America that whatever disagreements they may have, what they are fighting for is the America that al Qaeda and Kirk’s killer sought to destroy.

Should Republicans triumph in November, there will be plenty of time for policy debates. But unless unity can achieve that victory, all the arguments will be for naught, as victorious Democrats will surely spend two years blocking everything the Trump administration sees to do.

World.title: MLB great Roger Clemens recalls George W Bush's iconic 9/11 World Series first pitch: 'A perfect strike'
World.content:
President George W. Bush was America’s starting pitcher on Oct. 30, 2001.

In the wake of 9/11, the New York Yankees were playing the Arizona Diamondbacks in Game 3 of the World Series, and Bush threw out the first pitch. Roger Clemens, the Yankees’ starting pitcher that night, described the unforgettable moments that led up to Bush’s first pitch.

"I was actually in the bullpen warming up getting ready for the game with my pitching coach Mel Stottlemyre, and I told Mel let’s stop, I want to watch this," Clemens said during a recent appearance on Fox News’ "Fox & Friends."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"We have the best view, the whole stadium is going to light up, 55,000, whatever it was. You could see the snipers on top of the stadium, and he came out and threw a strike in front of the world, not just there at Yankee Stadium. It was for the world to see and it was nothing but spectacular."

Clemens was particularly impressed by Bush’s perfect strike, given the conditions of the mound and the equipment he had on.

"I could only imagine what President Bush was thinking when he was coming out of that dugout, bulletproof vest on. He threw from the top of the mound, and they dressed the mound with some dirt and mixture, and he’s in dress shoes. And so, to even go out there and not slip and be able to kick his leg up, like I said bulletproof vest and windup and throw a perfect strike right down Broadway," Clemens said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Clemens said he interacted with Bush in the clubhouse and gave the president a hug. The seven-time Cy Young Award winner said Bush was looking for a place to warm up when he received some sage advice from Derek Jeter.

"At the old Yankee Stadium you got to go out the clubhouse door and go to the right about 60-70 yards, and he went down there, and Derek Jeter, pretty well-known story, they had some small talk and Derek told him whatever you do Mr. President, don’t bounce it, you’re in Yankee Stadium, they’ll boo you," Clemens said.

"And I think he got a little nervous then. It was an awesome moment that I know I’ll never forget."

Clemens hopes that America never forgets 9/11 either.

"I can’t believe it’s been 25 years, I hope these kids that weren’t born then, I hope maybe our generation learned about Pearl Harbor that they learn about and keep 9/11 right there in the forefront of their mind," Clemens said.

For the 11-time All-Star, playing baseball during that time was a way to give grieving families and friends a chance to escape for a few hours each night. He recalled the late George Steinbrenner bringing family members and friends of those who were lost to the game.

For the 25th anniversary of 9/11, the New York Mets will play the Yankees on Friday night at Yankee Stadium.

A cargo ship docked for repairs at a port on the northeastern coast of China caught fire Thursday, killing at least 25 people who were on board at the time, according to Chinese state media.

The ship was being fixed by Beihai Shipbuilding Co. in the port of Qingdao — one of the country's major shipping hubs — when it caught fire at approximately 11:15 a.m. local time, the Xinhua news agency reported.

A total of 42 people were on the vessel at the time of the blaze, and 12 of them were safely rescued, Xinhua reported. Five others were injured and taken to the hospital, where they are in stable condition.

The Associated Press reported that the fire was extinguished at around 2:30 p.m., a little over three hours after it started. Videos online showed plumes of white smoke billowing from the ship.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation. Chinese authorities have not said what sparked the blaze while the vessel was undergoing repairs.

China’s President Xi Jinping called for "intensified efforts" to provide support for those who were affected by the fire, Xinhua reported, adding that Premier Li Qiang said "trapped people" needed to be rescued.

World.title: How a podcast community helped restore the controversial 'Gator Bait' chant for Florida football team
World.content:
For anyone who went through it, 2020 felt like living in a parallel universe.

The year was dominated by the Covid craziness that swept through the world as well as the myriad "cancellings" that took place, and college football in particular felt the effects of both.

Games and traditions alike were severely altered or outright shut down as a result of the pandemic and its accompanying lunacy, and the Florida Gators' football program especially felt the brunt of this.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL'S FIRST FULL SATURDAY IS HERE AND IT'S A CELEBRATION OF AMERICA AT ITS BEST

Sure, the Gators still played a ten game, All SEC slate, but access to Ben Hill Griffin Stadium was greatly limited, as the stadium which normally seats upwards of 90,000 fans on gameday had its attendance whittled down to less than 20,000.

In the wake of all of this, a tradition known affectionately around campus and throughout the community as "Gator Bait" was given the axe.

School officials cited "racial undertones" as the reason for removing the chant, linking back to late 19th and early 20th century depictions of using African-American children as bait for alligators.

The chant, at least in the context of the Florida football team, has much more innocent origins, being popularized in the 1990s by defensive back Lawrence Wright.

THESE ONCE-ANNUAL COLLEGE RIVALRIES USED TO DEFINE COLLEGE FOOTBALL AND NEED TO MAKE A COMEBACK ASAP

No one is more familiar with "Gator Bait" than James Di Virgilio, the popular podcast host of the "Gator Nation Football Podcast."

Di Virgilio and his co-host, Allen Williams, started the podcast back in 2014 as a break from the monotony and blind homerism that is abundant in the local sports talk radio shows around Gainesville, where the two reside.

Both are Florida graduates, and when they heard the news that "Gator Bait" was being shelved, Di Virgilio was perplexed.

"I think, like any Gator fan, it was surprising at first," said Di Virgilio. "As far as anyone could tell, no one who had ever used the chant at Florida... had any idea there could be any connection to anything other than a gator eating our opponents, so to speak, in a humorous way."

The GNFP host mentions other schools like LSU saying "Tiger Bait" as a rallying cry while receiving little to no backlash.

"I think it was a chant that many Gators (fans), especially those who are maybe 90s or 2000s Gators, have fond memories of chanting at opponents when you're winning national championships, etcetera, therefore it conjured up those memories of yesteryear," he opined.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL IS FINALLY BACK AFTER MONTHS OF NCAA LAWSUITS, NIL DRAMA AND CONGRESSIONAL FIGHTS

Despite the seemingly innocuous nature of the cheer, "Gator Bait" was officially banned in 2020 out of what Di Virgilio deemed "an abundance of caution" during a time of heightened scrutiny.

Meanwhile, in those years since the banning, the GNFP audience continued to grow.

Williams and Di Virgilio's analytical lens mixed with their obvious love and passion for the team they covered endeared them to tens of thousands of Gator fans, which presented them with a unique opportunity a few seasons ago.

At first, it started with a couple of comments here and there directed towards Di Virgilio about whether he thought "Gator Bait" could ever make a comeback.

OPINION: SPORTS IS ONE OF AMERICA'S GREATEST TRADITIONS AND A POWERFUL FORCE THAT UNITES US

"For two straight seasons, I basically polled our audience, which may or may not be representative of all of Gator Nation, to say 'does anybody really not want this?' Write to me," he explained.

Di Virgilio said in two full seasons of pushing for responses, he only got one message that was against bringing it back against hundreds that were in favor.

These messages, as he explained, came from a wide and diverse group of Gator fans, all of which cited very wholesome reasons for wanting the chant back in The Swamp.

"It wasn't just young people, it wasn't just old people. It wasn't just people of a certain skin tone," Di Virgilio mentioned. "It felt like it was a very pure, wholesome reason for wanting it."

Being a numbers guy, Di Virgilio had enough data to make his next move.

The University of Florida hired Dr. Stuart Bell to be their new president in July of this year, and since the decision to reinstate "Gator Bait" was up to the head man himself, Di Virgilio saw his opportunity to act.

"I had written to Dr. Bell a couple of weeks before we had everyone write to (him)," Di Virgilio said. "Here's my stance: I have limited information. You might have more information than I have. I would never want to do this if it was going to be divisive towards (other) Gators. I have no desire for that."

"But if you do the research and you find that this is something a majority of Gator fans want... then on your own merits, maybe think about reinstituting it."

With that, the die had been cast.

Countless fans of the GNFP took Di Virgilio's call to action to heart and wrote impassioned pleas to the university president asking for their beloved chant back.

They cited memories, tradition, and just the fact that it's a really catchy tune.

But as the emails piled up in Dr. Bell's inbox and the season drew nearer, something must have finally swayed the new president.

On the Friday before their first game against FAU, a clip was leaked of the Fightin' Gator Marching Band playing the familiar notes of "Gator Bait" on the practice field.

Lo and behold, the following day, 90,000 rabid Florida fans led a full-throated rendition of the once-banned cheer.

"Gator Bait" was back.

Di Virgilio wants to be very clear: he doesn't want the credit for bringing the chant back to The Swamp.

"I may have had 0.0001% to do with it," he explained. "Whether we were instrumental or not, someone else could have done it. I have no idea. We just felt like we wanted to push for something that brought back a lot of fond memories for us."

Regardless, he and his podcast community can certainly say they at least had a hand in ushering back one of the best cheers in college football.

"For me this is very apolitical," Di Virgilio said. "I think you want to do things that the majority of people want to do as long as it's not clearly violating any kind of legal or ethical boundary."

As he explains, Di Virgilio recognizes that not everything will be universally loved, including the "Gator Bait" chant.

Despite how popular the cheer's return has been on social media and in the Gator football community, some of the more vocal minority have bristled at the idea of "Gator Bait" making a comeback.

"I hope that if you're on the side of, you don't love it, you understand that those that (do) want it, want it for very traditional Florida reasons," said Di Virgilio. "And obviously, if you love it, you're not lording it over someone."

"Ultimately, we are all Gators."

In the end, it felt like a win for free speech, as the majority voiced their opinions and were rewarded accordingly.

It's a fact that is not lost on Di Virgilio.

"This is a really cool thing to know as podcasters, as a community of people, if you care about something you can take a second to write about it, on any side," he states.

"You may or may not have an influence, but at the end of the day, 'we the people,' so to speak, we do have a voice to share what we want... that's what this is really about. The beauty of articulate free speech and opinion, and also the willingness when you're wrong to just say, 'I was wrong.'"

World.title: Supreme Court blocks Missouri’s attempt to use newly drawn GOP congressional map
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday blocked an attempt by a Republican state official in Missouri to use a newly drawn GOP congressional map for this year’s elections.

The court, in a brief order with no noted dissents, granted an emergency request brought by a group called People Not Politicians, led by activist Richard von Glahn.

The decision puts on hold a decision by Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, who ruled on Tuesday that the new map must be used, notwithstanding the Missouri Supreme Court reaching the opposite conclusion.

The swift action from the justices likely signals the end of the battle over which congressional map to use in the midterm elections this November, with the state likely to use the previous map from 2022 that includes six seats currently held by Republicans and two held by Democrats.

The new map sought to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo.

“The law is the law, the Missouri constitution is clear, as was the Missouri Supreme Court,” von Glahn said in a statement.

Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican who led the effort to use the new map, “has shown that he cannot effectively do the job he was elected to do,” he added.

Hoskins’ lawyers told the U.S. Supreme Court justices just minutes before the decision was issued that only Clark’s order is “preventing the disenfranchisement of hundreds of thousands of voters” who participated in the primary election using the new congressional map.

With little time before the November election, it is the only way that Missouri can “conduct congressional elections that comply with the federal election calendar,” they added.

The Trump administration also filed a brief backing Hoskins, saying that if the justices were to block Clark’s ruling, it would “jeopardize state officials’ ability to conduct a timely and lawful federal election.”

This is the second time the underlying fight has reached the U.S. Supreme Court. On Tuesday, Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected a request from Hoskins seeking to block the Missouri Supreme Court ruling.

In a separate hearing on Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court gave Hoskins a cool reception as it considers whether to hold him in contempt for defying its previous ruling.

With Hoskins appearing in person, the judges peppered his lawyer with questions about whether he will now comply and use the 2022 map. They seemed dissatisfied with some of the responses.

William Seidleck, a lawyer with the Missouri Attorney General’s Office representing Hoskins, said his client would comply with the state court order requiring use of the 2022 map “unless and until” there is an intervening federal court decision. Hoskins is still “evaluating next steps,” he added.

Chief Justice Brent Powell told Hoskins not to “venture far from Jefferson City” while the court considers the contempt motion. He also pressed Hoskins to issue updated guidance to local election officials.

“We just want to make sure the law is followed,” Powell added.

Among his concerns is that if the legal fight continues, it could lead to ongoing issues after the election over whether the congressional delegation should be seated.

“We are in a precarious situation,” Powell said.

The broader clash is over a congressional map Missouri Republicans enacted in 2025, part of a nationwide redistricting push led by President Donald Trump.

The legal fight began when opponents of the new map gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would undo the GOP-drawn map and put it on hold for the 2026 election.

But Hoskins delayed a decision on whether to include the measure on the ballot, waiting to the last minute before rejecting the plan, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to voters’ approval.

The Missouri Supreme Court, which has a majority of Republican appointees, disagreed, saying there was nothing in state law that exempted congressional maps passed by the Legislature from being vetoed by voters via the referendum process.

The federal lawsuit was filed by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district currently held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo. and two voters. Clark then ruled Tuesday that the state must use the map that people voted in during the primary.

The drama was playing out even after Tuesday’s deadline to finalize Missouri ballots ahead of this fall’s elections. First ballots are set to go out in the state on Sept. 19.

World.content:
Jimmy Kimmel announced on Wednesday night that his show would not air his upcoming interview with Texas’ Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico on television, citing the Trump administration’s threats against ABC.

Kimmel said that during President Donald Trump’s administration, the Federal Communications Commission “has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.”

“Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas, who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” he said.

The interview, set for Thursday, will be posted on the YouTube channel for “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” instead, he said. Talarico, a Democratic state representative in Texas, is locked in a competitive Senate race with Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. Brandon Bell / Getty Images file

The Talarico campaign and the FCC did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment. ABC Entertainment declined to comment.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, condemned “FCC intimidation” in a statement reacting to Kimmel’s announcement.

“No host, local affiliate, or network should have to weigh federal retaliation before booking a guest for a newsworthy interview,” Gomez said in the statement. “Any attempt to pressure broadcasters into self-censorship undermines both press freedom and the public’s right to hear from candidates in their communities seeking public office.”

Kimmel’s announcement marks the latest apparent instance in which pressure from the administration has affected content aired on an entertainment show. Stephen Colbert said in February that CBS did not air his interview with Talarico out of fear of the FCC.

“He was supposed to be here, but we were told in no uncertain terms by our network’s lawyers, who called us directly, that we could not have him on the broadcast,” Colbert said at the time.

CBS said in a February statement that “the show was provided legal guidance that the broadcast could trigger the FCC equal-time rule for two other candidates.”

Trump has publicly targeted Kimmel in the past, calling multiple times for the comedian to be fired.

About a year ago, ABC pulled Kimmel’s show following the comedian’s comments about conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated in September of last year. The show returned nearly a week later, and Kimmel said in his monologue that “it was never my intention to make light of the murder of a young man.”

The FCC, under Chairman Brendan Carr, announced in April that Disney’s eight local television stations owned and operated by ABC needed to file broadcast license renewals early. The Walt Disney Co. sued over the decision last month.

In January, the FCC issued a memo saying that late-night and daytime talk shows must adhere to the equal time rule, which requires broadcasters to offer equal opportunities to other qualified candidates who are running for the same office. The memo marked a change in the FCC’s position. Twenty years earlier, a decision found that late-night and daytime talk shows were exempt from the rule.

Trump himself was interviewed by Kimmel in 2015, when he was running for president. Kimmel recalled the interview during his Wednesday show.

“At that time, when he was the one sitting next to me, he seemed to have no problem with the idea of talk show hosts interviewing candidates,” he said. “In fact, he was very eager to come back for another interview, which he did just before he became the nominee in 2016.”

“But for some reason, and I can’t seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed,” he said, tongue in cheek.

World.title: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee loses Democratic primary to businesswoman Helena Foulkes
World.content:
Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee has lost his Democratic primary to former CVS executive Helena Foulkes, NBC News projects, after facing a significant spending disadvantage and voter discontent with his tenure.

In an election season that has seen a wave of anti-incumbent energy, McKee, 75, becomes the first governor to fall in a primary this year — and the first in eight years.

Public polling had shown McKee, who was running for a full second term, trailing by double digits heading into Tuesday. And Foulkes, 62, outspent him on the airwaves by 3-to-1, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

The primary was a rematch of 2022, when Foulkes narrowly lost to McKee, who had replaced Gov. Gina Raimondo after she was selected for President Joe Biden’s Cabinet in 2021.

McKee’s 2023 decision to close the Washington Bridge, a commuter thoroughfare in Providence, hung over his campaign. The bridge closure came after state engineers discovered major structural problems that could have eventually caused it to collapse. Three years later, the bridge remains under construction.

Dan McKee; Helena Buonanno Foulkes. Getty Images

An Emerson College poll in August found that 63% of likely Rhode Island voters disapproved of McKee’s handling of the Washington Bridge, with just 18% saying they approved.

In her campaign ads, Foulkes said the state had “the worst roads and bridges.” She also touted her plans to boost the state’s economy and housing market.

McKee has defended his decision to close the bridge, saying he prioritized safety over politics, and he has said construction will be completed by 2028.

The last time a sitting governor lost a primary was in 2018, when Kansas Republican Jeff Colyer was defeated by then-Secretary of State Kris Kobach, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump. Hawaii’s Neil Abercrombie was the last Democratic governor to fall in a primary, losing by 35 points to David Ige, who was a state senator at the time, in 2014.

Eleven House members and two senators have lost primaries this year.

Given the heavy focus on local issues, the Rhode Island primary did not attract the level of national attention other Democratic contests around the country — which centered on fierce ideological and generational battles — have attracted this year.

Still, Foulkes does have connections to powerful Democrats. Thomas Dodd and Chris Dodd, her uncle and grandfather, were both U.S. senators from Connecticut. And former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who was a college roommate of Foulkes’ mother, campaigned for her.

Foulkes will be the heavy favorite in the general election in the blue state, which has not elected a Republican governor since 2010. Kamala Harris carried it by nearly 14 points in the 2024 presidential election.

World.title: ‘We felt defeated’: Lindsay Clancy juror provides new details about the lone holdout
World.content:
A juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial provided new details Thursday about the lone holdout on the panel, including that he acted out the killings on a water bottle during deliberations.

Nick Dargie, 25, was one of the three men on the 12-person jury tasked with determining whether Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the 2023 strangulation deaths of her three young children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old. He told “Good Morning America” on Thursday about his frustrations with the holdout juror, who has yet to be publicly identified.

“I think we felt defeated,” Dargie said about the case’s conclusion. “We spent seven weeks on this trial, almost two months of, you know, all of our lives dedicated to it.”

He is among at least five jurors — and the first male — who have spoken out about the case and what happened inside the deliberation room at Plymouth Superior Court last week. After more than 38 hours, the jurors could not reach a unanimous decision, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial after they deadlocked three times.

On Thursday, defense attorney Kevin Reddington filed a renewed motion to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility on each of the three charges, arguing that the prosecution did not prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Clancy was not in psychosis at the time of the killings.

Dargie told “Good Morning America” that toward the end of deliberations, the holdout juror would not engage in discussions with others or provide evidence that supported his reasoning, instead choosing to scroll on his phone.

Ultimately, Dargie said, he confronted the holdout juror after the man mimicked the killings, tying an exercise band entered into evidence around an empty water bottle and pulling it tight. Dargie said he is not sure why the man did that.

“I was shocked. It didn’t make any sense to me,” Dargie said. “We’re not in here to play detective or it’s not a game of Clue. This is serious.”

Nick Dargie on "Good Morning America." ABC News

Throughout the trial, Clancy’s defense attorney argued that she was in a state of psychosis when she strangled the children with exercise bands and therefore was not aware of what she was doing. The prosecution, however, argued she was not actually experiencing postpartum psychosis and planned the killings ahead of time.

Three women on the jury told NBC Boston that the 11 jurors agreed to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. The holdout wanted to convict, they revealed, but admitted he expressed doubt in the prosecution’s case.

“It was definitely frustrating, mainly frustrating when [the holdout juror] explicitly said, ‘You know, I don’t know if the prosecution or the defense proved their case,’” Dargie told “GMA.”

Reddington in the motion also pointed to the fact that in this case, every juror except one — who did not apply the reasonable-doubt standard — came to that same conclusion.

“No rational jury could find beyond a reasonable doubt that she had no mental disease or defect when the Commonwealth’s own proof established that she did,” the motion said, noting the 11-1 jury split.

And at first, Dargie said, a number of jurors thought Clancy was guilty of the crimes, and at times the jury’s votes differed day to day.

A female juror who spoke with CBS Boston anonymously said many people on the jury were initially “firm in their beliefs,” and that she was one of the people who, at first, agreed with the holdout and thought Clancy was guilty.

She explained how there was so much “gray area” and doubt in the case, and that ultimately, she switched her tune because she thinks Clancy is mentally unwell and that she’d get better help in a state mental health facility than in prison.

Dargie told “GMA” that “once we laid out all of the evidence and how we saw it, that really brought everyone kind of on the same page, except for this one juror.” The female juror chalked it up to one person being unable to let go of their convictions.

When that one juror didn’t agree with the group, Dargie said, he asked him to show evidence that “helped to prove what he was saying, but he couldn’t.” That’s what led the jury foreperson to send a note to the judge about the holdout during deliberations, explaining that he wasn’t meeting the burden of reasonable doubt the prosecution must overcome.

Dargie acknowledged that it’s fair for someone to have a differing opinion, but said this particular juror would not engage and could not “find something to support his view.”

Now, prosecutors must decide whether they want to retry Clancy. The next hearing for the case is scheduled for Sept. 29.

Dargie, who was serving in the military overseas, said he’s “haunted” by the case. Specifically, he said, the recording of the 911 call made by Clancy’s then-husband, Patrick Clancy, when he found the dead children that night is seared into his memory. The recording was played in court and was not released to the public.

Patrick Clancy on the stand. David L. Ryan / The Boston Globe via Getty Images file

“I’ve never heard something like that, like a scream like that, come out of someone’s mouth,” Dargie said of the recording. “It’s horrifying.”

The anonymous female juror told CBS Boston that she will “never be the same after that 911 call.”

Dargie also rejected online conspiracy theories that Patrick Clancy was actually the one who carried out the killings, noting that if anyone had heard the 911 calls, they would change their mind.

“I think if they tried the trial again the way they did, I think nine times out of 10, I think the jury would come back with not guilty by reason of insanity, no doubt,” Dargie said.

World.title: Oil prices surge to $107 for the first time since May as bond yields jump
World.content:
The price of oil surged again Thursday, with Brent crude surpassing $107 per barrel for the first time since May and U.S. crude oil jumping above $100 per barrel, also its highest level since mid-May.

A primary driver of the move in oil prices was President Donald Trump’s comment Wednesday night that he is not looking for a deal with Iran. Trump also said that he did not expect oil prices to fall until “right after” the November midterm elections, despite having said for months that the war would be over quickly.

“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump told reporters Wednesday afternoon. “They’re going to be tumbling down, and we’ll get them down.”

Commodities experts warned earlier this week that oil prices as measured by Brent could rise to $120 or even as high as $150 per barrel if the stalemate with Iran continues to drag on.

Trump’s suggestion that the war would continue for many more months also puts global crude oil stockpiles in focus. Earlier this year, dozens of nations agreed to release 400 million barrels in order to keep a lid on prices in the early months of the war.

The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since the 1980s.

Additionally, Saudi Arabia informed OPEC that its crude oil output plunged to the lowest level since 1990 last month due to renewed hostilities with Iran, according to a report from Bloomberg News.

NBC News was not immediately able to confirm that report.

“The move reflects a market still pricing in persistent geopolitical risk, with Persian Gulf tensions showing no credible path to de‑escalation,” analysts at ING said Thursday.

As a result of those rising prices, the national average gas price rose another 5 cents overnight to $4.27. Diesel fuel, which powers everything from farms to trucking to trains, rose 3 cents overnight to $5.97.

Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury bonds continued to sell off, driving their yields higher. The 10-year Treasury yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, especially for mortgages, touched 4.93%, its highest level since 2023.

The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.07% Thursday, according to Mortgage News Daily. This is the highest rate since May 2025.

The 30-year Treasury yield spiked to 5.35%, its highest level since 2007.

The move in Treasury yields was driven mostly by the soaring price of energy, which has triggered renewed fears of an inflation crisis.

World.title: Spice Girls fans feel duped after social media tease wasn’t for tour, but a music re-release
World.content:
Spice Girls fans are telling you what they want — what they really, really want — and it’s a tour that they aren’t getting any time soon.

The disbanded girl group excited their followers on Wednesday with a social media post teasing a big announcement for the following day. A short clip posted to Instagram showed an issue of “The Stage” magazine left on a set of stairs before zooming into a clasified  seeking Spice Girls Fans who are a “superfan, a collector, a music lover.”

“No sheet music required but you will need a vinyl or cd player,” the ad said.

Fans immediately jumped to speculation on what it could be, with many hoping for a possible reunion.

“If it’s a world tour, I’m selling my house to buy tix,” one Instagram commenter wrote.

Another wrote, “please say it’s @spherevegas,” referring to the popular Las Vegas venue where the Backstreet Boys are currently in residency.

But some should have slowed it down and read the sign.

On Thursday, the Spice Girls account announced a re-release of “all the singles” with b-sides and surprises “from the vault” on CD and vinyl. A previously unreleased demo of a song called “Do You Think About Me” was also made available on streaming services Thursday.

The full collection will release in November and ranges in price from $128.99 to $380.99, according to the band’s website. The re-release is meant to honor the 30th anniversary of their single “Wannabe,” the hit that changed the trajectory of their lives.

It was a blow to the ‘90s band’s most loyal fans, who were ready to promise they would be there in the stands.

“Negotiating with my husband on my price cap for Spice Girls tickets today was for NOTHING,” one woman wrote in the comments.

“Guys we want two things- Spice World on streaming platforms and a tour with the full line-up,” another Instagram user wrote. “Please make it happen.”

“I hear the millennial sigh of devastation from across the world,” one person said.

00:15 Spice Girls drop a cryptic video spurring reunion rumors 00:00 00:00

The Spice Girls have been asked repeatedly about a tour in recent years in interviews, but it appears that a reunion performance with all five original members is a pipe dream. There was a small tour across the U.K. and Ireland in 2019 that didn’t feature Victoria Beckham, aka Posh Spice.

Beckham expressed her excitement to go watch her former bandmates even if she wasn’t going to be on stage. The fashion mogul has said in the last year that she hasn’t performed in years and doesn’t feel that she is the strongest singer or dancer.

She told Andy Cohen on his radio show in October that she didn’t think she could even make a world tour work with the demands of her business.

“Before I was in the Spice Girls, I was so self-conscious and they made me feel that I was good enough, but being on stage, I realized as fun as it is, you know, it’s not ultimately what I want to do anymore,” Beckham said.

Melanie Brown, or Scary Spice as she’s known to fans, reiterated that a tour was not happening in an interview with Hello! magazine published in April.

“I’m 50. You can’t be nagging everyone to go on tour if they don’t want to,” Brown said. “I laid that to rest when I turned 50.”

But the women are still close friends.

All but Beckham were in attendance for Melanie Chisholm’s wedding earlier this year. And though she couldn’t be there for Sporty Spice on her big day, Beckham designed the singer’s wedding dress, according to Vogue.

All five women were together earlier this year, according to social media. Beckham’s youngest son posted a video on Instagram in February of the Spice Girls singing their song “Viva Forever” around a dinner table while he played guitar for him. The video has been watched more than 13 million times.

“Love you all,” Beckham wrote in her son’s comment section.
