World.title: One year after Charlie Kirk's death, Turning Point USA faces an uncertain future
World.content:
One year after Charlie Kirk's death, Turning Point USA faces an uncertain future

toggle caption Alex Brandon/AP

When Jacob York found out that Charlie Kirk had been fatally shot, he was at baseball practice. Standing in the outfield, he broke down in tears. That night, he decided that Kirk's organization, Turning Point USA, should have a chapter on his campus. So he got to work starting one himself.

"I feel like there [were] many of us who had that wake-up call," said York, 21, who attends Olivet Nazarene University, a small Christian school south of Chicago.

"I think I submitted the request to start a chapter six times," he recalled. "There were so many requests that it kept saying, 'Oops, try again later.'"

Sponsor Message

Kirk's death one year ago on the campus of Utah Valley University was as stunning for his followers as it was painful. A little more than a decade earlier, he had founded Turning Point with the goal of getting more young people involved in conservative politics. By the time he died at age 31, he had become one of the most revered figures on the right, especially among Generation Z and millennial conservatives.

From students like York all the way to the upper echelons of the Republican Party, Kirk's death was seen as a call to action. In the days following the shooting, Turning Point reported an initial surge of interest among college and high school students looking to start chapters.

His widow, Erika Kirk, spoke about that momentum in her first public remarks, just days after his death.

"If you thought that my husband's mission was powerful before, you have no idea," said Erika Kirk, who has since taken over as Turning Point's CEO. "You have no idea what you've just unleashed across this entire country, and this world."

But, as Charlie Kirk's young supporters reflect on the past year, some paint a more complicated picture of the organization he left behind. Rather than a unified and growing coalition of young voters, they describe a movement facing questions about its future — one that has yet to fully coalesce around a new leader and that is grappling with the same issue divides causing friction within the Republican Party more broadly.

Sponsor Message

Fractures amid growth

The fractures have been felt acutely by young conservatives like 23-year-old Dino Fantegrossi.

"Charlie Kirk got it. He spent all of his time on college campuses talking to people my age, whether he agreed or disagreed with them," said Fantegrossi. "He knew — because he was so plugged in — what bugged young people, what needed to be addressed. There's no one else that was quite at that level of plugged in."

Fantegrossi, a recent graduate of the University of Arkansas, had led his school's Turning Point chapter for more than two years. That is until last spring, when he decided to break with the organization and start a new group, Young American Revival, which he said aims to be "a positive vehicle for students to take out their frustrations in a manner that actually brings about change within our state."

toggle caption Melissa Majchrzak/AFP via Getty Images

"One of the big problems that has happened since Charlie's death is that I think a lot of the youth have kind of felt lost," said Fantegrossi. "They're not really sure how to channel their frustrations, and that oftentimes — when it's not put in check or pointed in a positive direction — can manifest itself in some very nasty ways."

In a statement, Turning Point spokesman Andrew Kolvet acknowledged that the group is facing "a confluence of challenges" but attested that "the organization is still growing in nearly every conceivable way," saying it's "a testament to Charlie's enduring legacy."

Turning Point says in a fact sheet that it saw "unprecedented expansion" in the 2025-2026 school year, with over a million involved students across 3,500 high school clubs and 1,500 college chapters.

"In many ways the challenges our students and chapters face have never been more obvious or pronounced, but so too are the opportunities," Kolvet said.

A missing leader for young conservatives

At the time of his death, Kirk was seen as one of the most influential voices within the conservative youth space and broader Republican Party. Supporters have credited him for the gains that then-candidate Donald Trump made with young voters in the 2024 presidential election, a crucial bloc that helped propel him to a second term.

Sponsor Message

Kirk's influence extended into Trump's second administration, as Kirk maintained close relationships with top White House officials while continuing to engage with the Make America Great Again movement's newly expanded youth coalition.

For his followers, his influence meant their views had a direct pipeline to the president. For the administration, he was a trusted messenger on policy decisions, even when they split the MAGA base, as with the strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in the summer of 2025.

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

But for as much as Kirk was revered on the right, he was reviled on the left, facing pushback for comments disparaging immigrants and transgender people and questioning the qualifications and capabilities of women and Black Americans. He also amplified conspiracy theories about COVID-19 and falsely claimed the 2020 presidential election was fraudulent.

The criticism did not faze Kirk, as he visited campuses across the U.S. to debate his positions at "Prove Me Wrong" events that were central to the image he cultivated for himself as a defender of free speech, free markets and limited government. It was the same type of event he was taking part in last year when he was assassinated at Utah Valley University.

"He was unique in terms of his connection to a not-insignificant number of younger people," argued John Della Volpe, a Democratic pollster who has spent decades researching young Americans.

Della Volpe, who observes and conducts focus groups of Gen Z voters, said Kirk's death could be another factor fueling a growing belief among young people that they lack political agency.

"His name is mentioned on an ongoing basis, literally every single month. But it's framed as 'He was someone who understood me, who heard me,'" Della Volpe added. "People feel like he listened to them and he's been taken from us. So therefore, why does it matter anymore?"

Sponsor Message

The divides playing out within Turning Point

That kind of direct connection has felt missing for many of Kirk's followers. Turning Point leaders vowed to continue holding campus visits in Kirk's stead, organizing more formal events that largely veered away from direct debate and instead featured a range of keynote speakers, including the group's new leader, Erika Kirk, and Vice President Vance. But the events have drawn mixed and, at times, lackluster turnout.

Filling Kirk's shoes isn't the only challenge facing Turning Point. There's also the daunting task of keeping young conservatives engaged at a time when many of them are unhappy with party leaders.

That includes Trump, whose youth coalition has increasingly soured on him. At the start of his second term, 92% of Trump voters under 35 approved of his job as president, according to data from Pew Research Center. By late April 2026, that support had dropped to 57%.

toggle caption Pool/Getty Images

Student organizers say the Iran war and the administration's relationship with Israel have been major tension points. Gen Z and millennial Republicans are much less likely than older generations to hold favorable views on both topics.

To Hazel Roberts, 18, a first-year student at Grand Canyon University who started a Turning Point chapter back in high school, these intraparty rifts are a painful reminder of why Kirk's leadership mattered.

"That's what Charlie loved about Turning Point. We could all have different perspectives and not hate each other for it, and we can talk about it. And since Charlie's passing, there has been a lot of hate from the right," she said. "Charlie was the glue that held us together."

Misinformation about Turning Point could cloud its future

The divides go past just policy rifts, and for some student activists on campus, they had made organizing efforts more of a challenge.

"The conspiracies revolving around Charlie Kirk's assassination [have] really tanked the credibility of Turning Point," said Alex BirdSong, 19, a junior at Georgia State University, referring to the slew of unfounded claims made by right-wing influencers, namely podcaster Candace Owens, to millions online over the past year.

Sponsor Message

BirdSong, who joined his school's Turning Point chapter following Kirk's death and now serves as its president, hopes that this school year he can help change how people think about the organization.

"We've had people come up to us who are Candace Owens fans and get mad at us for being Turning Point, and so that's what the climate is," he explained. "It's going to be a huge challenge for Turning Point and the right if, one, the right can't unify and, two, if the [Trump] administration can't get the controversies under wraps."

Some students admit that the confluence of challenges has caused momentum to fizzle.

toggle caption Win McNamee/Getty Images

"I would say the interest in conservative organizations is low right now, even if it did rebound when Charlie Kirk got shot," said Max Williams, 20, a junior at the University of Richmond, where he leads the school's Turning Point chapter. "I think that Charlie not being there, the Trump administration not being popular right now — I think that it is definitely slowed down a bit and maybe even is going in the opposite direction."

Williams said there's a part of him that's not excited to participate in organizing on campus again this year, as he too has grown frustrated with Trump.

"Some of this stuff is just infuriating, and you can't defend any of it. And I don't even try anymore," he added.

His plan for talking with students on campus: Emphasize the issues they care about, instead of focusing on Trump.

But without Kirk, that might not be as easy as it once was.

World.title: Democrats blast $5,000 payment promise ahead of Trump, Vance speeches in Dallas
World.content:
Democrats blast $5,000 payment promise ahead of Trump, Vance speeches in Dallas

toggle caption Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, President Trump made a stunning and implausible pledge: to send every American adult a $5,000 cash dividend. But only if his party maintains control of the House and the Senate in November's midterms.

"If the Republicans win, you win with us," Trump said to applause. "And it will be called the 'Trump dividend'. Congratulations. Now all we have to do is win."

That's a big "if." Republicans are facing significant political headwinds.

"We might not win," Trump admitted.

Sponsor Message

Quick math puts the bill for this proposed "dividend" at more than $1 trillion. Plus, it's illegal to pay or be paid to influence voting.

House Democrats in Dallas Thursday to counter program the convention quickly attacked the announcement.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., called the president a "known liar."

"The dividend is not happening," Garcia added. "[Trump] promised a dividend on tariffs. That didn't happen. He promised a dividend on DOGE. That didn't happen. He promised some strange, new dividend from Air Force One, what six months ago? That never happened."

"There's no one in the country that thinks somehow this new dividend is actually going to happen," he said.

Trump's address last night was a wide ranging, rally-style speech where he did everything from defend the Iran war to criticize the fashion sense of one Republican Senate candidate. He attacked Democrats as communist and extremists and begged Republicans to vote in November as if he were on the ballot.

"Please pretend that I'm running," he said. "If we don't have the majorities, so much can be lost."

Trump spoke for an hour and 44 minutes, far longer than scheduled.

He will deliver closing remarks tonight as well.

"But I'm not doing a big deal like this," he joked. "I gave you a lot of material. I don't have to do it twice."

Sponsor Message

The two-night event, hatched by Trump, was meant for Republicans to energize the base ahead of the midterms.

"It took a little imagination to think of it," Trump said of the first ever Republican midterm convention.

In a preview of what to expect tonight, the focus on Trump was clear as the event kicked off Wednesday, with a lineup of Republican lawmakers, candidates and everyday Americans, praising the president and his policies. It was capped off by Trump's headlining speech.

Speaking to an arena with whole sections of empty seats, Trump rallied the party faithful.

"The midterms are not supposed to be won by [the party of] the sitting president, and we're going to change that," Trump said, promising to visit the states and districts of every Republican facing a close race.

Tonight, Trump will share the convention's final hour with Vice President Vance. By the time Republicans hold their next convention in 2028, Trump will no longer be the center of the party's attention. There will be a new nominee and de facto party leader charting a course for Republicans.

The program tonight will include a tribute to the late republican activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated one year ago, and an observance of the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks, which is Friday.

MAGA celebrities and cabinet members will also grace the stage tonight. Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt is set to speak, along with Donald Trump Jr. and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Over the course of the convention, 19 Republicans in competitive House and Senate races will deliver short stump speeches. Many of them have used the stage to position the Republican Party as the party of the American people, painting Democrats as aligned with "socialism" and "communism."

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running to represent the state in the US Senate made those points, but also used his speech to ask for money.

"I need your prayers, your vote and your support," Paxton said. "If we lose Texas, we lose the common sense revolution. If we lose the common sense revolution, we lose America."

His Democratic opponent, state Rep. James Talarico has a campaign cash advantage but Trump's Super PAC, MAGA Inc. just committed to spend $10 million, propping up Paxton and hitting Talarico. A Republican shouldn't be in a tight race in Texas, but Paxton has been plagued by scandal and weak fundraising.

Sponsor Message

Trump, in his remarks, urged Texans to vote for Paxton despite what the president considers to be his flaws.

"Some may not like the way he dresses. I don't," Trump said as part of a lengthy and lighthearted critique of the man he endorsed.

NPR's Stephen Fowler contributed reporting.

World.title: Scientists say August was Earth's hottest month they've measured
World.content:
Scientists say August was Earth's hottest month they've measured

toggle caption Ahn Young-joon/AP

WASHINGTON — Earth cooked to its hottest month on record in August, blowing far past a key climate threshold, due to the dangerous double whammy of human-caused climate change and a supersized El Nino, according to the European climate service Copernicus.

August's sizzle also helped push the globe and the United States to swelter through the hottest Northern Hemisphere summer scientists have measured.

Last month the world averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit (16.96 degrees Celsius), which technically was one-hundredth of a degree Celsius more than the all-time global mark set in July 2023, but because that's also the uncertainty level, it's considered a tie, said Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for Copernicus.

"It is now time to stop acting surprised that our warming planet keeps getting warmer. This is occurring exactly as forecast by scientists literally decades ago," Texas A&M University climate scientist Andrew Dessler said in an email. "The interesting question is not whether we will keep breaking heat records (we will), but whether we're going to do anything about it or just stand there while the climate train runs us over."

Sponsor Message

Globally, August was 1.65 degrees Celsius (nearly 3 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, far exceeding the longer term 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold set by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. The eight hottest months on record have all been from July 2023 on, according to Copernicus data.

"Our climate system is really operating well outside the range we would have expected just a decade ago," Burgess said Wednesday from a United Kingdom that has been beset with heat waves. "We've transitioned from climate being very abstract and perhaps impacting the global South or far away places to climate impacting and disrupting our daily lives with schools closing, hospitals being overwhelmed, roads melting, train lines buckling. And the reality is we will get more of these conditions that we've seen this summer."

Global monthly ocean temperatures in August tied a March 2024 all-time record for warmest month recorded, while Aug. 22 set a record for hottest day recorded in the world's seas, according to Copernicus.

An extra hot summer hits

"This summer has really been exceptional. We've seen records that existed for close to 100 years be broken, in the U.S. in particular," Burgess said.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration on Wednesday announced that for the first time, summer in the Lower 48 states was hotter than during the peak of the devastating Dust Bowl in 1936. June through August of 2026 in the contiguous United States averaged 74.37 degrees (23.54 degrees Celsius), nearly four tenths of a degree warmer than the mark set 90 years earlier. Globally, this past summer also tied, with 2024, for the hottest on record, according to Copernicus.

Sponsor Message

In the U.S., August smashed heat records by more than half a degree Fahrenheit, averaging 75.58 degrees (24.21 degrees Celsius) and the average daytime high was a blistering 88.56 degrees (31.42 degrees Celsius), also a record. July was similarly record hot in the U.S., erasing another long-standing Dust Bowl mark.

That records are regularly getting broken, and that August and not July which is traditionally warmer set an all-time record, are signs that human-caused climate change is accelerating, Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather said.

Copernicus data goes back to 1940. NOAA data for the United States goes back to 1895 and global data, which generally matches Copernicus data but takes longer to calculate, dates back to 1880.

Fossil fuels, El Nino blamed

Several scientists said while El Nino is a factor, this natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps and warms weather globally is nowhere as big a cause as the heat-trapping gases emitted as humans burn coal, oil and natural gas.

"While El Nino is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels. Climate change makes every El Nino hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming," said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London.

Burgess said El Nino generally adds only one or two tenths of a degree Celsius (two to four tenths Fahrenheit) to the global temperature with the overwhelming rest of the heat coming from the burning of fossil fuels.

This El Nino is forecast, however, to break records for strength in the coming months. And as temperatures continue to rise, heat waves, storms, floods and wildfires will get more frequent and more dangerous, said Texas Tech climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe.

According to Hausfather, "it is increasingly likely that 2026 ends up beating 2024 as the warmest year on record, and almost certain that 2027 beats both, potentially reaching as high as 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels on the back of an unprecedentedly-strong El Nino event."

Sponsor Message

Some days may hit an even higher climate threshold, 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above mid 1800s, Burgess said.

"Until humanity stops burning colossal amount of coal, oil and gas, the pollution this causes will keep baking our planet, and extreme heat will keep smashing all-time records, killing millions and costing trillions, hitting transport and health systems, and pushing up prices for household basics like food," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said. "This is the spiraling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling."

World.title: Trade war, Alberta referendum loom large as Carney charts cabinet's year forward
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Prime Minister Mark Carney gathered leaders of the world's foremost economies in Kananaskis Country's picturesque mountainside last spring for the G7, it was fresh off his election win, a wind seemingly at his back as he met with U.S. President Donald Trump to talk trade, and the threat of the province's separation from Canada was a remote hypothetical.

"Our primary focus will be on trade and trade with Canada," said Trump at the time, standing side by side with Carney in his first visit to this country since 2018. "I'm sure we can work something out."

A little more than a year later, Carney is once again holding high-level meetings in the Rocky Mountains of the province where he grew up, this time to plan the upcoming parliamentary sitting with his cabinet, fresh off three byelections where his governing Liberals cleaned up.

But there is little else in common with the optimistic outlook of 2025.

Trade tensions between Canada and the U.S. only continue to intensify, while the danger of Alberta's departure from federation has become much more real.

While Abacus Data founder and CEO David Coletto said there's little indication Canadians are blaming the prime minister for the trouble facing the country at this time, they are still looking for answers on the way forward.

"I think there's always risk when the impact might be job losses or the cost of things going up because we are in the midst of a cost of living crisis, you know, the No. 1 issue for most Canadians right across the country," Coletto told CBC News.

WATCH | Carney releases video saying U.S. wanted 'dependency' in too many areas: Carney releases video saying U.S. wanted 'dependency' in too many areas | Duration 1:48 In an excerpt from a 15-minute explanatory video released by Prime Minister Mark Carney's office on Tuesday, Carney says U.S. trade negotiators wanted Canada 'to become even more reliant on them, not less.'

The prime minister continues to defend his decision to reject the proposed new trade agreement with the U.S. in order to protect Canada's sovereignty, as officials from the Trump administration try to convince the public that Carney walked away for political reasons.

Carney is close to peak popularity, with poll numbers stronger than his predecessor Justin Trudeau at this point in his mandate, according to Coletto, who says there's no sign personal attacks from the White House are going to change that anytime soon.

"The likelihood that Canadians would trust what Donald Trump says over Mark Carney is very low," Coletto said.

"I think we've always assumed that there would be a best-before date on the public's patience and I now question that because I think as long as people overwhelmingly believe that the greatest threat to their quality of life is coming from Washington and not from policy out of Ottawa that that's going to continue to buy the prime minister and the government time."

Pivot away from U.S., national unity on the agenda

As the two-day cabinet planning forum with cabinet ministers and secretaries of state kicks off, there's no announcement yet on whether Ottawa will match the Trump administration's latest retaliation.

The White House is adding more Canadian products to its list of those subject to tariffs of 50 per cent, including mattresses and motorboats, and also planning to ban certain Canadian goods, including most alcoholic drinks, some dairy products and motorcycles by the end of the month.

That itself is a response to Ottawa imposing retaliatory tariffs on more than $27 billion worth of U.S. imports – a counter to 50 per cent levies the Trump administration placed on an equivalent amount of Canadian goods last month, after Carney called off trade talks.

WATCH | Ottawa considers next moves in U.S. trade war: Government assesses U.S. trade war damage, says Canada in 'a position of strength' | Duration 4:57 Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada is still assessing the damage from the escalating trade with the U.S., but it's doing so from 'a position of strength.' Meanwhile Conservatives repeated calls to reconvene Parliament early.

The cabinet planning forum will focus on the pivot Carney says he is trying to lead, steering Canada away from its over-reliance on the U.S. — its largest trading partner — shoring up the economy and strengthening partnerships with other countries.

It's expected that ministers and secretaries of state will arrive prepared to defend their performance on their files and propose solutions as the country deals with what Carney describes as an unprecedented crisis.

The forum will also tackle separatism, coming as it does a little more than a month ahead of a referendum where Albertans will answer, among other questions, whether they want to stay part of Canada or have an eventual vote on secession.

Some of Carney's top ministers fanned throughout the province ahead of the cabinet meeting, including Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson, who was in Clive to break ground on a carbon-capture project.

"We are in a trade war, a trade war that we did not ask for, but that we must win," he said. "Canada didn't ask for a world where energy security equals economic security, equals national security. But that's the world we're in today."

WATCH | Canada faces more U.S. trade war escalation: At Issue | Canada faces more U.S. trade war escalation | Duration 22:33 At Issue this week: With Canada's $28 billion tit-for-tat counter-tariffs sparking further U.S. tariffs and outright bans on some Canadian products, the At Issue panel breaks down Canada's strategy, what it might do next, and what all the trade chaos means for politics and national unity.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, at an armchair discussion hosted by the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce, was asked about the possibility of restarting talks with the U.S.

"At the right time, there will be further engagement with respect," Champagne said. "Canada's a big nation, Canada's a G7 country, Canada's a NATO country … and Canada is a big customer. We buy more from the United States than Japan, England and Germany combined."

"Any action taken will affect both sides of the border."

Guests scheduled to brief cabinet reflect the concerns about both the trade war and Alberta separatism.

The list includes the mayors of Calgary and Red Deer, pollsters including Janet Brown — known for her insights into the Alberta political landscape — and Ian Bremmer, the founding political scientist of Eurasia Group.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who landed in Calgary Wednesday, will also briefly address cabinet in Banff.

Missing from the list is any expert on affordability or pocketbook issues, unlike in January 2026, when Carney and his ministers heard from Food Banks Canada CEO Kirstin Beardsley.

An apparent ambivalence toward pocketbook issues might become a weakness for Carney in the long term, Coletto said.

"I think that thing that Canadians are looking for more than anything is reassurance," Coletto said. "Reassurance that their government understands the risks seized by them and is doing everything it can to mitigate them at the same time as finding ways of looking long term to how to strengthen Canada."

World.content:

Earth cooked to its hottest month on record in August, blowing far past a key climate threshold due to the dangerous double whammy of human-caused climate change and a supersized El Niño, according to the European climate service Copernicus.

August's sizzle also helped push the globe and Canada to swelter through the hottest Northern Hemisphere summer scientists have measured.

Last month the world averaged 16.96 C, which technically was one-hundredth of a degree Celsius more than the all-time global mark set in July 2023. But because that's also the uncertainty level, it's considered a tie, said Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for Copernicus.

"It is now time to stop acting surprised that our warming planet keeps getting warmer. This is occurring exactly as forecast by scientists literally decades ago," Texas A&M University climate scientist Andrew Dessler said in an email.

"The interesting question is not whether we will keep breaking heat records (we will), but whether we're going to do anything about it or just stand there while the climate train runs us over."

This graphic shows that August 2026 was the hottest month ever recorded globally. (C3S/ECMWF)

Globally, August was 1.65 C above pre-industrial levels, far exceeding the longer term 1.5 C threshold set by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. The eight hottest months on record have all been from July 2023 on, according to Copernicus data.

"Our climate system is really operating well outside the range we would have expected just a decade ago," Burgess said Wednesday from a United Kingdom that has been beset with heat waves.

WATCH | Millions across Europe facing record temperatures from major heat wave: Millions across Europe facing record temperatures from major heat wave | Duration 2:21 Much of western Europe saw another scorching day on Saturday amid a deadly heat wave that has already broken temperature records in Britain, France and Spain. The heat is moving east across the continent, with one expert warning Switzerland's glaciers are set to lose a massive amount of ice due to the heat wave.

"We've transitioned from climate being very abstract and perhaps impacting the Global South or faraway places to climate impacting and disrupting our daily lives with schools closing, hospitals being overwhelmed, roads melting, train lines buckling. And the reality is we will get more of these conditions that we've seen this summer."

Global monthly ocean temperatures in August tied a March 2024 all-time record for the warmest month recorded, while Aug. 22 set a record for the hottest day recorded in the world's seas, according to Copernicus.

An extra-hot summer hits

"This summer has really been exceptional. We've seen records that existed for close to 100 years be broken, in the U.S. in particular," Burgess said.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on Wednesday announced that for the first time, summer in the lower 48 states was hotter than during the peak of the devastating Dust Bowl in 1936.

Until humanity stops burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, the pollution this causes will keep baking our planet, and extreme heat will keep smashing all-time records, killing millions and costing trillions. - United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell

June through August of 2026 in the contiguous United States averaged 23.54 C, nearly four-tenths of a degree warmer than the mark set 90 years earlier. Globally, this past summer also tied with 2024 for the hottest on record, according to Copernicus.

Burgess said El Niño generally adds only one- or two-tenths of a degree Celsius to the global temperature with the overwhelming rest of the heat coming from the burning of fossil fuels.

The numbers are expected to climb as more data is collected.

This El Niño is forecast, however, to break records for strength in the coming months. And as temperatures continue to rise, heat waves, storms, floods and wildfires will get more frequent and more dangerous, said Texas Tech climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe.

World.title: Poilievre tells U.S. TV Canadians are 'wounded' and 'confused' to be in America's crosshairs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is telling Americans their northern neighbours are feeling "wounded" and "confused" over how Canada and its economy became a key target for U.S. President Donald Trump.

"I think we feel a little bit wounded," Poilievre told reporters on the U.S. network CNBC on Thursday during a trip to New York where he is advocating for a return to normal trade relations.

"We're kind of confused as to how it is, suddenly, that Canada ended up in the crosshair."

The Conservative leader said Canada and the U.S. have a deeply interconnected economic relationship that has delivered peace and prosperity for decades and the only way forward should be tariff-free trade.

"Both countries are going to have their grievances," he said. "America had buy-America policies that prevented us from selling into subnational procurement markets and tariffs on our softwood lumber.… But the bottom line is: let's sit down and work them out for the mutual benefit of our people."

WATCH | Poilievre appears on CNBC:

In a statement Poilievre said he went to New York to fight against tariffs and for jobs on both sides of the border.

He said he will be meeting with investors and business leaders but his "main audience is the American people" to which he is making the case "that both our countries can be safer, richer and more affordable if we trade freely."

Poilievre also said he will stay in New York for the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Friday, to honour the victims and highlight "how Canadians and Americans stood together after the terrorist attacks."

'Politics ends at the border': Poilievre

That national spirit was on display during Poilievre's CNBC interview, when he refused to be goaded into answering a question about whether he believed Prime Minister Mark Carney was acting in good faith during the recent round of trade negotiations.

"I'm not going to attack my prime minister on foreign soil. It's just not something I'm going to do," he said. "My mission here is to fight for my country, not to score political points domestically. Politics ends at the border."

Poilievre said Canada needs to leverage the "single biggest asset Canada has in the U.S., which is our friendship with the American people who overwhelmingly love Canada."

Co-host Joe Kernen said he respected Poilievre for refusing to criticize Carney while abroad, noting that politicians in opposition in the U.S. do not maintain that standard.

"You actually have a little bit of class," Kernen said.

When Kernen pressed Poilievre on Canada's economic performance over the last decade, the Conservative leader also avoided criticizing the country, saying Canada has had "a lot of good public policy successes by different levels of government."

Going forward Poilievre said rivals and risks to the U.S. are "slowly mounting" and rather than combat them on their own, the U.S. should rebuild the Western alliance that won the Cold War rather than fighting with friends.

"I think the United States would be better off if it united with those countries that believe in free speech, free markets, free trade and free people," he said.

"We could build an incredible North American fortress with the resources that we have on this continent, but it's going to take a collaborative relationship to do it."

World.title: 97-year-old Guelph, Ont., man skydives in quest to 'learn as much as I can about life'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Guelph's James Gordon, 97, recently went skydiving for the first time, jumping from about 4,200 metres. He spoke with CBC K-W’s Diego Pizarro about the experience and his desire to keep trying new things.

'An experience never to be forgotten': 97-year-old Guelph man goes skydiving

At 97, James Gordon of Guelph, Ont., is proving you’re never too old for a new adventure.

In his first time skydiving, the resident of the Village of Riverside Glen retirement community jumped from a plane at an altitude of 4,200 metres last month.

“I wanted to do it because it’s an unusual experience,” he said. “I just wanted the experience and to say I’ve done something else. I want to learn as much as I can about life.”

The retirement community partners with Skydive Swoop in Dundas so residents can try skydiving.

Gordon is the oldest resident to take on the challenge. He says the jump is part of his quest to live an “exciting and thrilling” life.

He said he was eager to get up in the air, but did begin having second thoughts the night before.

“I was really, really caught up with feeling very unsure if I wanted to continue. But my wife was there, so I behaved with a little bit of courage and just waited for the next morning.”

He said that when it came time to jump, he was no longer afraid.

“The next morning when I had to go get on the plane, my golly, I didn’t feel a thing. I was just interested."

'I feel that if you push yourself and you do things, you keep your mind working and you keep your body working, the more chance you have that you will live longer,' Gordon says. (Skydive SWOOP)

Taking the plunge

On Aug. 21, Gordon piled into a plane with three others.

He was strapped to an experienced skydiver.

During the leap, Gordon said, he was immediately caught off guard.

“I never knew I’d be tumbling, turning and twisting. I spun over, round and round, all over the place.”

Once he stabilized, he was able to enjoy the view.

“I really loved it, looking around, seeing things at a far distance. There were mountains, the hills, the lakes — everything you could wish to see."

Kimberly McCarthy, manifest manager at Skydive Swoop, said skydiving when older isn't as rare as some people may think.

Gordon hopes to skydive again we he turns 100. (Skydive SWOOP)

"There's no age limit on skydiving," McCarthy said. "There are quite a few people out there that are still skydiving regularly and they're in their 80s."

McCarthy believes Gordon is the oldest skydiver Swoop has ever had. She didn't get to see the jump itself, but she was there when he landed.

"We were really excited for him. We all came running up to him, and gave him handshakes and high-fives. It's getting me choked up just thinking about it. I'm kind of getting old there myself, and so it just kind of gave me the feeling that I still had a whole half of my life coming my way."

Gordon was caught off guard when be began spinning around after jumping from the plane. (Skydive SWOOP)

A life of adventure

Daring experiences have always been a part of Gordon's life.

For five years, he worked as a game warden in Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe.

His daughter, Gillian Bakar, said she remembers countless stories from her childhood.

"His dog was eaten by an alligator at some point. He ran from elephants and escaped from lions. He had serious adventure back when the wild was truly wild."

Gordon also made contact with a number of tribes and built relationships with members.

Gordon is shown in Zimbabwe, getting a bone reading about the trajectory of his life from a member of the Shangaan tribe. (Submitted by Gillian Bakar)

When it came time for Gordon to take to the sky instead of the jungle, Bakar said, there was no hesitation on her end.

"My first thought was at 97, if you want to have an adventure like that, absolutely run with it," she said.

"I just feel absolutely happy for him. He's managed to do something that he is so incredibly proud of."

As for what's next, Gordon hopes to publish a book recounting his adventures in the jungle.

The book has been over 50 years in the making.

"His lifelong wish has been to get that book published," Bakar said.

Always in search of the next thrill, Gordon said he plans to skydive again when he turns 100.

He believes his hunger for adventure is his secret to a long life.

"I feel that if you push yourself and you do things, you keep your mind working and you keep your body working, the more chance you have that you will live longer. And here I am at 97."

World.title: Canadian bank CEOs can't stop bragging about AI. Are job cuts next?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scotiabank CEO Scott Thomson says artificial intelligence saved his bank roughly 24,000 days' worth of work over about four and a half months. At TD Bank, CEO Raymond Chun recently said AI has reduced the time it takes to pre-process mortgages from about 15 hours to three minutes.

Canada's Big Five banks employ nearly 400,000 full-time-equivalent workers. That's more than double the number of employees in Canada's auto assembly and parts manufacturing industry. TD Bank workers alone outnumber Canada's active military force.

According to a study by Toronto Metropolitan University, 98 per cent of financial sector workers are highly exposed to AI technologies. That's far higher, they say, than the 56 per cent estimated for the Canadian workforce overall.

Last month, the Bank of Canada estimated that one‑third of jobs may "undergo substantial changes" because of AI integration, given today's capabilities. The central bank found that banking, insurance and other financial clerks are among the most exposed.

"AI is a big opportunity for us, a transformational opportunity both from an effectiveness, and an efficiency perspective," Thomson said on Wednesday at the annual Scotiabank Financials Summit in Toronto.

RBC CEO Dave McKay, who has led the bank since 2014, says AI is affecting every part of its business and that he uses it each morning to generate custom reports from RBC's internal data. (Kevin Van Paassen/Bloomberg)

His enthusiasm is shared by his C-suite peers.

"There isn't a part of our business that's not being impacted by AI," RBC CEO Dave McKay told an audience at an industry conference hosted by his bank earlier this year. At an event in June, he spoke about using AI every morning to generate custom reports based on RBC's internal data.

Last month, BMO CEO Darryl White said predictive AI modelling in his bank's insurance business can make underwriting decisions in as little as 10 seconds. The industry standard is at least 28 days, he noted.

Stock market analyst John Aiken covers the banking industry for New York-based Jefferies Financial Group. He sees top executives at Canada's Big Five — Royal Bank, TD Bank, Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank, and CIBC — brimming with excitement over the billions of dollars they've invested in AI in recent years.

What's unclear, he said, is how rank-and-file bank employees will feel the impact.

"This isn't a little pet project," Aiken told CBC News. "The funny thing is, it's the CEOs themselves that are bringing it up unprompted.

"Strangely enough, we're not seeing head count reductions from the banks. You're presumably going to see lesser demand for lower skilled workers ... the front-line staff at the branches."

OpenAI and Anthropic logos are seen in this illustration taken June 11, 2026. (Reuters/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo)

Questions about how AI will affect some of Canada's largest private employers come amid a much broader debate over how the technology could shape humanity as a whole.

Earlier this week, an artificial intelligence researcher quit his job at Anthropic, accusing the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of irresponsibly "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence."

On Tuesday, another Anthropic employee wrote on the social media platform X that, "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade."

On Wednesday, federal AI Minister Evan Solomon said "there are real concerns" at the frontier of AI development

WATCH | AI Minister Evan Solomon says AI safety a top priority: Existential warnings about AI 'are not new,' minister says | Duration 5:23 AI Minister Evan Solomon said 'there are real concerns' at the frontier of AI development, when asked about an Anthropic researcher who quit the firm, citing existential safety risks. 'Our No. 1 concern always is safety, full stop,' Solomon said.

Jon Pinkus, a partner at Samfiru Tamakin LLP who specializes in employment law, sees jobs at risk throughout the white-collar world because of AI. However, he said he has yet to see a clear-cut instance of humans being replaced.

"I have real generational anxieties for the incoming workforce. Not just this generation, but for generations to come," he said.

"I think there are going to be certain positions that just don't exist, particularly more junior positions, entry-level positions.

"A lot of those entry level tasks are the ones now being done by AI ... [it does] them well enough for many organizations to say, 'Why are we going to pay this person $80,000 per year?'"

Jeff Lanthier, director of media relations at RBC, told CBC News in response to questions about AI's impact on staffing levels that people and relationships would always be at the core of the bank's strategy.

"We see AI as an enhancement, not a replacement," Lanthier said.

The other Big Five banks did not respond to requests for comment in time for publication.

At its investor day last year, RBC announced plans to generate $700 million to $1 billion in enterprise value through AI-driven benefits by 2027. TD Bank is similarly targeting $1 billion in annual value from its artificial intelligence initiatives. Both banks have in-house AI research labs, called RBC Borealis and Layer 6, respectively.

CIBC president and CEO Harry Culham, left, greets German Vice-Chancellor and Federal Minister of Finance Lars Klingbeil before a CIBC roundtable with the German-Canadian Chamber of Industry and Commerce in Toronto, on Friday, May 8, 2026. (The Canadian Press/Sammy Kogan)

CIBC CEO sees staff levels rising

CIBC CEO Harry Culham said his bank's new AI workspace is more like a "co-worker" than a chatbot. Even so, he predicts the bank will add employees overall.

"We actually see head count growth over the next five years," CIBC CEO Harry Culham said on his bank's Aug. 27 earnings call with stock market analysts. "We're using it all over the entire organization, and we've got thousands and thousands of people being educated."

Kiridaran Kanagaretnam, an associate dean at York University's Schulich School of Business in Toronto, sees the Canadian banking industry's overall employee numbers drifting higher, absent a major financial crisis.

He recommends students pursue professional designations in accounting and finance to boost their value to employers.

"Everything is changing at a rapid rate," he said. "But that doesn't mean things are bleak."

World.title: N.L. residents helped Muslims feel safe amid post-9/11 prejudice, says association leader
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the anniversary of 9/11 marking 25 years, many are remembering the events that shook the world that morning in New York. For Muslims living in Newfoundland and Labrador, one says that September day brought out the best and the worst in people. But in the years that followed, Haseen Khan — the president of the Muslim Association of Newfoundland and Labrador — says the province’s Muslim community was supported by their neighbours. The CBC’s Adam Walsh reports.

When Haseen Khan looks back on his memories around the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, he often begins on the shock it brought.

It's a "grave wound" that is still open for many.

"It was beyond imagination. It was beyond anyone's imagination, that humanity can fall that low," Khan told CBC News Wednesday.

"A loss of one innocent life is loss of the entire humanity. And that's a very strong reminder, and that's what was going through our minds at that time."

But Khan also looks back on how it impacted Newfoundland and Labrador's Muslim community at the time.

Twenty-five years after the attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon, Khan is president of the Muslim Association of Newfoundland and Labrador. Back then, he was part of a growing population in the province — one that has grown from 50 people in 1989 to more than 4,000 residents as of the 2021 census.

He said he remembers the tragedy bringing out both the best and worst in people. It rallied the world closer together, he said, but it also changed how Muslims were viewed globally.

"These perpetrators, they associated themselves with Islamic faith. And that created lots of anxiety and fear among Muslims and, unfortunately, the entire community," Khan said.

"Sometimes, you see people react to the situation and they don't, kind of, respond to the situation. That kind of had some lasting impact that led to Islamophobia. And that resulted in, kind of, fear, injustice, and [a] sense of insecurity."

The attacks stoked fear across parts of Canada, which led to Muslims being targeted in some parts of the country.

A 2003 report from the Canadian Islamic Congress showed more than 170 anti-Muslim hate crimes were reported to the group in 2002 — a 1,600 per cent increase from the just 11 reports made in 2000.

In the days that followed Sept. 11, then-prime minister Jean Chretien publicly condemned the attacks while visiting a mosque in Ottawa, saying he turned his back on Canadians who took part in shaming or attacks.

Muslim people who spoke with CBC News in the years that followed shared they often faced threats while in the United States, questioning their safety, security and voicing a desire to find a new home where they could freely embrace their Muslim identity.

WATCH | Three Muslim people spoke with CBC News in 2021 about life as a Muslim post-9/11: Muslims in Canada on why they left the U.S. after 9/11 | Duration 6:06 The rise in Islamophobia in the U.S. after 9/11 prompted these three Muslims to move to Canada. Now after two decades, they see worrying signs emerging here.

But Khan said he also remembers the support that came from Newfoundlanders and Labradorians in the years that followed.

He's felt residents have historically been quick to support the community in times of need. He specifically cited support following a shooting at a mosque in Quebec City on Jan. 29, 2017, when residents formed a human chain around the St. John's mosque during prayers in the following days.

"Our fellow Newfoundlanders and Labradorians showed a very strong, kind of, support that, 'We are with you. You should not feel, you should not have any type of concern," Khan said.

"The support of local people and their welcoming attitude, I think that has been a source of reassurance and confidence."

The Suleman Dawood Mosque was opened in St. John's in 2025. What began as a community of around 50 people in the late-1980s has blossomed into a Muslim population upwards of 10,000 residents across Newfoundland and Labrador. (Katie Breen/CBC)

Looking ahead to Friday, Khan said he believes his thoughts will be on the response following the tragedy.

He encouraged other spiritual leaders to think the same, hoping the community can continue to invest in interfaith community building.

"In order to understand and respect our differences, and to find common ground for collaboration, [we have] to build a stronger, safer and united community so that future generations will inherit a world defined by unity. Not division."

World.title: Marvel's Wolverine is a relentlessly bloody game with a sincere soap opera at its heart
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

You can't fault Sony for continuing to expand its video game-specific take on the Marvel Universe.

Its Marvel's Spider-Man games for the PlayStation consoles, by veteran in-house studio Insomniac Games, have been some of the platform's best-selling and reviewed games and indeed some of the most successful open-world games over the past decade.

Now, they're following up with Marvel's Wolverine, a more grizzled take on their original continuity starring the Canadian(ish) antihero James Logan Howlett.

The result is a relentlessly paced action game that eschews an open world for constant forward momentum — and may initially shock players with the bloodiest combat seen in a modern comic book adaptation other than Ryan Reynolds's R-rated Deadpool films.

A linear story with a rapid pace

Marvel's Wolverine nominally takes place in the same world as Insomniac's Spider-Man games, but you won't see any shocking crossovers here — appropriate, as we're telling a very different story.

The X-Men as we know them don't exist in this story; instead, we join the grumpy mutant with metal claws and a healing ability as part of Team X, a small commando group also including shapeshifter Mystique and Sabretooth (like Logan but bigger and angrier) under the mentorship of Nathaniel Essex, who instantly gives off vibes of a more sinister analog to Professor X.

The young mutant Leech, left, meets Team X's leader Nathaniel Essex in Marvel's Wolverine. (Insomniac Games/Sony Interactive Entertainment)

You'll run into antagonists like Bolivar Trask, the scientist behind the mutant-hunting Sentinel robots, and Lady Deathstrike — Logan's sometimes-girlfriend, sometimes rival — here leading the Hand order of ninjas.

Instead of Spider-Man's open-world facsimile of Manhattan, Wolverine takes you more or less in a straight line through multiple locations including Tokyo and Marvel's fictional Southeast Asian nightlife town of Madripoor.

Longtime X-Men heroes and villains Mystique, Wolverine and Sabretooth begin the story as teammates. (Insomniac Games/Sony Interactive Entertainment)

It will take most players roughly 12 to 15 hours to complete, whereas players could feasibly stretch the Spider-Man games to nearly double that. This game feels more like a globetrotting action film, or a comic book miniseries with a new location or villain subplot for each chapter.

It's bloody … very bloody

Unlike the Spider-Man games' teen-rated combat, Wolverine uses his claws to full effect, earning the game's Mature rating and then some.

With just a few button presses, Logan eviscerates, dismembers and impales humanoid enemies with breathtaking speed and savagery, fountains of blood splattering the landscape and his uniform alike.

Combat in Marvel's Wolverine is fast, brutal and very, very bloody. (Insomniac Games/Sony Interactive Entertainment)

Combat is fluid and mostly intuitive to the player, with most attacks mapped to the square and triangle face buttons; combining the controller's triggers and other buttons activates powered-up moves like spinning Logan's claws in a cyclone, or launching himself like a flying drill.

Most important is maintaining momentum; by continuously leaping at enemies and parrying incoming attacks you'll build up a rage meter that increases your damage and unlocks critical strikes that dispatch most low-level goons in one hit. Slow down your approach and you'll lose most of the bonuses, making things harder in the long run.

The game isn't as bloody when Wolverine uses his claws on mutant-hunting Sentinel robots. He does the same thing to squishier human enemies, though. Use your imagination if you really need to. (Insomniac Games/Sony Interactive Entertainment)

You'll break up the fighting with quieter moments like exploring Team X's headquarters or mingling with mutants at the Princess bar in Madripoor, but don't expect complex multilayered espionage like in the recent 007 First Light. They're mostly just there to give you a breather before you're thrown into yet another wave of enemies to eviscerate.

This is a Jean Grey story, too

Anyone familiar with Wolverine's lore across the screen and pages will know that he's often caught in a love triangle with fellow X-Men Cyclops and Jean Grey.

Jean, the uber-powerful user of telepathy and telekinesis, is the most important supporting character of this saga, while Cyclops is completely absent.

Fellow mutants on the run Jean Grey and Logan a.k.a. Wolverine share a rare quiet moment in the fictional Marvel city of Madripoor. (Insomniac Games/Sony Interactive Entertainment)

That makes way for a love story with more complexity than usual between Logan and Jean that slowly becomes the centrepiece of the game's narrative.

Jean will also accompany Logan through much of the back half of the game, levitating rubble to make traversable paths or aiding the player in combat by trapping enemies in place for you to attack, for example.

Canada in the (brief) spotlight

Most versions of Wolverine are nominally Canadian, having been born in Alberta and serving as part of the country's secret Weapon X program and crossing paths with Alpha Flight — the Canadian equivalent to the Avengers.

None of that history is relevant here, but we do spend some time in the Canadian North, where Team X's secret headquarters is based. You'll also take a walk in the snow before downing some off-brand Canadian rye whisky in Logan's log cabin, and first meet Jean in Vancouver before leaping into a motorcycle chase sequence along the Sea-to-Sky Highway.

Wolverine takes a brief walk through the snow on the way to his log cabin, but it's not long before the fighting begins again. (Insomniac Games/Sony Interactive Entertainment)

Insomniac's art directors went to great lengths to make sure the landscape was accurately portrayed, including the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh sníchim (Squamish language) on highway signs.

The action moves so fast and furiously in this sequence, though, that you likely won't notice them as you leap from truck to truck and fling enemies to their deaths.

WATCH | New Wolverine video game includes several parts of B.C.: Marvel's Wolverine video game features Squamish Nation's language | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 7:01 The new Marvel's Wolverine video game features B.C. landmarks and Sḵwx̱wú7mesh sníchim, the Squamish Nation's language, on highway signs. Senior art director Gavin Goulden explains why including the language was important for authentically representing the region.

A narrative that outpaces the gameplay

Insomniac's Spider-Man games stood out for their stories that remixed well-known characters' origins in a way that can surprise even the most well-read comic book fan, and Wolverine is no different.

(While review spoiler guidelines prevent a full account of the story, it does some novel things with Jean's background that X-Men fans will either find intriguing or infuriating.)

It's easy to get sucked into the game's final chapters and narrative crescendo — to the point that when the non-interactable cutscenes end and you're thrown back into control, it can feel like an obligation or a chore.

Some cutscenes have a cinematic style that feels plucked from an action film, and other brief shots take a slow-motion pause to pay homage to certain famous pages or cover art from Marvel's comic books. (Insomniac Games/Sony Interactive Entertainment)

It doesn't help that some boss fights, while visually spectacular, aren't mechanically different enough from other fights; they just take longer to pummel into submission.

It's a credit to Insomniac's visuals and direction team that I found myself thinking about the actors' performances as much as I have for any other narrative-heavy game.

Most of the main characters' faces are based at least somewhat on their performance actors' real-life likenesses. They're animated with impressive realism — Liam McIntyre's Wolverine in particular emotes with convincing rage and puppy-dog empathy alike, especially opposite Krizia Bajos's Jean Grey.

They impart a whiff of the uncanny valley, though, as the rest of the world feels ripped from the more stylized pages of a modern comic book.

Logan finds a mask worn by an enemy from The Hand order of ninjas after a particularly bloody battle. (Insomniac Games/Sony Interactive Entertainment)

Despite the shorter run time and narrower scope, Insomniac did not water down the experience for its first X-Men foray. Indeed, Marvel's Wolverine might be the purest distillation of the character's gnarliest comic book appearances — heavy on the uncensored violence but also the yearning soap opera at the core of many X-stories.

If you have a PlayStation 5 — and the stomach for a bloodier outing than most — it's not one to miss.

Marvel's Wolverine is available exclusively for Sony's PlayStation 5 and PlayStation 5 Pro on Sept. 15.

World.title: Ontario premier announces cabinet shuffle, moves embattled labour minister to infrastructure profile
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford made several changes to his cabinet Thursday, including moving embattled minister David Piccini from the labour portfolio to infrastructure.

Piccini is under investigation by the integrity commissioner after the auditor general raised questions about his handling of the $2.5-billion Skills Development Fund.

Ford has defended Piccini and the success of the fund.

Kinga Surma, who previously served as the minister of infrastructure, is now the Treasury Board president, a role left vacant after Caroline Mulroney resigned earlier this year.

Trevor Jones, who had served in the agriculture portfolio, is the new labour minister, and Sam Oosterhoff moves from an associate minister role to fill the agriculture job.

Zee Hamid, who was previously the associate minister of auto theft and bail reform, becomes the new minister of tourism, culture and gaming, after Stan Cho resigned from the job as he came under fire for spending $16,000 in Toronto hotel stays despite living in the city.

In a news release, the province said the associate minister of auto theft and bail reform's mandate had been fulfilled after changes were implemented to Ontario's bail system and auto theft rates decreased provincially.

Brian Saunderson, a former Olympic rower, becomes the new minister of sport, a portfolio left vacant after Neil Lumsden retired last month.

The new role of associate minister of artificial intelligence adoption has been created and is being filled by MPP Vijay Thanigasalam. The province's release stated the role would help businesses adopt new technology and help workers displaced by AI adoption.

Ford's office framed the announcement as putting Ontario on solid ground amid U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with ombudsman over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.
