World.title: How Celine Dion became a pop culture icon across generations
World.content:
As the global star kicks off her anticipated Paris residency, here's how Celine Dion managed to gain younger followers while keeping her loyal older fans.

On September 12, Celine Dion kicks off a series of 26 sold-out concerts, part of a Paris residency held through May 2027. Some 500,000 people are expected to attend the performances, marking the global star's highly anticipated return to the stage following a prolonged break.

In 2022, she announced that she was battling a rare and incurable neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome. The health issues led her to cancel her world tour.

In the summer of 2024, she returned to the spotlight atop the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics, her resilience giving hope to fans worldwide.

Now, in the days ahead of her Paris concerts, Dion has been thrilling hundreds of fans gathered in front of her hotel, taking the time to chat with them for a few minutes every day, sometimes even joining them in spontaneous sing-alongs and dances.

Charming her fans with candid moments at the Royal Monceau Hotel in Paris Image: Cyril Pecquenard/SIPA/picture alliance

The best-selling Canadian artist of all time, Dion has released a total of 27 studio albums, sold more than 200 million records worldwide and earned multiple Grammy Awards.

Even though her most defining hits date back to the 1990s, she is more than a nostalgia act, as her appeal is now skyrocketing with Gen Z and millennial listeners.

How did that happen?

'It's All Coming Back to Me Now:' Her power ballads are surging in popularity again Image: Joel Goodman/ZUMA/picture alliance

A modern fashion darling

In her daily exchanges with her fans on her way to rehearsal, she's always wearing fresh couture pieces: an asymmetrical Loewe gown, a bold blue Givenchy leather dress by Sarah Burton or a striking jacket by Tom Ford.

"Celine Dion is turning the streets of Paris into her runway," wrote Vogue magazine in reaction to her stylish outfits.

"She's always really been into fashion, already in the 1990s, even though we long didn't know this," says Quebec cultural reporter Stephane Leclair, author and host of a podcast series on the star's "D'eux" album. "You know, Celine Dion was never considered 'cool.' She's always had that slightly corny, slightly goofy side. But through her genuine interest for fashion, she’s managed to revamp her image quite a bit."

A notable move came in 2016: Dion admired Zendaya's edgy red carpet looks so much that she tracked down her stylist, Law Roach, and asked him to team up with her. She credits Roach with transforming her into a modern fashion darling.

But that's just one aspect that explains her ongoing — and renewed — popularity.

A rags to riches story

Born on March 30, 1968, Celine Dion was the youngest of 14 children of a poor family in French-speaking in Quebec, Canada. As she proudly notes on her official website, the house was so full that, as a baby, she had to sleep in a drawer instead of a crib.

She grew up surrounded by music, and recorded her first song at the age of 12. It impressed music manager Rene Angelil so much that he mortgaged his house to pay for her first record. She quickly emerged as a child star in Quebec.

Her winning performance at the Eurovision Song Contest in 1988 Image: dpa/picture alliance

Inspired by Michael Jackson, she decided that she wanted to become a megastar. She won the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 1988 and launched her first English-language album, "Unison," in 1990.

This, however, sparked cultural tension among French-speaking fans in Quebec, who felt she was neglecting her roots to pursue American and international superstardom.

"We were between two referendums on Quebec's independence at the time," points out Leclair.

But even after she became a global star, Dion proudly kept identifying as the "little girl from Charlemagne," the small town near Montreal where she grew up.

"People in Quebec quickly understood that it didn't change anything, that she would always remain one of them, and that it only added another layer to her career," notes Leclair.

Indeed, she also kept working in French all while building her career as a global pop artist. Teaming up with popular French song-writer Jean-Jacques Goldman, they released "D'eux" in 1995. It became the best-selling French-language album of all time.

The theme song for "Beauty and the Beast" (1991) won her both a Grammy and an Academy Award, while her best-selling "My Heart Will Go On" (1997) for the blockbuster film "Titanic" cemented her status alongside music's greatest vocalists.

Adding groundbreaking edge to Las Vegas

While other aging stars would head to the Las Vegas Strip to finish their careers, Dion revolutionized the music industry with "A New Day...," her high-profile residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace: With a total of 714 performances from 2003 to 2007, she demonstrated how such residencies could be modern, cutting-edge — and extremely lucrative.

It served as a blueprint for Las Vegas residencies by younger stars, such as Britney Spears and Adele.

Viral authenticity

"The world's biggest stars are often dead set on protecting a perfect, untouchable image. Celine, on the other hand, is incredibly accessible. She isn't afraid to let her true, authentic personality shine through," points out Leclair.

"And Celine's die-hard fans just love her humorous side," he adds. "They love the fact that she's a bit wacky. It makes her really relatable."

Famous for spontaneously breaking into song during interviews, those moments, as well as various over-the-top scenes from her 1990s music videos, have been picked up in Internet memes and TikTok trends.

Encouraged by her teenage sons, she launched her own official TikTok account in January 2026. She went viral with a "What's in My Bag?" video where she pulls out a mix of everyday essentials and completely unhinged items.

Writing a new chapter

But beyond the humor, she's also ready to share her most vulnerable moments.

In 2016, she lost her husband — her manager, Rene Angelil — and a brother to cancer within the same week. Her 2019 album "Courage" focused on loss and recovery.

Their 26-year age gap and the fact that Dion was only 12 when she met her manager and future husband made headlines, but they stayed together until his death Image: Ryan Remiorz/empics/picture alliance

Her 2024 documentary "I am: Celine Dion," in which she looks back on her life and career all while addressing how she deals with her stiff-person syndrome diagnosis, has been praised by critics as intensely sincere and visceral.

One scene of the film follows her as she suffers from a painful spasm.

"I don't think many stars of that caliber would have agreed to be filmed — and have the footage included in the final cut — in such an unflattering state," notes Leclair. "It was partly out of a desire for transparency, to explain to her fans why she had to step back."

And her fans highly value this authenticity, as well as her resilience.

She is now undergoing physical and therapies to manage her symptoms and be able to perform again for this series of more than 2-hour-long concerts. They will feature 18 musicians and four backing singers; a live choir will also join them on stage for several songs.

Additionally, Paris will mark the start of the concert series with two giant karaoke sessions on September 11. A total of 10,000 people are expected to take part in the participatory event celebrating her four decades of songs.

Edited by: Sarah Hucal

World.title: El Supremo ve en la ‘ley de nietos’ un “peligro fundado, real y serio” de afectar a la “objetividad” de las elecciones
World.content:
La Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo ha notificado los autos por los que suspendió el derecho al voto de los nacionalizados por la Ley de Memoria Democrática

El Tribunal Supremo considera que la inscripción en el censo electoral de los nacionalizados por la Ley de Memoria Democrática, la llamada ley de nietos, genera “un peligro fundado, real y serio de poder afectar gravemente a la objetividad y transparencia del proceso electoral”. Y esa posibilidad causaría “un daño irreversible a la rectitud y corrección de aquel”, sostiene el Supremo, que teme que otorgar el derecho al voto a los nuevos nacionalizados afecte al “resultado electoral deseado por los españoles que ya figuran inscritos correctamente en el censo electoral”. Así lo expone la Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo en los autos que han dado lugar a la suspensión del derecho al voto de quienes han obtenido la nacionalidad por ser hijos o nietos de españoles que abandonaron el país entre el 18 de julio de 1936 y el 31 de diciembre de 1955. La magistrada Alicia Millán ha emitido un voto particular en el que discrepa de sus compañeros.

El alto tribunal anunció este martes una decisión que ha dejado en el aire el voto de las más de 2,4 millones de personas que han pedido acogerse a la ley de nietos y que ha causado un enorme terremoto político y jurídico y ha avivado las críticas del Gobierno al Poder Judicial, una situación que este jueves ha reprochado la presidenta del alto tribunal, Isabel Perelló, en el acto de apertura del año judicial. Pero faltaba por conocerse el contenido de los autos en los que el Supremo acuerda esa controvertida medida. En estos escritos (uno en respuesta al recurso planteado por Vox y otro al del partido Iustitia Europa) la sala argumenta su decisión en que la posibilidad de obtener la nacionalidad que abre la ley de nietos va a suponer un “incremento extraordinario” del Censo Electoral de Residentes Ausentes (CERA) que pone en riesgo la transparencia del proceso electoral, lo que aconseja suspender el derecho a voto de esos españoles hasta que el Supremo resuelva sobre el fondo del litigio planteado por los dos partidos de ultraderecha.

El pleito abierto por Vox e Iustitia Europa se dirige contra un acuerdo de julio pasado de la Junta Electoral Central (JEC), que rechazó pronunciarse sobre los efectos electorales de la Ley de Memoria Democrática. Esta norma, aprobada en octubre de 2022, establece que “los nacidos fuera de España de padre o madre, abuelo o abuela, que originariamente hubieran sido españoles, y que, como consecuencia de haber sufrido exilio por razones políticas, ideológicas o de creencia o de orientación e identidad sexual, hubieran perdido o renunciado a la nacionalidad española, podrán optar a la nacionalidad española”.

Entrada de la Embajada de España en Ciudad de México (México), este martes. Sáshenka Gutiérrez (EFE)

Seis días después, el 25 de octubre, el Ministerio de Justicia dictó una instrucción con las “directrices” sobre cómo debía interpretarse la ley en las oficinas del Registro Civil para otorgar las nacionalidades. Y este nuevo texto estableció que no hacía falta acreditar ser hijo o nieto de exiliado, sino que “se presumirá” esa condición a “todos los españoles que salieron de España entre el 18 de julio de 1936 y el 31 de diciembre de 1955″. La inscripción inmediata en el CERA de los nacionalizados bajo el paraguas de esta instrucción es la que ahora ha limitado el alto tribunal hasta que dicte sentencia sobre el recurso presentado por los dos partidos de ultraderecha.

El Supremo da por buenos los datos de incremento del censo que aportó en su recurso Iustitua Europa, que cifra en 408.262 los nuevos inscritos en el CERA desde las elecciones generales de 2023 hasta el 1 de julio de 2026. Sin avanzar cuál va a ser la decisión que finalmente adopte sobre los efectos electorales de la ley de nietos, el tribunal advierte de que ese “progresivo incremento del CERA” fruto de la interpretación que la instrucción del Ministerio de Justicia hizo sobre la norma aprobada por el Parlamento, “no parece ajustarse, tampoco, al contenido de la propia norma legal que interpreta”. La decisión ha sido acordada por cinco de los seis magistrados que han debatido el recurso: Luis María Díez-Picazo, Antonio Jesús Fonseca-Herrero, José Luis Requero, Manuel Delgado-Iribarren y Antonio Narváez.

Los autos del alto tribunal estiman parcialmente la medida cautelar que habían solicitado Vox y Iustitia, que en una vista celebrada el pasado lunes acusaron al Gobierno de estar inflando el censo de forma irregular con descendientes de emigrados durante la dictadura. La Fiscalía y la Abogacía del Estado rechazaron ese extremo y advirtieron de que la admisión de la suspensión cautelar supondría restringir para miles de nacionalizados el derecho al voto, un derecho fundamental recogido en la Constitución.

Uno de los argumentos que emplearon los dos partidos de ultraderecha es que, si el CERA sigue acogiendo a españoles nacionalizados por la ley de nietos y el Supremo acaba declarando irregular todas o algunas de esas inscripciones en el censo, se puede producir un daño irreversible en el proceso electoral. Y el Supremo ha acogido esta tesis e invoca el principio del “periculum in mora” (“peligro en la demora”), que rige en los tribunales para la adopción de una medida cautelar. Los magistrados consideran que, en este caso, se aprecia “la existencia de un riesgo” de “alteración del censo electoral por la vía de un incremento excepcional de la cifra de nuevos inscritos en el CERA, que afecta también a su regularidad jurídica”.

El tribunal recalca la necesidad de preservar “la corrección, claridad y transparencia de todo el proceso electoral y, en concreto, del censo correspondiente”, como un “presupuesto indispensable” para el ejercicio del derecho de sufragio y “para la eficacia y prevalencia de la expresión de la voluntad popular”. “Por la magnitud de las cifras de incremento del CERA ofrecidas, la afectación al derecho de sufragio y al resultado electoral deseado por los españoles que ya figuran inscritos correctamente en el censo electoral, podrían quedar también gravemente comprometidos”, apunta.

Frente a esto, señalan los magistrados, cualquier medida cautelar que se pueda adoptar para asegurar “la eficacia” de la futura sentencia sobre el recurso planteado por Vox y Iustitia, “tendrá un carácter meramente temporal”, de tal manera que el efecto sobre el derecho al voto de los ya inscritos en el CERA o quienes hayan solicitado estarlo “no resulta desproporcionado en relación con los intereses generales” que se trata de preservar.

Además de cuestionar la interpretación de la Ley de Memoria que hizo la orden de Justicia, el tribunal ve también “una controversia jurídica seria y fundada sobre la naturaleza, alcance y contenido del acuerdo de la JEC” impugnado por Vox y Iustitia. Los jueces creen que la postura del órgano electoral a fiscalizar “pudiera no corresponderse con las competencias de control funcional y de dirección y supervisión” de la Oficina del Censo Electoral que la ley confiere a la Junta.

World.title: ¿Puede el casero obligarme a contratar un seguro del hogar que incluya responsabilidad civil por daños a terceros?
World.content:
Pregunta. ¿Es legal que en un contrato de alquiler de vivienda haya una cláusula que obligue al arrendatario a contratar y costear un seguro del hogar? Si lo es, ¿puede dicha cláusula obligar al arrendatario a asegurar el continente de la vivienda o su obligación se limitaría a asegurar el contenido?, ¿y estaría el arrendatario obligado a que su seguro del hogar incluya responsabilidad civil por daños a terceros? Pedro Milla

Respuesta. Sí, es legal que un contrato de arrendamiento incluya una cláusula que obligue al inquilino a contratar y asumir el coste de un seguro de hogar, siempre que ambas partes lo pacten de forma voluntaria al firmar el contrato.

No se trata de una obligación impuesta por la ley. La Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos (LAU) no exige al inquilino la contratación de un seguro de hogar. Esta posibilidad se fundamenta en el principio de libertad de pactos recogido en el artículo 4 de la LAU: “Respetando lo establecido en el apartado anterior, los arrendamientos de vivienda se regirán por los pactos, cláusulas y condiciones determinados por la voluntad de las partes, en el marco de lo establecido en el título II de la presente ley y, supletoriamente, por lo dispuesto en el Código Civil”. En este mismo sentido, y al amparo de lo dispuesto en el artículo 20 de la LAU y en el artículo 1255 del Código Civil, las partes pueden establecer las cláusulas y condiciones que consideren oportunas, siempre que no sean contrarias a la ley. Por tanto, si el contrato se firma incluyendo esta obligación, el inquilino deberá cumplirla.

Respecto al objeto del seguro, lo habitual es que el inquilino asegure el contenido de la vivienda, es decir, sus pertenencias, muebles, electrodomésticos y demás enseres de su propiedad. Por su parte, el continente (paredes, techos e instalaciones fijas) corresponde, en principio, al propietario como titular del inmueble. No obstante, como hemos indicado, es válido que las partes acuerden expresamente que el arrendatario contrate o asuma una póliza que cubra también el continente, o parte de este, si así se establece en el contrato.

En cuanto a la obligación de incluir una cláusula de responsabilidad civil es totalmente legal y, además, muy frecuente en la práctica. Esta cobertura protege al inquilino frente a los daños que pueda causar accidentalmente a terceros, como una fuga de agua que afecte a una vivienda colindante o un incendio originado en el inmueble arrendado. En ausencia de esta cobertura, el arrendatario deberá responder personalmente con su patrimonio de los daños y perjuicios que pudiera ocasionar.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Por qué hay que visitar Enciña da Lastra: no parece Galicia, pero lo es
World.content:
Una encina gigante da nombre al parque natural más desconocido y sorprendente de la comunidad, de clima y paisaje mediterráneos. Es la puerta de entrada a la comarca de Valdeorras, donde se hacen excelentes mieles, vinos y aceites

Si uno se duerme yendo a Galicia por la autovía A-6 a la altura de Ponferrada (León) y el que conduce se desvía sin previo aviso por la carretera N-120 y lo despierta solo un cuarto de hora después en el mirador de Cobas (Ourense), creerá que está en el cielo, porque lo que ve es paradisíaco: un ancho río que no sospecha que es el Sil represado en el embalse de Peñarrubia, en cuya tersa superficie se refleja como sobre un espejo el sol naciente y un cañón bordado de árboles majestuosos y riscos dorados. Lo que no creerá, desde luego, es que está ya en Galicia, porque los árboles no son eucaliptos, sino encinas. Los riscos no son de granito o de pizarra —lo habitual allí—, sino de roca caliza. Y aquel alimoche común que sobrevuela este idílico panorama es tan poco gallego como una tortilla de patata con cebolla, muy hecha y sin sal.

Lo que descubre el viajero desde el mirador de Cobas no parece Galicia. Pero lo es. Es Enciña da Lastra, el parque natural más desconocido de la región, de clima mediterráneo y sustrato calizo, un paraíso de las orquídeas —hay 25 especies— y una puerta de entrada magnífica a la comarca de Valdeorras. Parque y comarca son el extremo oriente de Galicia, donde Ourense linda con León y Zamora. Tan extremo oriente es que se parece más a Castilla y León que a la propia Galicia. Al mejor amigo del hombre, los valdeorreses le dicen perro, no can. A la ventana, ventana, no fiestra. Al vino sí lo llaman viño, pero para conservarlo tienen tropecientas bodegas subterráneas, como si esto fuera la Ribera del Duero. Y lo dicho: en lugar de eucaliptos, que no hay monte en Galicia sin ellos, lo que uno encuentra al entrar en Valdeorras son majestuosas encinas, las que dan nombre al parque natural.

La guardiana de un tesoro oculto

Poco más abajo del mirador de Cobas —o de Covas, pues de las dos formas se escribe—, en la última curva que hace la carretera antes de entrar en la aldea del mismo nombre, proyecta su sombra de 25,60 metros de diámetro una encina monstruosa de 16,90 de altura y con un perímetro de 8,80 en la base de su tronco trifurcado. Es la Aciñeira de Covas o Enciño de Fontenouva, el único ejemplar de Quercus ilex reconocido y protegido por la Xunta de Galicia como árbol singular, y eso que hay 151 catalogados de otras especies. Esta encina de edad incalculable —entre 200 y 500 años— es la guardiana de la aldea, del parque natural y de la comarca. Y, según dicen, también de un tesoro oculto entre las rocas calizas donde hunde sus raíces. Allí, cuentan, lo escondieron o dejaron olvidado los mouros, seres fantásticos de la mitología gallega que habitaban bajo tierra rodeados de riquezas antes de que llegaran los humanos.

La encina centenaria que da nombre al parque de Enciña da Lastra. Andrés Campos

En Cobas se puede bajar paseando en 10 minutos a la orilla del embalse para refrescarse en las aguas del Sil y para ver somormujos lavancos, garzas reales y, en septiembre y octubre, cuando pasan camino de sus cuarteles de invierno andaluces y africanos, águilas pescadoras. O bien echarse a andar por la pista forestal que es prolongación de la calle principal y que va ganando suavemente altura, a unos 200 metros sobre la superficie del embalse, hasta Vilardesilva. Son unas tres horas de camino, siguiendo una ruta circular sencilla de 11 kilómetros.

Si somos más de ir observando la flora y la fauna que de andar por andar, con llegar hasta un antiguo horno de cal que hay a media hora del inicio ya está bien. Por el camino y al pie mismo del calero, florecen en primavera la orquídea araña (Ophrys sphegodes) y la piramidal (Anacamptis pyramidalis), dos de las especies más llamativas de este orquidario natural, y en un escarpe calizo que hay poco antes de cruzar el arroyo de Pereda y de avistar la enorme mole troncocónica del viejo horno, arraigan plantas como la Armeria rothmaleri y la Petrocoptis grandiflora, que no lo hacen en ningún otro lugar del planeta.

El antiguo horno de cal en el parque natural Enciña da Lastra. Andrés Campos

Hay que acercarse también al centro de visitantes del parque natural, en Biobra, donde se informa con detalle de cuanto hay en él y de las rutas más curiosas, como la de Tras os Penedos —la mejor para observar mariposas— o la de As Dúas Vertentes. Recorriendo esta última, se ven en lontananza las minas romanas de Las Médulas y, en el cielo, el alimoche común, que en Galicia es un ave muy poco común, valga la redundancia. Si se viaja en un grupo de al menos ocho personas, se puede hacer las rutas acompañados por un guía del centro de visitantes sin pagar nada, solo escribiendo con antelación a su correo electrónico (servizo.conservacion.natureza.ourense@xunta.gal). Pero hay que tener en cuenta que el centro solo abre de jueves a domingo y que echa el cierre desde mediados de septiembre hasta Semana Santa. Así no es de extrañar que este sea uno de los parques naturales más desconocidos de España.

Dos pueblos ‘enxebres’: Vilardesilva y Pardollán

Además de la naturaleza inaudita de Enciña da Lastra, en el centro aconsejan visitar Vilardesilva y Pardollán, dos de los pueblos más enxebres, más auténticos, con más encanto del parque y de Valdeorras, una región donde el desarrollismo y los marmolistas han causado estragos. El feísmo apenas ha hecho mella en ellos.

Una de las calles del pueblo de Vilardesilva. Andrés Campos

En Vilardesilva abundan las casas de piedra caliza bien labrada, con galerías de madera hermosamente tallada y con buenas historias a sus espaldas. Historias como la que fue propiedad de Paco González, que emigró con sus padres a Alemania, donde fue fontanero y luego payaso —el primero titulado de Europa—, y que volvió regularmente en verano a esta aldea de su Valdeorras natal para hacer un alojamiento rural —Chao do Prao— y dar cursos de clown. Así, hasta que Paco murió en 2017 y su casa rural y su escuela se perdieron. El cercano mirador da Cruz es un buen lugar para olvidarse del triste final del sueño de verano de Paco, admirando el paisajazo —el espolón calizo de Peñarrubia aflorando de las aguas quietas del Sil como la aleta dorsal de los peces acorazados que poblaban este rincón de Galicia hace 400 millones de años, cuando era un cálido mar tropical— y oliendo a tomillo salsero, una planta tan exótica en Ourense como un clown valdeorrés en Alemania.

Pardollán, por su parte, tiene un lugar especialmente cuidado, que justifica por sí solo la visita: la céntrica plaza donde todos los vecinos —43; 10 más que Vilardesilva— beben y llenan sus regaderas en una preciosa fuente de tres caños, rodeada de macetas floridas, pinturas murales y casas con galerías azules. Este colorido rincón, más que de una aldea del interior de Galicia, diríase de un pueblo marinero de las Rías Altas.

El pueblo gallego de Pardollán. Andrés Campos

La ‘alvariza’ que surgió del fuego

En el centro de visitantes del parque también recomiendan, si se va a pasar más de un día en la zona, acercarse a conocer la empresa apícola familiar O Marquesado, en O Porto. “Apicultores desde 1896”, reza un cartel en la fachada de la casa-taller, pero enseguida se da uno cuenta, viendo y oyendo a los dueños, Antonia Franco y Jens Kleinwächter, de que no llevan tanto tiempo en esto y tampoco en Valdeorras. Antonia, hija de emigrantes gallegos en Alemania­ —y prima de Paco, el clown—, volvió hace 12 años a la tierra de su padre con su marido y ambos decidieron seguir el dulce oficio del tío de ella, que iba a retirarse.

Antonia Franco en el taller de miel de O Marquesado, en O Porto. Andrés Campos

El caso es que hacen lo mismo que otras cuatro generaciones de apicultores de su familia —una miel con un sabor especial, gracias al microclima mediterráneo de este rincón de Ourense—, pero con una técnica y una precisión alemanas, como se ve en la limpieza y el orden del taller, de la tienda y de la sala de catas. “En Alemania”, explica Jens, “aprendimos a trabajar con la dócil abeja cárnica y aquí tuvimos que aprender de nuevo con la negra ibérica, que es mucho más nerviosa, más defensiva, más brava”. Una abeja a la que no tranquiliza y vuelve más manejable y productiva el cambio climático y tampoco los graves incendios que sufrió la comarca en 2020 y 2025. “Mi tío”, explica ahora Antonia, “producía siete toneladas al año con 150 colmenas. Nosotros, con el doble, solo cuatro”.

Para compensar, y porque no saben parar, estos emprendedores de cabeza alemana y corazón español llevan a los visitantes que lo desean a hacer de apicultores por un día en alguno de los terrenos donde tienen sus 300 colmenas. Por el camino, van parando aquí y allá para admirar los soutos, montes de castaños productivos que han sido estos últimos años eficacísimos cortafuegos. En una ladera no tan limpia, la maleza ardió como la yesca en agosto de 2025, durante el incendio más grande registrado hasta entonces en España, y entonces apareció una alvariza, una muralla circular que se usaba hace más de un siglo para defender las colmenas de los osos. “Un convenio entre la Xunta y la Fundación Reina Sofía”, informa Jens, “va a permitir recuperar en breve esta estructura patrimonial: nosotros la devolveremos a la vida, llenándola de colmenas. Ya solo queda abrir un camino para poder llegar en un 4x4 allá arriba”. Mientras tanto, Jens lleva a los apituristas al pie del monte donde reapareció la alvariza, en Oulego, y la observa de lejos con la mano en el corazón.

Jens Kleinwächter, frente a la 'alvariza' de Oulego. Andrés Campos

Beber en una cueva y comer en otra

Otra cosa que se hacía en Valdeorras desde siempre, además de miel, es vino, pero poca gente de fuera se fijaba en esta denominación de origen hasta que uno de Rafael Palacios, Sorte O Soro 2020, obtuvo 100 puntos en la guía Robert Parker Wine Advocate. Ahora todo el mundo vuelve los ojos y los paladares hacia esta comarca y alucina con sus montes llenos de vides de Godello —la uva autóctona, la más apreciada, con la que se elaboran vinos frescos, afrutados y elegantes, que se beben solos— y de cuevas. Se decía que había muchas, más de mil cuevas, y un reciente estudio de Carina Rodríguez y Cristina de la Torre, As covas de Valdeorras, ha confirmado que no es una exageración: han catalogado 1.103.

Una cueva bien conservada, que da gusto visitar, es la de Adega Melillas, una bodega familiar creada a principios de siglo por emigrantes retornados de Suiza a su pueblo natal, A Rúa. ¿Y por qué se llama Melillas? Pues porque así llamaba al abuelo de Sonia Prada —copropietaria, gerente y quien explica la saga a los enoturistas—, que hizo la mili en Melilla. Arriba se degustan y se compran los vinos —el mejor, el Lagar do Cigur Godello 2025— y abajo se entra casi a tientas en la cueva, que no es de clara roca caliza, sino de negra pizarra. Cuando los ojos se acostumbran a la oscuridad, se descubre una de las cuevas más altas de Valdeorras, con techos de más de cuatro metros, donde antiguamente el vino se conservaba bien en los veranos de clima tan poco gallego de esta comarca, igual que en una vinoteca.

Sonia Prada en la cueva de bodega Melillas, en A Rúa. Andrés Campos

Mayor aún es una cueva de Seadur, la segunda que vale la pena visitar: tan grande es, que cabe en ella un restaurante, Cova da Xabreira, con 42 comensales dando cuenta en sus mesas de las berenjenas con queso de O Cebreiro y miel de O Marquesado, el chuletón de vaca madurada Simmental y cuanto va saliendo de las brasas. Para beber, nada como el rosado Viñas de Seadur As Fontelas que elabora la misma propiedad con la autóctona y muy escasa uva brancellao. Y para elucubrar en la sobremesa: ¿cómo abrirían semejante boquete en la roca madre del monte? Porque es puro granito. No hay huellas de barrenos. Fue a pico.

Dormir a orillas del Bibei y del Sil

Después de mucho comer y elucubrar, no es mala idea dirigirse a As Ermidas, en O Bolo, para dar una cabezada en la playa fluvial del río Bibei, el principal afluente del Sil por su orilla izquierda, o un paseo por los alrededores, viendo cómo Diego de la Torre cuida los viejos olivos que se retuercen en las escarpadas márgenes, muchos de los cuales debieron de ser plantados en 1624, cuando se creó el santuario barroco de As Ermitas que hay en lo alto. Con las aceitunas que con arduos trabajos obtiene de estos y otros olivos centenarios de Valdeorras, Diego produce con cuentagotas el AOVE Terras Gigurras, que sale a 56 euros el litro y se agota en un amén. Ahora mismo hay que esperar dos meses a que los olivos y este oleicultor heroico hagan más.

Quien quiera algo más que una siesta en bañador —una con pijama—, puede volver a Seadur y alojarse en A Rectoral, la casona de 1783 donde vivía y prácticamente teletrabajaba el cura de la localidad: solo tenía que levantar la voz para decir misa en la vecina iglesia. El lugar, que tenía también algo de cueva, con sillares ciclópeos y rincones sombríos por doquier, ha sido reformado a fondo y decorado alegremente por sus propietarios, Isabel Val y Lucas Presedo, que han tenido el acierto de colgar en casi todas las habitaciones y apartamentos lienzos de la artista de A Rúa Carina Rodríguez, que evocan las máscaras y los trajes del Entroido orensano. Otro acierto: el apartamento A Lareira, con la moderna cocina y un antiguo escaño con mesa abatible integrados a modo de office dentro de la monumental campana de la vieja chimenea.

Una buena opción también para alojarse y para poner a esta ruta punto final —o aparte, porque hay que volver para seguir explorando el extremo oriente de Galicia— es el hotel rural A Pontevella, en Sobradelo. Está en un lugar difícil de creer: a orillas del Sil, junto a un puente seiscentista de 90 metros cuyos siete ojos han visto cosas tremendas —como la crecida de 2010 o como la francesada, que para detenerla se derribó su arco central en 1810—. Soraya Docampo, su propietaria, levantó con sus propias manos este hotel boutique de acabados impecables, como solo puede hacerlo alguien que antes se dedicó a la construcción. Además de buena obrera, es buena cocinera y amena anfitriona.

El puente sobre el río Sil, en Sobradelo. Andrés Campos

Mientras los huéspedes se chupan los dedos —muy ricas, las croquetas de cecina artesanal y la lubina al horno con vino Godello—, les cuenta cosas maravillosas de este pueblo que es la capital de uno de los municipios más ricos de Galicia, Carballeda de Valdeorras, el mayor productor mundial de pizarra. Las piscinas naturales de Sobradelo tienen playa de arena fina, mucha pizarra —¡claro!— y hasta hidromasaje. Mañana habrá que ir a probarlas.

World.title: Four people with long Covid euthanised in NL last year
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Four people died by euthanasia last year after suffering with long Covid, according to the Dutch regional euthanasia review committee.

The youngest patient was 51-years-old, the other three were over 65. In another six cases, long Covid played a role in the decision to end their lives but was not the primary factor.

An estimated 400,000 people in the Netherlands currently suffer from long Covid, many of them have severe symptoms that stop them working or being able to enjoy basic everyday activities.

The Dutch Health Council this year urged the government to give more clarity around the situation with long Covid and do more to help treat those suffering from it.

Last month, a national research and investigation centre was launched by the Long-Covid Foundation, to help prolong work into treating the illness.

Government funding of €40 million dried up, so the foundation raised €500,000 to give to seven scientists to keep researching possible treatments.

World.title: Roof of PM’s office is original 16th-century flat-plack
World.content:
The roof of the Torentje, or Little Tower, at the Binnenhof in The Hague was built in 1547 as a construction kit and has been largely untouched since, broadcaster NOS reported on Thursday.

The research on the eight-metre-high spire above the office of the prime minister was carried out by the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf, the government’s property agency, during the ongoing renovation of the complex.

The ceiling was opened last year to check the area for asbestos, which was found, revealing the oak roof structure behind it.

The wooden construction has needed practically no repair work in 478 years.

An inspection revealed that the beams were sawn by hand, typical in the days before the widespread use of sawmills. The wood came from an oak tree felled in southern Sweden around 1546.

Roman numerals are also chiselled into the beams, indicating that the roof was built in a workshop, taken apart and transported to the building site. The numerals show which parts belong together, like the instructions for a piece of Ikea furniture.

The tower itself is older: the earliest records date from 1497, and Emperor Charles V had it completely rebuilt in 1547, when the spire was added.

The renovation of the Binnenhof began in 2021. The work was initially expected to take five years and cost €475 million, but the bill has since risen to at least €2.7 billion and completion has been postponed until 2031.

Earlier this year, archaeologists found an early 14th-century city gate at the site.

World.title: Parents as “customers” fuelling school disputes, council says
World.content:
Parents are falling out with schools and turning to dispute committees to settle grievances, according to the the government’s independent education council. This is happening partly because parents are being turned into “customers” of the education system, where they can publicly compare and select schools.

The council was asked to look into the problem by the former education minister and sent its findings on Thursday.

Tension between parents and schools is usually blamed on social media, polarisation and a more individualistic society, it said, but that explanation leaves out the part played by law and policy in setting the two sides against each other.

Policy changes, such as the 2014 passend onderwijs reform, which leaves parents and schools to agree between themselves when a child qualifies for additional support, have raised tensions. Previously, an outside committee would make these decisions.

Websites allowing parents to compare schools on performance data, such as exam pass rates and the share of pupils recommended for pre-university education, have also created a customer and provider dynamic, the report said.

Disputes taken to the national dispute committees for schools rose steadily until 2024, with a slight dip last year. The number of secondary teachers who say dealing with parents is giving them stress is rising, and in primary schools a third of all teachers say the same.

The council’s two main recommendations are that ministers should consider what a policy will do to the relationship between parents and schools before introducing it, and that parents should be given more say collectively rather than only as individuals with a complaint.

World.title: Calves shipped from Ireland go 50 hours without milk, NVWA says
World.content:
The Dutch food and product safety authority NVWA is taking enforcement action against four Irish livestock transporters over the treatment of very young calves shipped to the Netherlands, broadcaster NOS reported on Thursday.

The calves are given almost nothing to drink during a journey of at least 50 hours, which breaches EU animal welfare rules, the NVWA said. The transporters have been given a year to change their working methods or face financial penalties.

The animals, mostly bull calves under two months old, are loaded onto trucks in Ireland and put on a ferry to France. After a 19-hour crossing they are unloaded to rest and drink, then driven on to the Netherlands.

EU rules say animals must be fed during transport where “necessary”, which the European Commission and the NVWA interpret as at least every 12 hours. The Irish authorities disagree and have not intervened.

According to the NVWA, the trucks have no drinking systems suitable for milk, and calves of this age have to be helped to drink. The Irish government has itself said that is “practically impossible” on the ferry.

“That means the animals can no longer go directly from Ireland via France to the Netherlands in one go,” NVWA inspector Annebeth van Aartsen told NOS. “The transport would have to be organised differently.”

The Dutch veal sector said earlier it wanted to stop the Irish imports in 2026 because of the suffering involved, but a NOS investigation this year found the transports were still going on.

The NVWA had previously said it could not act because most of the violations take place at sea, outside Dutch jurisdiction. The action follows an enforcement request by animal welfare groups Eyes on Animals and Dier&Recht.

World.title: Amsterdam fails to get EU backing to limit Airbnb rules
World.content:
Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema has failed to persuade the European Commission to help crack down on people renting out their own homes to tourists.

Halsema travelled to Brussels in the spring with the mayors of other big European cities that struggle with mass tourism – like Barcelona and Paris – to lobby for tougher powers to regulate holiday rentals through sites like Airbnb.

But the EU Affordable Housing Act, presented on Wednesday, would not ban or limit holiday lets but instead establishes a standard for when an area is under “housing stress” – defined as one where house prices are at least eight times per capita disposable income and have risen over the past decade.

It then gives local authorities a legal basis to restrict commercial short-term rentals and second-home purchases in those areas.

Combating local damage

Amsterdam had asked the commission for two things, according to the Telegraaf: more powers to act against people letting out the home they live in, and for the right to intervene once an area’s liveability has been damaged by tourist rentals.

The commission seemingly dismissed both requests. The text of the act explicitly excludes a host’s primary residence from any restriction, on the grounds that renting out your own home does not take housing off the market. It also only covers measures justified by affordability and availability, not neighbourhood nuisance.

“It is questionable whether this proposal is going to help us,” Amsterdam housing alderman Zita Pels told the paper. Dirk Gotink, an MEP for the centre-right NSC, also told the Telegraaf: “we don’t need a European law to solve local problems.”

Amsterdam already restricts renting your own home through sites like Airbnb to 30 nights per year but has tried to go further in the past. In July 2020 the council banned holiday rentals outright in the red light district and part of the canal ring.

The Amsterdam district court overturned that ban in 2021, and the Council of State, the highest administrative court, upheld the ruling in 2023, saying a total ban was disproportionate and the city should first have tested less drastic measures, such as a lower night limit.

For people in the Netherlands with a second home in Spain, Portugal or France, nothing will change for now. The law would allow local authorities in stressed areas to restrict purchases of homes not used as a primary residence, but only for property bought after the measure takes effect.

The proposal must first be negotiated by the European Parliament and member states, a process likely to take a year or more.

World.title: Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite
World.content:
Exports from the Netherlands to the United States fell by 25% in the first half of this year, knocking the US out of the top five destinations for Dutch goods.

Dutch companies sold €13 billion worth of goods to the US between January and June, €4.3 billion less than in the same period last year, figures from national statistics office CBS show. The decline began after the Trump administration imposed a general import tariff of 15% on goods from the EU in August last year.

Almost every type of product was affected. Machinery and transport equipment, the biggest category of Dutch exports to the US, accounted for nearly half the fall. Sales of medicines and other chemical products dropped by more than 30%, and manufactured goods such as medical instruments fell by almost a quarter.

As a result, the US now takes 4% of Dutch goods exports, down from 5.5% a year earlier. Italy has overtaken it as the fifth-biggest market, with Spain also catching up. Exports to Belgium, Germany, France, Spain and Italy all rose over the same period.

Trade in the other direction has grown – imports from the US were up 19% to €27.6 billion, although most of that increase was oil and other fuels, which have become more expensive because of the conflict in the Middle East. Other kinds of imports rose by 6.7%.

The tariffs have been costly for the US as well. The country’s Supreme Court ruled in February that most of the levies Donald Trump introduced last year were illegal, and Dutch companies are now claiming back more than €1 billion in duties.

Philips has already received €186 million, and Heineken and Ahold Delhaize are expected to recover hundreds of millions between them.

In 2024, before the tariffs were introduced, the Netherlands exported more than €38 billion worth of goods to the US, nearly 6% of all its exports.

World.title: Library membership tops 3.8 million as more adults sign up
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

More than 3.8 million people were members of public libraries in the Netherlands in 2025, a 3% increase over the year before according to new numbers by national statistics office CBS.

The number of adult library members rose by 46,000 to nearly 1.4 million.

In particular, an increasing number of younger adults, those between the ages of 18 and 30, are joining libraries.

In total, 9% of adults are library members. That statistic is dwarfed by the number of children who are library members. Nearly two-thirds of kids, 74%, are members of a library.

The number of children joining a library has also increased in 2025. Last year saw a rise of 2.4%, or over 57,000 more kids with a library card.

The Netherlands had 802 library locations in 2025, an increase of 35 on the year before. This is due to an increase in funding from the national government, according to CBS.

The number of physical books checked out by patrons has remained stable but the number of e-book loans rose. Nearly 6 million e-books were borrowed via the online library, 3% more than in 2024, and audiobook loans rose 11% to 2.9 million.

Divers have recovered the body of a man who fell out of a boat in the IJ in Amsterdam on Wednesday.

The 47-year old went overboard near the Schellingwouderbrug, which connects Amsterdam East and Amsterdam Noord, at around 12:30PM, the regional safety board reported.

Multiple diving teams and rescue boats were dispatched as well as a helicopter equipped with a thermal camera.

After an hour of searching, the operation was scaled back as it was unlikely the man would be found alive.

Divers found his body late Wednesday evening.

It is not clear how the man ended up in the water. The police are investigating.

Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment

Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation was in Poland this week to visit potential locations for the base and discuss the issue further. World.title: “We remember where Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,” says Polish FM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. Europa się budzi, a establishment wpada w panikę. Wynik AfD pokazuje, że ludzie mają dość dyktatu Brukseli, Zielonego Ładu i niszczenia państw narodowych przez nielegalną imigrację. Polityczne trzęsienie ziemi dopiero się zaczyna. Piękna, biała Europa narodów wkrótce powróci. — Włodzimierz Skalik (@Wlodek_Skalik) September 7, 2026 One party that has been unambiguously positive in its response to AfD’s victory is the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian group that broke away from Confederation last year and is currently polling support of around 9% “Europe is waking up, and the establishment is falling into panic,” wrote KKP’s deputy leader, Włodzimierz Skalik, on social media. “A beautiful, white Europe of nations will soon return.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Robots “protest” in Warsaw to demand regulation of AI and automation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. But that headline figure does not tell the whole story, with experts arguing that the Polish labour market is actually in good shape, writes @AlicjaPtak4 https://t.co/Pk4y7BqGrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. The candidate of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja), one of Poland’s main political groups, has been disqualified from Kraków’s mayoral election after over 2,000 of the signatures from local residents collected in support of his candidacy were found to be invalid. One of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, admitted that the situation was an “embarrassment” and “catastrophe”. He responded by dismissing the candidate, Bartosz Bocheńczak, as head of his party’s local structures in Kraków and launching an investigation into how the blunder occurred. Podobnie jak i wielu naszych działaczy, wolontariuszy, sympatyków i wyborców, czuję się bardzo zawiedziony brakiem rejestracji kandydatury Bartosza Bocheńczaka w Krakowie. Przyczyną braku rejestracji było to, że spośród około 5000 zebranych podpisów, ponad 2000 były błędnych.… — Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) September 7, 2026 Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, is holding a mayoral election this month after the previous incumbent, Aleksander Miszalski, was removed mid-term in a rare recall referendum earlier this year. Over a dozen potential candidates announced plans to stand. But, in order to be registered, they had to collect at least 3,000 signatures from residents of the city supporting their candidacy, then submit them to the municipal electoral commission by 3 September. Twelve candidates made such submissions, after which the commission began assessing all signatures to ensure that each candidate had at least 3,000 that were valid. On Monday, reports began to emerge that, although Bocheńczak had submitted just over 4,600 signatures, the commission had found that fewer than 3,000 of them were valid. That evening, the candidate himself confirmed the news. Mentzen, who is leader of the far-right libertarian New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja) party that makes up one half of Confederation, revealed that over 2,000 signatories had listed their address as their place of residence rather than where they are officially registered as living. In Poland, it is common for people to live somewhere different from where they are officially registered. That is particularly the case for young people, who are often registered at their parents’ address while residing elsewhere. Confederation is particularly popular among young people, and Kraków has a large student population. Moja kandydatura na Prezydenta Krakowa nie została zarejestrowana. Zabrakło ważnych podpisów. Nie będę snuł teorii spiskowych, szukał winnych ani przerzucał odpowiedzialności na kogokolwiek. Uważałem, że złożenie niemal 5000 podpisów zapewni nam wystarczający margines… — Bartosz Bocheńczak (@BBochenczak) September 7, 2026 Mentzen said that the regulations regarding collecting signatures for candidates are “absurd”, yet admitted that Bocheńczak’s campaign should have done a better job of complying with the rules. There must now be “consequences from this embarrassment”, said Mentzen, who announced that Bocheńczak had been dismissed as New Hope’s local leader in Kraków and that a party commission would “determine responsibility for this disaster”. Confederation also faced scrutiny last year when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected its financial report for the 2024 European elections after it found irregularities. The party also failed to submit the required documents on time. As a result, it lost access to state subsidies. The Supreme Court has rejected an appeal by the far-right Confederation against the electoral commission's decision to reject its financial report for last year's European elections due to irregularities. The group will now lose access to state subsidies https://t.co/hNGu2Zvzii — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 14, 2025 Bocheńczak is not the only candidate who has struggled with collecting signatures. Last week, just days before the deadline, it emerged that over 3,000 signatures collected in support of the favourite in the elections, Łukasz Gibała, an independent, were invalid because the word “Kraków” was missing from the form. Gibała – a perennial candidate in mayoral elections who finished runner-up to Miszalski in 2024 – quickly scrambled to collect more signatures, and his team managed to gather an additional 9,000 in three days. On Monday this week, it also emerged that three other independent candidates, Marian Banaś, Stanisław Kułach and Marta Ratuszyńska, had failed to gather enough signatures. All three have taken up their right to appeal against the commission’s decision to reject their candidacies. Dziś złożymy dodatkowe podpisy do komisji wyborczej – ponad 9 tysięcy (oprócz wcześniejszych 5,5 tys.). Skala Waszego zaangażowania i pomocy była bezprecedensowa – w 3 dni zebraliśmy więcej podpisów niż którykolwiek z naszych rywali przez 3 tygodnie 💪 Bardzo Wam dziękuję i… — Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) September 3, 2026 Six candidates have so far been accepted, including Gibała; Monika Piątkowska, who is supported by the centrist Civil Coalition (KO) and Polish People’s Party (PSL); Michał Drewnicki of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS); Aleksandra Owca of the left-wing Together (Razem); and Michał Klimek of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). Two candidates, Daria Gosek-Popiołek of The Left (Lewica) and Sławomir Pietrzyk of Social Democracy of Poland (Socjaldemokracja Polska), are still awaiting confirmation from the electoral commission that they submitted enough valid signatures. A decision is due to be announced today. The first round of the election will take place on Sunday 27 September. If any candidate receives over 50% of the vote, they will become mayor. If not, a run-off between the top two candidates will take place on 11 October. There has been little polling on support for candidates, but one survey by the Opinia24 agency for Polityka Insight two weeks ago showed Gibała with 25.2%, ahead of Piątkowska (15.3%) and Gosek-Popiołek (8.7%). World.title: Poland urges EU to deny asylum to migrants who violently cross its borders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
