World.title: Farnworth can’t forget his finals heartbreak. His fab five can right those wrongs
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Farnworth can’t forget his finals heartbreak. His fab five can right those wrongs Nick Wright September 10, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The scars from his last foray in finals football may linger, but Herbie Farnworth enters the 2026 series as a changed man, and a key member of arguably the most lethal backline in the NRL. The Dolphins centre looms as his side’s X-factor in their maiden finals campaign, which begins on Saturday in New Zealand when they play a Warriors side with a parochial crowd behind them. Farnworth hasn’t featured at this point of the season since he played with the Brisbane Broncos in the heartbreaking 2023 grand final defeat at the hands of a Nathan Cleary-inspired Penrith Panthers. Dolphins’ ‘Fab Five’: (from left to right) Selwyn Cobbo, Jamayne Isaako, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Herbie Farnworth, Jack Bostock. Getty While the Englishman has new ambitions in delivering silverware to Redcliffe – and holds no bittersweet feelings that Brisbane got the job done in 2025 – those memories still linger and serve as motivation.



“It’s definitely a hard one to get over, I’d be lying if I said I hadn’t thought about it a fair bit,” Farnworth revealed. “But I feel like I’ve grown a lot as a person and as a player from it. Obviously, the boys [Broncos] ended up putting it right in the end, which was good to see – it was a lot of good mates who worked really hard. “Obviously, I didn’t get a ring, so hopefully, it’s our time this year. I know how hard all those boys work, I’d been with a lot of them since the under-20s, so it was nice to see them go on and do well.” Since arriving at his former club’s nearest rival, Farnworth has gone from the best up-and-coming centre in the game to a clear standout. Despite being positioned out wide, he leads the competition for offloads (72) and tackle busts (150).



Related Article NRL 2026 A week after a fatal crash, Chester drove the same road. That was just the start of his battles He has helped his team become one of rugby league’s most attacking sides, cementing a top four place ahead of finals. “I’ve obviously got some very good players inside me in Izzy [Katoa] and Kodi [Nikorima] putting me in good spots to break those tackles and make those offloads, so the credit probably goes to those guys,” Farnworth said. Fullback Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow chimed in: “He [Farnworth] doesn’t want to get tackled even more than me, I think that’s where I get it from. “Just watching him play and how he goes about his game, he’s a special talent.”



Dolphins’ attacking style has had a ripple effect for the rest of the side, with the work of the ‘Fab Five’ – Farnworth, Tabuai-Fidow, Selwyn Cobbo, Jack Bostock and Jamayne Isaako – complementing a forward pack built on speed and skill rather than size. No team in the competition this year has run for as many metres as the Dolphins’ nearly 43,800. The backline quintet has run for more than 16,800 of them, with only the ladder-leading Panthers running for more collectively among the teams named for the first week of the finals. The more mobile and creative members of the Dolphins forward pack – Max Plath, Kurt Donoghoe and Morgan Knowles the leading examples – have expanded the side’s attack; producing faster play-the-balls and an interchange of passing to combat the increasing pace of the contest due to the six-again set restart laws. “It should be the other way around, shouldn’t it?” Dolphins forward Felise Kaufusi said with a laugh, when asked about the mountain of work his backs get through.



“We’ve got some mobile and fit forwards, and the way the game is going – and how fit and fast it is – I think you need that from your middles. Those big bodies we have in our backs, they’re like extra forwards anyway, so I think we complement each other pretty well.” Related Article NRL 2026 How an AFL great has unlocked rugby league’s next great halfback Tabuai-Fidow credits the “special bond” shared between the squad for contributing to the on-field cohesiveness. He said he had “no regrets” about his move to Redcliffe from a North Queensland Cowboys’ outfit which had just reached the 2022 preliminary finals. “It all comes down to working hard for each other. We have that special bond and that connection where the back five will do the hard yards, and the forwards will tackle for us – it’s a trade-off there where we work together and make our jobs easy,” Tabuai-Fidow told this masthead. Isaako added: “Our forward pack is not as big as most forward packs in the comp, we’re a little bit of a smaller forward pack and a bit more mobile, and that sometimes means when the ball is kicked inside our 10, 20 metres zone we have a job to take the first three of four carries to get to our kick.



“It’s something we pride ourselves on is making sure we get the ball down the other end, and having a good kick-chase. In order to do that, we need our forwards to be in that chase line, so [we need to] do as much work as we can coming out of the backfield and make it easier for them.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Work-from-home laws are in purgatory, and the Liberals fell right into Labor’s trap
World.content:
Analysis NationalVictoriaVictorian Parliament Work-from-home laws are in purgatory, and the Liberals fell right into Labor’s trap Chip Le Grand September 10, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the end, the Labor Party has exactly what it wanted out of its promise to give people a legislated right to work from home two days a week. The laws, in all likelihood, will never come into existence. On Thursday, they were condemned to a form of legislative purgatory – an upper house select committee for inquiry. There, it will dwell in darkness until this parliament is prorogued and the bill expires along with all the other unloved, forgotten and forsaken legislation of the past four years. Ben Carroll has got everything he needed from the work from home legislation. Eddie Jim This was never really about changing the law. All along, the main game for Labor was to draw the Liberal Party into a stoush about working from home.



Remember, this, along with promising nuclear power, are the two greatest reasons the federal Liberal Party is currently in opposition. Related Article Victorian Parliament ‘Final nail in the coffin’: Parliamentary twist derails work-from-home laws It is an embarrassing outcome for the government – for perhaps a day or two. Beyond that, it is an electoral gift to Premier Ben Carroll, who despite mouthing support for people’s right to work from home since he replaced Jacinta Allan, was never enamoured with her pet policy. We should all be thankful for the Victorian opposition for being guileless enough to make all this possible.



Working from home is wildly popular, but the one thing missing from the debate was compelling evidence that it needs to be protected by law. Related Article Opinion

Work therapy I can’t get a job because I can work only from home. What can I do? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor Thanks to the depth and duration of our COVID lockdowns, Melbourne remains one of the world’s most liveable cities for workers who prefer to clock on from the comfort of their homes and elastic-waisted trousers. Employers have embraced, by necessity, WFH accommodations. When disputes arise, there is a growing body of Fair Work Commission case law to help resolve them. This is not something that should concern Victoria’s lawmakers, who 30 years ago ceded to the Commonwealth their right to regulate employment conditions. The Victorian government’s plan to somehow bolt a right to work from home onto our anti-discrimination regime always seemed too clever by half.



Had the government scrounged a couple more votes in the upper house and passed these laws, it would have faced an almost certain High Court challenge. It is difficult to imagine a greater waste of the court’s time. Instead, with the Jess Wilson-led opposition now a firm favourite among the pollsters and bookies to win the November election, WFH can reclaim its central purpose – a wedge for her. Carroll feigned disappointment at what took place in the parliament’s Legislative Council, where Jeff Bourman from the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party – a political species on the endangered list – enlisted the help of the Coalition and some crossbench pals to delay the bill beyond this parliament’s final sitting day. Privately, he couldn’t have hoped for a better outcome. From here until November 28, he will pin on the Liberals a debacle entirely of Labor’s making.

World.title: Watch: The horrifying moment roof collapses at Curtin University worksite
World.content:
NationalWACourts Watch: The horrifying moment roof collapses at Curtin University worksite Rebecca Peppiatt September 10, 2026 — 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The moment a glass ceiling collapsed underneath two men, killing one of them, has been released by a Perth court after the company responsible for the roof’s construction pleaded guilty to criminal negligence. Apprentice glazier Jonathan Hartshorn, 23, was killed at Curtin University’s Bentley campus in October 2020 after falling 20 metres from a partly constructed, five-storey glass roof. Loading Workmate Rikki Issitt was also seriously injured during the same incident, on Wednesday telling Perth Magistrates Court his life had been irrevocably changed as a result. Steel fabrication company Elsdon was held responsible for the workplace incident after it was determined their staff had inadequate welding qualifications that led to poorly created steel trusses that were designed to hold the glass in place.



But it has taken six years for justice to be served, the company only pleading guilty to the charge of failing to ensure the safety or health of a person who is not an employee on Wednesday. Related Article Courts Survivor’s guilt and devastation: Court hears toll of fatal Curtin University roof collapse A second charge of failing to provide safe plant and caused death as a result was dropped and charges against the roof’s design company were also dropped earlier this year. On Thursday, Perth Magistrate Andrew Matthews released footage of the moment the roof collapsed that had been shown in court and seen by Hartshorn’s devastated mother. Susan Chappell told media outside court that watching the moment her son died was “horrible” and earlier criticised Elsdon for the length of time it took them to take responsibility for the 23-year-old’s death.



“Jonnie should be here, fulfilling his dreams, living the sweet life that he wanted,” Chappell said. “Instead his future was torn from underneath him along with mine. Now left with the wreckage.” Issitt also addressed the court and spoke about the moment he fell through the roof and thought he was going to die. “I looked up and saw the ceiling hanging above me,” he said. Issitt suffered significant injuries including breaks to both arms and legs, a fracture spine and broken pelvis.



He has been unable to work since. “The emotional consequences have been devastating,” he said, before adding that he had suffered survivors guilt following the death of Hartshorn.

A writer in the Herald travel section, recently mentioned unnecessary translations in phrasebooks, such as ‘Help!’” notes Geoff Gilligan of Coogee. “One of the most needless I can recall was from a Greek phrasebook. In the chapter, ‘At The Hairdressers’ was, ‘The water is too hot, you are scalding me.’ That said, I don’t know if it can match, ‘My postilion has been struck by lightning’.”

“The things one sees,” muses Paul Koff of Glenhaven. “I was taking a morning stroll when I spied a young lady jogging towards me. Bedecked in designer lycra, she carried, in the crook of her arm, an open laptop, into which she was cheerfully conversing. A case of working from (near) home?”

Beverley Fine of Pagewood thinks the renaming of the world in the image of the US (C8) may take on a sometime corporate bearing and provides some excellent examples: Tentariff, States Of HormUS, Paypalgeria, RusCIA, Chile Dog and Costco Rica.

It’s a Strait flush, according to Eric Scott of Bondi Junction: “Since the Strait of Hormuz seems to be open and closed at the same time it can join the list of renamed locations as The Strait of Schrödinger.”

“Moving to the St George district to escape dragonflies is not advisable (C8),” says Sean Lenehan of Kogarah. “On Saturday, my wife called me out to the backyard where there was a swarm of them and on Sunday I encountered them on the 5th hole at Bexley Golf Course. I blamed them for my woeful round.”

World.title: On parenting, teachers should not have to carry the responsibility
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters On parenting, teachers should not have to carry the responsibility September 10, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Davidson To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Columnist Jenna Price sounds angry in her article on parental responsibility (“Teachers aren’t here to raise your kids. That’s your job”, 9/9). We can’t blame her. For a long time, teachers have been expected to do many things apart from teach the curriculum. We have all sorts of different medical conditions now that weren’t diagnosed in the past, including autism and ADHD. There has been demand on teachers for increased amounts of time for admin. As Price indicates though, many parents expect teachers to teach values and behaviours that parents themselves need to teach.

Parents are so much more involved with their children now than in decades gone by and children are protected sometimes from consequences of their bad behaviour. Baby Boomers were parented with benign neglect: “come home when the street lights go on”. From my experience with working with parents, many of them want to be the friend of their child. You cannot be. Your role, especially in the early years and up into the teens, is to set boundaries and help your child to stay within them. There can be negotiations, but there must be consequences. Your child will respect you and ultimately themselves. It takes some courage I guess, but the time for a different relationship with your children is when they are adult.

Jan Marshall, Brighton What are the parents doing?

Jenna Price’s article is very timely. Whenever I read or hear about young teens, even preteens, committing home invasions, car stealing and joy riding in the early hours of the morning, I think where are their parents? I always knew where my young teens were at those times. Parent effectiveness training needs to be ramped up and even made compulsory for some parents.

Georgina Simmons, Mornington The lessons begin in the home

Much has been written recently in relation to how schools and teachers need to tackle toxic masculinity, misogyny and the “manosphere”. As a secondary school teacher with more than 40 years’ experience, I can tell you that if you believe this, you are deluding yourself. From the moment a child leaves the womb, the strongest socialising agent in their lives, especially in those early formative years, will be their parents. Parents are responsible for instilling in their children traits such as respect, compassion, empathy, and resilience. Most parents are aware of this responsibility; however, a growing number believe they can abrogate it to others, usually schools and teachers.

Every time a teacher sets foot in a classroom, they are already modelling and reinforcing the character traits that youth require to navigate life beyond school; however, if parents have not adequately prepared them in those crucial early years, it is often too late, and if they have provided their children with smartphones and watches before age 15, they are doing them a huge disservice.

Gary Warren, Eltham



Perhaps, a licence is required

″⁣Teachers aren’t there to raise your kids. That’s your job″⁣ – the headline that I have been waiting to see. Well done Jenna Price. Before people decide to have children, all prospective parents should think long and hard about the lifelong commitment they are undertaking. A parenting licence would be more relevant than a marriage licence.

Jane Washington, Frankston South Step up, and raise the children

Hear, hear, Jenna Price. Parents need to step up and actually raise the children they created. Feeding and clothing them is the least of it.

Helen Boér, Balwyn North If it’s good enough for puppies . . .

Jenna Price aptly states that respectful relationships begin at home. Unfortunately, although there are courses to learn about almost everything, there don’t seem to be any when it comes to parenting. Nowadays to register your dog some councils require proof of puppy school attendance, which is really a course showing humans how to bring up respectful pooches. Dare it be suggested that a Parenting Certificate could be introduced?

Judith Hudson, Elwood THE FORUM Explain AI benefits

The Allan Labor government spoke of being ″⁣ruthless″⁣ in attracting data centre jobs and making Victoria ″⁣the data centre centre″⁣. Faced with unexpected outrage from affected communities, the Carroll Labor government is sounding a little less gung-ho. The recently appointed AI Minister, Anthony Carbines, wants data centre developers to ″⁣share the benefits″⁣ (″⁣Anger over $1.5b West Gate data centre as AI minister issues warning to sector″⁣, 10/9). It’s hard to know what benefits there are to be shared. I doubt the minister means that the energy-gorging, water-guzzling data centre behemoths themselves have any possible benefits to share. But if he means that the secret AI computing taking place inside the data centres offers us benefits, he should start ascertaining and explaining in detail what those benefits are, beyond the usual nebulous ″⁣cure for cancer″⁣.

Richard Barnes, Fairfield



Accusation irony

It’s ironic that Israel has been accused of ethnic cleansing, given that Jews lived for millennia in what had been called Judea and Samaria before they, themselves, were ethnically cleansed from the ″⁣West Bank” in the 1948 Arab-Israeli war. If the government is to apply trade sanctions on Israel in the future, it would need to explain its hypocrisy in not having done likewise with China and Turkey, who have long illegally occupied Tibet and northern Cyprus, respectively. In 2005, Israel withdrew all of its settlements from Gaza in pursuit of peace, and this ultimately resulted in October 7. Israelis are understandably reluctant to repeat this approach with the West Bank. As past Israeli PM, Golda Meir put it, “Better a bad press than a good epitaph”.

Geoff Feren, St Kilda East Embargo calls

All those in Australia and other countries making calls for an embargo on imports from Israeli settlements on the basis of alleged human rights abuses, will no doubt be following them up with demands that we cut off imports from perpetrators of massive and unambiguous human rights abuse, such as China.

Bill James, Frankston Snobbery abounds

My great-great grandfather, Henry Russell, was born in Henry Street, East Collingwood, in 1857.

East Collingwood now goes by the name Abbotsford, so snobbery has existed in Melbourne for more than 160 years.

Rob Prowd, Box Hill South No faith to begin with

Your correspondent (Letters, 9/9) talked of losing faith in the outcomes of privatisation. Anyone who ever analysed privatisation never had this faith to begin with. Economics writer Kenneth Davidson in the time of Jeff Kennett’s government wrote numerous articles in The Age demonstrating that the overall cost to the community of delivering services had to increase by virtue of the need for profit; the higher interest rates paid by private industry (hence support from the banking sector) and the costs of contract preparation and supervision.

For a politician there was the joy of creating deniability and the appearance of action.

For the community there now is the vastly increased cost, the complete inability to sheet home responsibility for failure, the confusion of how to seek redress for failure, and the lower standard of service. What’s not to love?

Laurie Comerford, Chelsea More bad habits

Promises by Premier Ben Carroll for greater transparency in government are now looking a bit shaky. There are at least two areas of concern.

IBAC reforms containing provisions for enhanced powers will not apply to issues previously covered by IBAC. In essence, it would prevent revisiting allegations associated with recent major scandals, including matters relating to the Big Build infrastructure program.

The other area is Labor’s action to block an attempt to establish a parliamentary committee into the proposed secret tax on public transport users, described as a ″⁣rail improvement″⁣ levy, through increased rail, tram and bus fares estimated to raise $8 billion to fund transport projects including the SRL.

Both moves are seen as attempts to protect former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan. Seems the bad habits of yesteryear are reasserting themselves.

Martin Newington, Aspendale



Factors in voting

Your correspondent (Letters, 10/9) states she will be voting for One Nation because its Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, has a similar history to her son, who is an outstanding citizen in his older life. I make no comment on Pickering’s background nor ability, however, I would want to consider how the few policies that leader Pauline Hanson postulates could possibly be ones that voters would see as an indication that her party was capable of guiding our country through very challenging times. Surely in casting her vote a little more consideration than a likeness of her outstanding son to a candidate is warranted.

Bill Pimm, Mentone No insight

In relation to One Nation, some of their major candidates claim they’re not politicians; past behaviour, however damning, is irrelevant; they’re not concerned with scientifically proven principles of climate change, although pestilence, fire and hurricanes surround them; they have simple black and white solutions to complex problems; they seem to espouse the “kick the superannuation can down the road” approach without a thought for future needs; instant gratification isn’t quick enough for them and finally, their overriding raison d’être is one finger pointing at the major parties without the awareness that three fingers are pointing right back at themselves.

Peter Russo, Brunswick West Medicare madness

I was referred by my rheumatologist to have MRIs on my shoulders and arms due to extreme pain. He wrote me the necessary referrals and when I rang the imaging group to make the appointments, I was told that Medicare would only pay for one limb per scan per day but they had a vacancy the next day and I could come back and have the other limb scanned and that would be OK with Medicare. What sort of madness is this? Where’s the logic? Can someone please explain this to me? I am 91 years old and I certainly don’t find it easy to travel back and forth twice. Apart from the inconvenience, the double paperwork involved is nonsensical.

Norma Zandle, Brighton East The 9/11 ripples

It is difficult to overstate the impact of the September 11 attacks on the world we live in today. The invasion of Afghanistan which followed was initially conducted for justified reasons, but ultimately failed to remove the Taliban. The fraudulent war in Iraq destabilised that country and paved the way for the rise of ISIS, which helped to exacerbate the civil war in neighbouring Syria. Despite its many crimes, Saddam Hussein’s regime helped to check Iranian power, and its removal left Iran free to dominate its neighbours, creating a recipe for permanent regional conflict. Subsequent Western military interventions in the region led to the gradual erosion of civil liberties at home, and to waves of mass migration to the West, creating significant unresolved problems with cultural integration and social cohesion, and contributing to the rise of political extremism globally. As we approach the 25th anniversary of 9/11, we must mourn the 2977 innocent people murdered by al-Qaeda on that fateful day, and reflect on the mistakes made by our political leaders since.

Nikhil Dhanabal, Clyde North How the land lies

One of your correspondents wonders why politicians can’t be forced to take polygraph tests (Letters, 8/9), while another (9/9) says polygraph machines are unreliable junk science.

The irony is, in Australia we have no legislation against lies in political advertising. Further, if a government changes its mind – due to public clamouring or sheer logic – it is branded a ″⁣liar″⁣. I’m thinking of Anthony Albanese’s sensible retreat on the stage 3 tax cuts that only benefited the wealthy in his first term, and cutting benefits to future residential property investors in this year’s budget.

On gambling advertising, Albanese has yet to prove himself – given he is standing out against the measures recommended in Peta Murphy’s report, and which have the support of MPs in both main parties and the backbench, as well as most Australians.

Caroline Leslie, Hawthorn



American idolatry

It’s now obvious that there is no limit to Australians’ indiscriminate worshipping of all things American. How else can you explain, in the home of the world’s finest version of football, the crowds rushing to the MCG to watch American gridiron – a ridiculous distortion of rugby, and easily the world’s worst form of football.

Geoff Dalton, East Malvern What cost SRL?

It is true that the SRL will benefit some if it is ever built, but at what cost? This hastily conceived project that lacks a business case and transparency will cost more than $50 billion for the first leg. The other cost will be to the hospitals, schools, health services, police, roads, infrastructure, plus the debt. Maybe a good idea but we can’t afford it.

Vince Vozzo, Elwood O, Canada

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is to be admired for standing up to the bullying of Donald Trump. It may well inspire other countries to do the same, which would represent an own goal by Trump.

John Walsh, Watsonia



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Society

If I get off my train at Southern Cross and connect to the 48 North Balwyn tram in Collins Street, do I end up in Balwyn or Balwyn North? Oh Melbourne, are you confused or just pretentious?

Gryff Jamieson-Ballard, Castlemaine Jenna Price (Comment, 9/9), thank you. Parents, (and I’m one) stop undermining teachers (and I was one). Work with teachers. We all want what is best for our children/students, don’t we?

Louise Madden, Geelong West I was so enthralled by a television news story on the NFL game, I forgot about the earlier story on the shocking condition of our country roads.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill



Politics

It’s not so much that Victorian One Nation leader Warren Pickering admitted to myriad misdemeanours in his younger days but the fact that he’s a conspiracy theorist in a one-trick party.

Dorothy Galloway, Mentone Fancy making crime and corruption illegal (″⁣Hanson gives her support: Who has not tried drugs?″⁣, 10/9). Now that’s a masterstroke.

John Guy, Elsternwick Furthermore

King Canute couldn’t hold back the tide, and if the RBA increases interest rates to roll back inflation that’s largely caused by wars, it will also fail.

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood I am sure Donald Trump has his 9/11 story wrong. He would have carried two firefighters, one on each shoulder to safety, instead of modestly claiming they saved him.

Ian Anderson, Ascot Vale Commentators have said UK’s banning of West Bank imports is only symbolic. There are times when symbolism beats inaction.

Dan Drummond, Leongatha Finally

Myra Fisher (Letters, 10/9), your sense of humour often gets me laughing, especially in the morning. Sets me up well for the day.

Tris Raouf, Hadfield

World.title: Farnworth can’t forget his finals heartbreak. His fab five can right those wrongs
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Farnworth can’t forget his finals heartbreak. His fab five can right those wrongs Nick Wright September 10, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The scars from his last foray in finals football may linger, but Herbie Farnworth enters the 2026 series as a changed man, and a key member of arguably the most lethal backline in the NRL. The Dolphins centre looms as his side’s X-factor in their maiden finals campaign, which begins on Saturday in New Zealand when they play a Warriors side with a parochial crowd behind them. Farnworth hasn’t featured at this point of the season since he played with the Brisbane Broncos in the heartbreaking 2023 grand final defeat at the hands of a Nathan Cleary-inspired Penrith Panthers. Dolphins’ ‘Fab Five’: (from left to right) Selwyn Cobbo, Jamayne Isaako, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Herbie Farnworth, Jack Bostock. Getty While the Englishman has new ambitions in delivering silverware to Redcliffe – and holds no bittersweet feelings that Brisbane got the job done in 2025 – those memories still linger and serve as motivation.



“It’s definitely a hard one to get over, I’d be lying if I said I hadn’t thought about it a fair bit,” Farnworth revealed. “But I feel like I’ve grown a lot as a person and as a player from it. Obviously, the boys [Broncos] ended up putting it right in the end, which was good to see – it was a lot of good mates who worked really hard. “Obviously, I didn’t get a ring, so hopefully, it’s our time this year. I know how hard all those boys work, I’d been with a lot of them since the under-20s, so it was nice to see them go on and do well.” Since arriving at his former club’s nearest rival, Farnworth has gone from the best up-and-coming centre in the game to a clear standout. Despite being positioned out wide, he leads the competition for offloads (72) and tackle busts (150).



Related Article NRL 2026 A week after a fatal crash, Chester drove the same road. That was just the start of his battles He has helped his team become one of rugby league’s most attacking sides, cementing a top four place ahead of finals. “I’ve obviously got some very good players inside me in Izzy [Katoa] and Kodi [Nikorima] putting me in good spots to break those tackles and make those offloads, so the credit probably goes to those guys,” Farnworth said. Fullback Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow chimed in: “He [Farnworth] doesn’t want to get tackled even more than me, I think that’s where I get it from. “Just watching him play and how he goes about his game, he’s a special talent.”



Dolphins’ attacking style has had a ripple effect for the rest of the side, with the work of the ‘Fab Five’ – Farnworth, Tabuai-Fidow, Selwyn Cobbo, Jack Bostock and Jamayne Isaako – complementing a forward pack built on speed and skill rather than size. No team in the competition this year has run for as many metres as the Dolphins’ nearly 43,800. The backline quintet has run for more than 16,800 of them, with only the ladder-leading Panthers running for more collectively among the teams named for the first week of the finals. The more mobile and creative members of the Dolphins forward pack – Max Plath, Kurt Donoghoe and Morgan Knowles the leading examples – have expanded the side’s attack; producing faster play-the-balls and an interchange of passing to combat the increasing pace of the contest due to the six-again set restart laws. “It should be the other way around, shouldn’t it?” Dolphins forward Felise Kaufusi said with a laugh, when asked about the mountain of work his backs get through.



“We’ve got some mobile and fit forwards, and the way the game is going – and how fit and fast it is – I think you need that from your middles. Those big bodies we have in our backs, they’re like extra forwards anyway, so I think we complement each other pretty well.” Related Article NRL 2026 How an AFL great has unlocked rugby league’s next great halfback Tabuai-Fidow credits the “special bond” shared between the squad for contributing to the on-field cohesiveness. He said he had “no regrets” about his move to Redcliffe from a North Queensland Cowboys’ outfit which had just reached the 2022 preliminary finals. “It all comes down to working hard for each other. We have that special bond and that connection where the back five will do the hard yards, and the forwards will tackle for us – it’s a trade-off there where we work together and make our jobs easy,” Tabuai-Fidow told this masthead. Isaako added: “Our forward pack is not as big as most forward packs in the comp, we’re a little bit of a smaller forward pack and a bit more mobile, and that sometimes means when the ball is kicked inside our 10, 20 metres zone we have a job to take the first three of four carries to get to our kick.



“It’s something we pride ourselves on is making sure we get the ball down the other end, and having a good kick-chase. In order to do that, we need our forwards to be in that chase line, so [we need to] do as much work as we can coming out of the backfield and make it easier for them.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Work-from-home laws are in purgatory, and the Liberals fell right into Labor’s trap
World.content:
Analysis NationalVictoriaVictorian Parliament Work-from-home laws are in purgatory, and the Liberals fell right into Labor’s trap Chip Le Grand September 10, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the end, the Labor Party has exactly what it wanted out of its promise to give people a legislated right to work from home two days a week. The laws, in all likelihood, will never come into existence. On Thursday, they were condemned to a form of legislative purgatory – an upper house select committee for inquiry. There, it will dwell in darkness until this parliament is prorogued and the bill expires along with all the other unloved, forgotten and forsaken legislation of the past four years. Ben Carroll has got everything he needed from the work from home legislation. Eddie Jim This was never really about changing the law. All along, the main game for Labor was to draw the Liberal Party into a stoush about working from home.



Remember, this, along with promising nuclear power, are the two greatest reasons the federal Liberal Party is currently in opposition. Related Article Victorian Parliament ‘Final nail in the coffin’: Parliamentary twist derails work-from-home laws It is an embarrassing outcome for the government – for perhaps a day or two. Beyond that, it is an electoral gift to Premier Ben Carroll, who despite mouthing support for people’s right to work from home since he replaced Jacinta Allan, was never enamoured with her pet policy. We should all be thankful for the Victorian opposition for being guileless enough to make all this possible.



Working from home is wildly popular, but the one thing missing from the debate was compelling evidence that it needs to be protected by law. Related Article Opinion

Work therapy I can’t get a job because I can work only from home. What can I do? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor Thanks to the depth and duration of our COVID lockdowns, Melbourne remains one of the world’s most liveable cities for workers who prefer to clock on from the comfort of their homes and elastic-waisted trousers. Employers have embraced, by necessity, WFH accommodations. When disputes arise, there is a growing body of Fair Work Commission case law to help resolve them. This is not something that should concern Victoria’s lawmakers, who 30 years ago ceded to the Commonwealth their right to regulate employment conditions. The Victorian government’s plan to somehow bolt a right to work from home onto our anti-discrimination regime always seemed too clever by half.



Had the government scrounged a couple more votes in the upper house and passed these laws, it would have faced an almost certain High Court challenge. It is difficult to imagine a greater waste of the court’s time. Instead, with the Jess Wilson-led opposition now a firm favourite among the pollsters and bookies to win the November election, WFH can reclaim its central purpose – a wedge for her. Carroll feigned disappointment at what took place in the parliament’s Legislative Council, where Jeff Bourman from the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party – a political species on the endangered list – enlisted the help of the Coalition and some crossbench pals to delay the bill beyond this parliament’s final sitting day. Privately, he couldn’t have hoped for a better outcome. From here until November 28, he will pin on the Liberals a debacle entirely of Labor’s making.
