World.title: Victoria's largest amateur football league denies 'gender bias' accusations
World.content:
Multiple Victorian Amateur Football Association (VAFA) clubs have expressed disappointment with how women's competitions are being handled this season, as players across the league say the women's competition is being treated as secondary.

The VAFA is the state's largest amateur Australian Rules football league with about 300 teams and 12,000 participants.

Last week, Fitzroy Football Club and St Mary's Salesian released public statements expressing disappointment over two separate incidents that affected their finals campaigns.

Fitzroy celebrated its final home-and-away season win, believing the victory put it into the top four and its first finals series of the premier women's division.

However, the league had declared an earlier season game between two other clubs, St Kevin's and Kew, "abandoned" due to an ineligible player, and recalculated the match ratio for the teams, putting Fitzroy outside the four.

The club said it was "bitterly disappointed" not just with how the league managed the competition, but with its communication with clubs.

"To say we are frustrated with the decision is an understatement," Fitzroy said in its statement.

"We're incredibly proud of their season and all they have achieved. The same cannot be said for the VAFA's handling of this matter, and it goes to a concern that this premier women's competition is not being as well run as it should be.

"The fact the top tier of the VAFA has only nine teams creates a situation such as this to occur. As one of the top levels of women's football in Australia, it beggars belief that an odd number of teams are in the division. Would this happen in the men's premier competition?"

Loading Instagram content

Fitzroy president David Leydon said the club took great pride in playing in the premier women's division, "a very prestigious competition" that has taken them a long time to get into.

He said making finals was a big moment for the club

"And to have that ripped away from us courtesy of an arrangement that we were unaware of until after our last game, I was heartbroken," Leydon said.

He said the abandoned game should have been communicated to all other clubs in the competition.

Earlier in division two, St Mary's Salesian won an important preliminary final but were later disqualified after a player was ruled ineligible for finals.

The St Mary's player had only played two home-and-away games instead of the required three, following a rule change that year.

VAFA changed the requirement to three games at the start of the season and updated its website. But St Mary's claim PlayHQ, the platform the VAFA runs every fixture, team list and season through, still stated the old eligibility requirement for division two women's finals as two in-season games, upon which the club relied.

St Mary's said it would never have selected an ineligible player in a final had they known.

Loading Instagram content

The player missed most of the season due to maternity leave.

The club says it was not notified of the rule change, and that the men's eligibility rule was updated on PlayHQ this year, but the women's was not.

VAFA's response

VAFA strongly refuted any "any gender bias" in applying the competition rules.

It said the club statements, and subsequent social media comments on the posts, brought the integrity of the competition into question and framed the issues as being gender-based.

"Whilst we understand the emotions that such commentary provokes, the inaccuracy of these club statements is misleading and being considered by the board for potential breaches of the VAFA's policies," the VAFA told the ABC.

It said the ineligible St Kevin's player was never a matter that would affect Fitzroy's ladder position or qualification for finals, so Fitzroy was not involved in the initial enquiries into the game result.

VAFA CEO Jason Reddick said he was in touch with Fitzroy on the Sunday of round 18, the final home-and-away round, both over the phone and in writing.

Fitzroy asked for an investigation into the matter on the Monday. The VAFA looked into it and released its findings on the Friday, the day before the finals series commenced.

In response to Fitzroy asking if something similar would happen in the men's, the league said it was not a fair question.

"This is not a gender-based issue," it said.

"The matter is about the VAFA Rules pertaining to the playing of an ineligible player. We have the example of stripping reigning Premiers Uni Blues of all their points and fining them $22k for playing ineligible players in their Premier Men's team in 2022, so there is clearly no gender bias when it comes to applying the Rules of the VAFA competition."

Regarding St Mary's statement, the league said member clubs presented and voted on any rule changes each year, so all clubs knew the finals eligibility rules at the start of the season.

It also said it sent out a reminder ahead of the finals through its portal to all clubs.

'Just looks like flat-out discriminatory'

Multiple women's players across various VAFA clubs, who wished to remain anonymous due to fear of repercussions from the league, said they were not aware of the finals eligibility rule changes this year.

One player from a premier women's side said the women's competitions were treated "1,000 per cent" like an afterthought, particularly in fixturing, scheduling and grounds.

More women are playing footy than ever before. Why are so many leaving? The women's team from Kyneton's 15-month public and bitter saga suggests it is the canary in the coal mine of a widespread issue for women's players across the country.

She gave the examples of the women's division one, two and three having their grand finals at 9:40am, 9:20am and 9:20am respectively last weekend, which she said was "just awful".

The men's competitions received their fixtures months in advance, whereas the women received theirs just weeks before their season starts, she said.

"I think if it was like at least some of the men's teams got s*** locations and times, it would be slightly more understandable, because I know that obviously the council plays a big part in that [and)]in getting access to grounds at certain times. But it just looks like flat-out discriminatory," she said.

She said the issues around player eligibility also came down to broad structural issues within women's football, where clubs were often low on volunteers and didn't receive "a whole lot of help or guidance from VAFA about how to deal with situations".

Fitzroy says it is frustrated with the league. (Supplied: Fitzroy Football Club)

"That's another issue with, and this is not VAFA's fault, but by default, women have less community support and less money, less financial support, which means that the burden often feels heavier on women's teams to make sure that they're on top of all of this admin," she said.

"It's normally someone random who has no idea how football works, who's doing the team management stuff, which is checking who the players are and if they've got their correct numbers and all of that admin that goes towards eligibility and selection and reporting and all of the flow and stuff.

"So I do think that there's also a bit of like a burden on VAFA also to make more of an active effort to communicate changes, knowing that like this is all volunteer-run clubs."

Earlier this year, the ABC reported that VAFA women's players found issues with inequitable resourcing and fixturing by the league.

'Very under-resourced'

A source who has worked in senior administrative roles across different VAFA clubs, and who wished to remain anonymous for fear of repercussions at their club, said there were many issues with how the women's competitions were run.

"Firstly … it's tough for them. I think they're very under-resourced," they said.

"They're essentially set up as a men's competition traditionally and historically, and they've added women, you know, 10 years ago. And so that's always going to come with a need for serious transition and a need for serious recalibration."

Fitzroy says the club was heartbroken to learn it didn't qualify for the finals. (Supplied: Fitzroy Football Club)

They said there wasn't a clear strategy for the women's competition, pointed to "anomalies" across the competition, highlighted "fixture mistakes", and said, "we're having administrators at the VAFA giving wrong information to clubs".

"So that's just a reflection of, well, they're not resourcing it enough, and they're not actually prioritising women's footy in their strategic goals and operations, and it's reflected in the under-resourcing, which means you have these mistakes," they said.

Leydon said after Fitzroy released its public statement, the support was overwhelming, including from other clubs in the league.

"Hopefully it turns into something positive, and we can try and fix the way the women's program is conducted and get everyone to take it a lot more seriously," he said.

Tech.title: Electric air taxis get the green light for test flights in Texas
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A new federal program to test the feasibility of electric, hybrid-electric, and autonomous aircraft kicks off today in Texas — before the rules governing this new technology have even been finalized.

Earlier this year, the Federal Aviation Administration’s Advanced Air Mobility and Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing (eVTOL) Integration Pilot Program (eIPP) selected eight state-led projects to serve as some of the first public tests of these new aircraft. The first one kicks off today in Texas, featuring three eVTOL companies: Joby, Beta, and Wisk.

For the next week, these companies will conduct test flights demonstrating future routes between cities and regional airports, including Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. The aircraft won’t carry any passengers, but regulators will be keen to see how the state’s air traffic control system handles the uptick in flight traffic. The companies, meanwhile, are eager to prove to the federal government that their aircraft deserve to be awarded type certification, which is required before any of them can carry passengers commercially in the US.

But type certification can take years to attain, which led to the White House to create this pilot program allowing these companies to demonstrate their new technology — even before the regulatory process has concluded. Through the eIPP, the companies hope to accelerate their path to market by getting a head start on data collection that will be needed for certification. Data from the program will also be used to “develop new regulations that safely enable this futuristic technology at scale,” the White House said earlier.

The companies say they are thrilled to demonstrate the future of electric and autonomous flight, which they argue will help reduce car traffic in cities and open up new mobility opportunities for consumers.

“I’m incredibly excited by the potential for vertical lift in Texas, a state with the infrastructure, expertise, and partnerships to help lead the next era of American aviation,” JoeBen Bevirt, Founder and CEO of Joby Aviation, said in a statement.

Several of these companies have conducted public test flights before — Joby’s egg-shaped aircraft demonstrated its future route between Lower Manhattan and JFK Airprot earlier this year — but these will be the first official flights under the White House’s new pilot program. Additional tests are being planned in New York, Utah, Pennsylvania, Louisiana, Florida, North Carolina, and New Mexico.

Legal in-fighting, however, could muddy the picture for electric aviation. Joby and one of its rivals, Archer, are currently suing each other for stolen trade secrets and corporate espionage. Technology limitations, including battery weight and sensor decisions, could also hamper the rollout.

Tech.title: Universal Music is launching an AI music platform with ElevenLabs
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Universal Music Group is launching a new AI-powered platform that will allow users to draw from its catalog of licensed music to create song remixes, mashups, and new takes on tracks, according to an announcement on Thursday. The record label is developing the platform through a multiyear licensing agreement with ElevenLabs, a company that specializes in AI voice and music generation.

UMG and ElevenLabs’ partnership will also include the “development of additional products and fan experiences in the months and years to come,” though the press release doesn’t include other details about what this might entail.

”By combining UMG’s global community and rights management expertise, with our AI models and products, we’ll enable artists and songwriters to create powerful new experiences for their fans, and ensure they are fairly compensated,” ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski says in the press release. The new AI music platform will remain separate from ElevenLabs’ Music API and ElevenMusic generator.

Tech.title: Where to preorder the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4
Tech.content:
While both new watches look similar to their predecessors, there are a number of updates under the hood that might intrigue some people enough to warrant a preorder. My colleague Victoria Song got hands-on with both smartwatches , and runs down the biggest changes, from the Audio Intelligence features made possible by the S11 chip (included in the Series 12 and Ultra 4), plus the possible impact of its improved sensors and tracking capabilities.

If you don’t want to wait for reviews to hit before you make the purchase, the Series 12 starts at $399 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Apple itself for the 42mm size ($50 more for the 46mm). Tech.title: Wolverine on the PS5 goes back to a simpler (and bloodier) style of action game
Tech.content:
Marvel’s Wolverine captures just how angry its lead character is. The latest PS5 exclusive from Spider-Man developer Insomniac, Wolverine is a straightforward action game that is at its best when you’re (literally) slicing through enemies or thrust into a sequence pulled from a blockbuster movie, like climbing the fuselage of a plane as it careens toward land or racing a motorcycle across rain-slicked city streets. It’s the kind of game that can really get your heart rate rising, and keeping Logan mad is a key part of the strategy. In many ways, it’s a throwback to straightforward action titles of the past — and it’s a refreshing change of pace in a medium saturated with live-service and open-world games.

Though it comes from Insomniac, Wolverine is very different from Spider-Man, which thrust the web-slinger into an open-world version of New York City. Instead, this is a much more linear experience that feels like a combination of two other PlayStation staples: God of War and Uncharted. Rather than follow Wolverine as a member of the X-Men, the story instead has him as an often reluctant member of Team X, a mercenary group with similar pro-mutant aims but a much more violent approach. Instead of heroes like Cyclops and Professor X, Wolvy is joined by more villain-adjacent characters like Sabretooth, Mystique, and Nathaniel Essex, before eventually connecting with Jean Grey. The story pulls Logan and his companions across the globe, but it starts out relatively simple, as they investigate a rash of mutant disappearances connected to a billionaire arms dealer.

The most important thing about both Wolverine the character and Wolverine the game is fighting. This is a hairy little dude who loves to scrap, and his mutant powers — healing and sharp claws — make it so that he is very good at it, able to both take a huge amount of damage and dish it out. And the best part of the game is how Wolverine-specific the action is. The combat is fast and violent and forces you to be aggressive. Wolverine can leap huge distances to take out foes and use his claws to both repel attacks and slice at enemies, often with very gruesome results. (At the end of a battle he’s usually coated in blood.) An important part of this is Wolverine’s rage level, which increases the more you fight. As his rage grows, it allows you to do two things: go absolutely berserk and kill a rash of enemies with a single blow, and use your healing power as a sort of extra life in case your health depletes. It’s a clever system that means you can’t sit back and play it safe. Wolverine isn’t chill, and you can’t be either.

Image: Sony Interactive Entertainment

That’s the God of War side of Wolverine. The Uncharted side comes in the form of all of the over-the-top set-pieces you’re thrown into. I’ll refrain from detailing some of the best ones for spoiler reasons, but I’ll say that, just like in Uncharted, these moments make it feel like you’re playing out a wild sequence from an action movie. There are chases across the rooftops of Tokyo, massive boss battles against some iconic comic book villains, and scenes where Wolverine is literally being ripped apart as he fights for survival.

The flip side is that, because of this setup, Wolverine is also much more restrictive than most of its contemporaries. In some ways this is a good thing; it’s refreshing to play a game that isn’t trying to do everything. But there are still some awkward elements. For instance, much like in Spider-Man, there are lots of collectibles that will reveal new bits of story or unlock new suits for Wolverine to wear. But exploration outside of the main path is extremely dull, so the only reason to track these down is if you have a completionist mindset. It’s also disappointing that Wolverine’s closet of outfits is much less fun than Spider-Man’s, and they often feel out of place with the game’s attempt at a more gritty tone.

Making matters worse is that, despite a promising start, the story ends up in a largely forgettable place, with few surprises, particularly if you have an even slight knowledge of the X-Men universe from comics or the animated series. Outside of combat and set-pieces, Wolverine skews generic AAA game; the voice acting, the cutscenes, and even some of the missions feel like standard video game fare, many of which seem out of place. Wolverine is amazing when you’re surrounded by ninjas trying to kill you. But when Logan is in a tux trying to spy on a fancy party? Not so much.

All that said, Wolverine’s return to a simpler and smaller style of action — I beat the game in around 13 hours — is still notable, particularly from Sony, which has had a rough few years after placing many ill-fated bets in the live-service space. But much like last year’s Ghost of Yōtei, Wolverine shows that PlayStation is still capable of the single-player blockbusters the platform is best known for. It’s also launching at perhaps the busiest video game release period in recent memory, going up against major titles including Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Control Resonant, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Gears of War: E-Day, Silent Hill: Townfall, Star Wars: Zero Company, and, soon enough, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Grand Theft Auto VI.

In that company, despite occasionally skewing generic, Wolverine’s bloodthirsty focus on action is something that makes it stand out.

Marvel’s Wolverine launches on September 15th on the PS5.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse AI works and creeps me out
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Meta has launched its new Muse assistant, marking the company’s first real foray into AI-powered productivity tools. The company says its AI agent can “take the busywork off your plate” by helping you with online shopping, emails, trip-planning, and more. I decided to try out the new tool and see how well it performed — especially from a company that previously prioritized entertainment over productivity. Though the AI assistant generally worked as I expected it to, the unnerving amount of information it autonomously gleaned about me largely overshadowed my experience.

One of the first tasks I assigned Muse, which carries out actions using a cloud-based virtual computer, was to sort through my Gmail inbox and delete messages I don’t need. That required me to connect Muse to my Google account and give it permission to access, read, and delete emails. The process didn’t go smoothly on mobile; the Google sign-in screen kept glitching and returning me to the Muse website instead of the app. I eventually got it working on my laptop, where it deleted thousands of promotional emails and updates. I didn’t feel good about permitting Muse to view all of my emails given Meta’s track record on privacy over the years.

Muse did a good job at clearing out my emails. Screenshot: The Verge

Meta says it designed Muse to only exchange data with third-party apps “that’s needed for them to work for you.” The company also says that it doesn’t share your information with advertisers. I still felt uneasy, but I pushed on anyway, linking my Amazon account to Muse. I asked the AI agent to pick out workout tops for me based on a specific size, style, and colors. Before placing the order, Muse noticed I had other items in my cart and asked if I wanted to remove them. The consideration pleasantly surprised me. Once I signed off on the purchase, it proceeded to successfully buy only the tank tops.

Shifting gears, I tried out some of Muse’s other capabilities, which allow it to generate AI podcasts similar to Gemini Notebook, create images and videos, as well as develop interactive webpages or documents called “artifacts.” Muse denied my requests to generate images of a “cartoon mouse with red pants” and a “cartoon guy with a red hat, blue overalls, brown hair, and a mustache.

However, it readily generated a video and several images of a product launch event featuring devices with Apple’s logo when asked. In one image, Muse created what looks like an iPhone-like foldable, an Apple Watch, and AirPods. Each device is propped up on a stand with Apple’s logo on it, while a presenter stands in front of a backdrop plastered with the company’s recognizable bitten apple. The phone even included Apple’s native app icons on the fake iPhone, though it hallucinated and named the App Store “Photos,” while calling Maps, Music, and the actual Photos app “Calender.” Muse refused to generate an image of an “Apple CEO.”

Muse wouldn’t generate an image of an Apple CEO, but it still plastered the company’s logo everywhere. Image: Muse

Then things got weird. I tapped over to the “Feed” tab, where Muse generates a news feed of sorts based on a text prompt. I submitted the prompt that Meta includes by default: “Make me a feed about my interests. Keep the tone clear and direct. Ensure it is quick to skim. Try to avoid clickbait.” It returned several AI-generated summaries of current events, including blurbs about Apple’s iPhone Duo launch event, the dangerous surf hitting California’s coast, and tankers destroyed in the Iran war. The app also listed several news stories from the state where I’m currently visiting my family, which Muse admitted it pulled from the shipping address on my Amazon order.

I dove deeper from there and asked Muse what else it might know about me based on the Instagram and Facebook accounts I signed up to use the AI agent with. It rattled off my very specific interests, ranging from anime and CrossFit to Labrador retrievers, Florida wildlife, and ’90s/2000s nostalgia — many of the same topics that frequently pop up in my Instagram Reels feed.

Curious, I asked Muse to tell me where it got that information. “Honestly, Instagram doesn’t show you that exact list anywhere in the app — I read it through the account’s API data, which surfaces more than the UI does,” Muse wrote. “The closest thing you can see yourself is your ad topics… That shows the topics advertisers can target you with, and you can remove ones you don’t want or choose to see less of them.” I checked the “Ad topics” list in my Instagram settings menu, and while it does include some vague categories, like workouts, music, and electronics, it’s not the same level of detail that Muse provided. The Verge reached out to Meta about the data Muse can access inside Instagram and Facebook but didn’t immediately hear back.

Muse says it accessed my specific interests through Instagram’s API. Screenshot: The Verge

Like some of the other agentic AI tools I’ve tried out, Muse does a decent job at performing low-stakes tasks. I also like that it generates a running list of “ideas” that give personalized suggestions on how to use the tool, like providing side-by-side comparisons of products, finding and cancelling forgotten subscriptions, and keeping track of the next release of Pokémon cards. Muse keeps a running list of “goals” to complete based on your conversations with the AI agent, too.

Muse delivered on its promise of handling life’s more mundane tasks in the background, but the level of personal details Muse scooped up from sources unavailable even to me was enough to leave me with an uneasy feeling about letting Muse sort through personal emails and handle my credit card. That level of suspicion is going to be the real hurdle for Meta to overcome.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo’s hardware doesn’t look special, but its software might be
Tech.content:
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has pulled off a familiar trick. It arrives into a mature Android foldable market with a handful of hardware features we’ve mostly already seen elsewhere, but paired with a level of software polish that makes a lot of them feel new again. It’s those software flourishes that have me excited to try the iPhone Duo when it launches next month, but I’m less convinced that its hardware will be anything special.

If Apple had gotten there first, the Duo’s biggest surprise would have been its squat, wide, passport-inspired shape. But its slow-moving supply chain meant that Huawei, Samsung, and Xiaomi all managed to beat Apple to market with similarly sized rivals, so the unusual design already feels fairly familiar — helped by Samsung’s aggressive efforts to market its new design.

More has been made of Apple’s efforts to eliminate the foldable display’s crease, which seem to have been largely successful. Apple attributes it to a 100-component hinge, custom adhesives that allow the display layers to “glide” over one another, and a matte finish that reduces glare and reflections to make the crease harder to spot. Trying the phone at Apple’s event yesterday, Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel said that you can’t really see the crease, but that “if you go looking for it, you can definitely feel one.”

It sounds, and looks, impressive, but Apple is far from the first to do it. Samsung made great strides in eliminating the crease on its Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra thanks to new titanium display layers. Before that, Oppo all but eliminated its Find N6 crease by using 3D printing to fill the minute gaps across the hinge. I’d have to see all those phones side by side to see which crease is subtlest, but even if Apple does win, it won’t be by much.

None of the iPhone Duo’s other standout hardware features are true firsts either. Google beat it to an IP68 rating, now even surpassed by Honor’s IP69. Samsung, Oppo, and Honor have all offered stylus support before — though Samsung has since dropped it. Samsung also moved on from the under-display selfie camera, which has always been hamstrung by poor photo and video quality and a distractingly visible patch on the screen.

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

In other ways, the hardware even feels behind the competition. The Duo is the thickest of this new wave of wide foldables, though at 5.2mm when open it’s still thinner than the iPhone Air. The weight is a more obvious issue: The 254g Duo is 26 percent heavier than the Z Fold 8 — a 53g difference — which is going to be pretty noticeable. You have to go back to 2022’s Z Fold 4 to find a Samsung foldable that’s heavier, TriFold excluded.

There’s also no evidence that Apple has adopted silicon-carbon batteries yet, which have allowed Samsung, Motorola, and other Android manufacturers to fit bigger capacities into the smaller spaces of foldable phones. Apple says the phone should still deliver a full 24 hours of regular use, but Honor’s Magic V6 uses silicon-carbon to deliver two days of life.

The rear cameras are pretty basic too, with a pair of 48-megapixel shooters and no telephoto. That’s almost an exact match for the cameras on the Z Fold 8, but Google, Motorola, Xiaomi and others are now providing capable triple cameras across their foldable lines, and the iPhone Duo already lags behind.

It looks as good as any Android foldable on paper, but it doesn’t look better than many of them

None of this is to say that the Duo looks like a bad piece of hardware. Every foldable phone is a compromise, and Apple has picked a similar set of compromises to Samsung in order to get this phone out the door at $1,999. It looks as good as any Android foldable on paper, but it doesn’t look better than many of them.

Where that might change is the software. Google has made an effort to make Android more flexible and adaptable to suit folding phones, while OEMs deliver custom solutions to push things further, but none have rewritten the rulebook quite like Apple.

The version of iOS 27 running on the iPhone Duo isn’t the same as on other iPhones, but it doesn’t match the iPad either. The biggest change takes the dock from the bottom of the display and lays it out vertically along the right-hand side. The Dynamic Island is turned vertical and thrown in here too, while the status bar collapses into a small circular icon in the top-right corner. This big change is bolstered by clever little touches throughout, like a dynamic blur effect that shifts as you open the screen, creating a fluidity no Android foldable has so far matched. It’s a total transformation of the iOS layout that specifically has foldables in mind.

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

The point of all that change is to ensure consistency between the outer and inner screens. Open the iPhone Duo on the homescreen and almost everything will stay in place, making the move between screens feel seamless. That effect won’t hold in full-screen apps of course, which will adapt to fill the space, but that right-hand UI rail will be fixed. Locking the whole phone interface to the right-hand edge doesn’t sound great for left-handed users though, who are likely to find the Duo unusually awkward to use unless Apple adds the option to flip everything to the other side.

StandBy mode has also been retooled for the Duo. Prop the phone down half-open and it will enter StandBy, letting you use it as a digital photo frame, smart display, or just get quick access to a few key widgets, like the clock. Finally, the $2,000 alarm clock you’ve always dreamed of.

Photo by Antonio Di Benedetto / The Verge

Not everything is as ambitious. Multitasking looks limited so far, with the option to run two apps in split-screen, including two windows of the same app, and save pairs to reopen together. Android rivals offer similar, but support three split-screen apps at once, and often more sitting in flexible, resizeable floating windows.

But Apple’s software power doesn’t only lie in its OS. It’s the only phone manufacturer with the influence to shift the app ecosystem at large, and with the Duo it hopes to push third-party developers to adopt its best foldable features. It already showed off Netflix, Slack, and Zoom apps with custom Duo support, in some cases adapting dynamically depending on how flexed the hinge is.

Photo by Antonio Di Benedetto / The Verge

Android foldable features are still rare, with most apps simply changing size to fit the varying screens. Even that has its limits — I found a few apps ran awkwardly on the Fold 8’s short outer display. Apple is likely to have an easier time ensuring developers optimize their apps to suit both of the Duo’s displays.

Most apps do little else to take advantage of dual displays, multiple cameras, or semi-open states like a tented mode. A few video apps adapt their playback controls when foldables are half-open, but that’s about it so far. Of course, some of those app developers might take their iOS foldable features and eventually roll them out to Android too, so Apple’s advantage might not last forever.

It’ll take more time with the Duo to see exactly how it stacks up against the latest models from the Android side of life. So far it doesn’t look like Apple has surpassed its rivals on the hardware side, but its total control of software may give it an edge regardless.

Tech.title: India’s Pocket FM doubles revenue run rate to $500M as AI powers 93% of audio content
Tech.content:
Pocket FM, an Indian audio storytelling platform, has doubled its annualized revenue run rate to $500 million over the past year as it increasingly turns to artificial intelligence to produce its content.

AI now powers 93% of Pocket FM’s overall catalog and is used to produce 99% of its new content, co-founder and CEO Rohan Nayak said in an interview.

The shift comes as generative AI makes deeper inroads into content production. However, Pocket FM, which started in 2018 as a platform for serialized audio stories, still relies on human creators for ideas and storytelling, while using AI to turn those concepts into finished content at scale.

“We want to create great IPs that last 100 years, and that needs humans,” Nayak told TechCrunch.

Pocket FM’s current approach focuses on building AI tools around the creative process instead of generating content autonomously. AI head Vasu Sharma, a former Meta and Tesla scientist, told TechCrunch that the startup has trained its own models for tasks including creative writing and text-to-speech, using years of production data and signals on how listeners engage with stories.

Economics have played a key role in Pocket FM’s push toward AI. The technology, Nayak said, has made its content production about 80 times cheaper. He added that 100 hours of content, which previously took about a year to produce, can now be made in a day.

The move toward AI has also led to a notable increase in the amount of content Pocket FM produces. Its more than 550,000 creators are now producing about 2.5 million hours of AI-powered content a year, Nayak said. Two years ago, the startup’s entire catalog comprised about 100,000 hours of content. The platform has overall built a library of more than 770,000 audio series.

The influx of content has helped Pocket FM improve its ability to retain listeners, Nayak said, noting that the startup’s 12-month revenue retention rate has risen to 76% from 44% two years ago. Nayak attributed that in part to having more stories available to match different listener preferences.

Pocket FM Co-founder and CEO Rohan Nayak Image Credits:Pocket FM

Pocket FM’s annualized revenue run rate stood at about $250 million a year ago before climbing to $430 million in April and $500 million now. (The startup calculates the figure by multiplying its monthly revenue by 12, rather than using contracted recurring revenue, Nayak explained.)

The growth came as Pocket FM ramped up its use of AI in content production, expanded into markets including the U.K., Germany, and France, and launched user-generated content in the U.S.

Some 96 titles on Pocket FM’s platform have now generated more than $1 million in revenue each, including 13 that have crossed $10 million, the startup said.

Beginning with India as its primary market, Pocket FM now has more than 250 million listeners across over 20 countries. The U.S. market, which grew around 70% over the past year, is its largest market, accounting for about 70% of its annualized revenue run rate.

About $85 million of Pocket FM’s annualized revenue comes from ads, while the remaining roughly $415 million comes from users paying to unlock individual episodes, Nayak said.

Moving beyond audio

Pocket FM’s parent company, Pocket Entertainment, is now looking to take its AI-driven content model beyond audio. Its three-month-old microdrama app, Pocket Saga, has reached an annualized revenue run rate of about $15 million, Nayak told TechCrunch.

The Pocket Saga app is currently available only in the U.S. and its content is entirely AI-produced, unlike Pocket FM, where humans remain involved in developing stories. The startup is also using successful Pocket FM audio stories to create AI-generated videos for Pocket Saga, with no traditional live-action production involved.

Pocket Saga on iOS Image Credits:Apple App Store

Pocket Entertainment plans to expand further beyond audio and microdramas, with plans to enter at least two more entertainment formats over the next five years. The company also aims to turn successful stories from its platforms into books, television, and movies through licensing deals.

Alongside the growth, Bengaluru- and Culver City, California-based Pocket Entertainment is in talks with investors about raising fresh capital. A recent report said the startup was seeking $100 million to $120 million at a valuation of about $2 billion.

Nayak did not deny the talks but said the startup was under no immediate pressure to raise capital. He declined to say how much it could raise or at what valuation but noted that a new round would primarily be used to invest further in AI and new entertainment formats.

Meanwhile, Pocket Entertainment said it is profitable and generating positive cash flow on an adjusted basis, but declined to disclose its profit, cash flow, or margins.

A public listing, however, is still some way off. Nayak told TechCrunch that Pocket Entertainment does not plan to go public in the next 24 months. It’s keeping its options open for an eventual listing in either India or the U.S., though.

Tech.title: Instagram’s latest feature lets you add tagged posts to your profile grid
Tech.content:
Instagram is rolling out a small but useful new feature that gives users a little more control over what appears on their profiles. Starting today, you can add posts you’re tagged in directly to your main profile grid.

While it’s not exactly a groundbreaking update, it’s one of those changes that a lot of people will probably find useful. Most of us have experienced coming home from a party, concert, vacation, or night out with friends and going through the shared album, only to realize one of them has already beaten everyone to the punch and posted one of the best group photos, tagging you in the process.

While you could post the same photo yourself, that feels a little awkward. So Instagram now has a solution.

You can add a tagged post to your grid from the DM notification you receive when you’re tagged, directly from the post itself, or through your Tagged tab. If you change your mind later, you can easily remove the post from your profile.

The original post stays exactly where it is. Adding it to your grid doesn’t delete or duplicate the original post, and you can remove it from your profile at any time without removing it from your Tagged tab.

Image Credits:Instagram

Instagram says the feature could also be useful for creator collaborations, giving creators another way to showcase posts they’ve been tagged in without having to republish the same content or use the “Invite collaborators” option. It could also come in handy for brand campaigns featuring multiple creators who want to highlight a piece of content they were all tagged in on their profiles.

The update is part of a broader push from Instagram to give users more control over how their profiles look. Back in June, Instagram introduced the “Reorder your grid” feature, allowing users to rearrange the content on their main profile grid.

Instagram has also been adding new tools to make creating and managing content easier. One recent addition is “First Draft,” a new editing feature that automatically trims selected video clips and removes pauses, pulling together the best moments into an initial cut.

There’s also the newly launched “Replace Audio” tool, which lets users update the music on an existing post whenever they want.

Tech.title: Google is making it easier to switch between password managers on Android
Tech.content:
In Brief

Google on Thursday introduced a new password manager switching experience on Android that doesn’t require you to download CSV files when migrating to a new app.

With the new feature, users will be able to move all of their passwords — and even passkeys — between apps seamlessly.

To use the new system, users first open their new password manager app and choose to import or copy passwords from the old manager app. Android will detect manager apps on the device and coordinate transfer between both apps. Users can review the information being transferred and approve it in a few taps.

Image Credits:Google

Because this method also supports passkey transfer, users won’t need to set them up again when moving to a new password manager app. Plus, the company said that this averts the risk of exposing data from a CSV file.

Google said the new experience is already available on select partners as well as in Google’s own password manager app. Bitwarden, 1Password, and Dashlane are currently supported, with more apps coming in the future.

The password manager switching feature will be available on all devices running Android 8 or above.

Tech.title: The Boring Company raises $3B in round led by UAE
Tech.content:
In Brief

Elon Musk’s tunneling company, The Boring Company, has raised a $3 billion Series D funding round that pushes its valuation to $23 billion.

The round was led by the United Arab Emirates. The Boring Company said Thursday that it now plans to dig more than 150 kilometers of tunnels in the Middle Eastern country. Andreessen Horowitz, Sequoia Capital, Human Capital, Vy Capital, and Valor Equity Partners also participated.

The Wall Street Journal reported in July that The Boring Company was looking to raise as much as $4 billion.

The Boring Company has done most of its digging to date in Las Vegas, Nevada, where it operates a handful of tunnels that connect hotel casinos and the convention center. It recently started work on a project in Nashville, Tennessee, that will involve a 10-mile “loop” underground.

The company has stated that its goal is to “solve traffic” by moving vehicle travel into an underground, three-dimensional network of tunnels.

Tech.title: AI agents are flooding public services with new requests
Tech.content:
As AI makes it easier to fill forms and file complaints, public services around the world are seeing enormous jumps in applications and other requests.

In the United Kingdom, complaints to the housing ombudsman more than doubled since the introduction of ChatGPT, rising from 2,600 in 2022 to just over 7,000 last year. The United States’ Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) saw 5x growth in complaints over the same period. There were similar jumps in Brazilian judicial petitions and German parliamentary petitions.

Researcher Chris Schmitz is tracking this rise as part of a broader trend he called “agentic flooding.” In a paper set to be presented next month at the AI Ethics and Society conference, he looks at 84 different cases of potential flooding across 11 jurisdictions, finding broad evidence that AI tools are changing the way people interact with public services.

The harder question is what to do in response. While some of the new filings are clearly adversarial, others are the result of legitimate applicants using AI to file claims that would otherwise be abandoned. While some might see the new applications as AI-generated spam, Schmitz sees it as a rare opportunity to remake social services for the AI era.

Schmitz looked at services ranging from welfare applications to official judicial appeals, but they all have online services that could be accessed by an AI assistant. (The full dataset is hosted here, for reference.) For methodological reasons, Schmitz’s paper stops short of saying AI is directly causing the surge of new applicants. But most of the 84 cases follow the same basic arc, where submissions were roughly flat before 2022, then rose at increasing speed as AI technology diffuses. Crucially, most cases have not seen that growth slow down, suggesting it will likely keep rising for years to come.

For Schmitz, it’s easy to see how the increasing skills and availability of AI would drive increased usage.

“People are finding out that this is something one can do, and incrementally, it is just getting easier to do it … before it might have been a question of a lot of dragging context together and prompting ChatGPT 3.5 very precisely, it may now be a question of just pasting or taking a photo of a letter with your Claude app and getting a pretty good response in one shot,” he said.

The jump in volume is similar to what many bug-bounty services also experienced last year, as companies found their inboxes flooded with low-quality reports generated by LLMs. The reports rarely contained significant security issues, but companies were still obligated to vet the reports as they came in, presenting a significant drain on resources. It’s easy to imagine public services facing a similar problem, as they manage 5x more applicants with the same budget.

But where the bug bounty programs were flooded with worthless submissions, Schmitz says most of the new applications to public services are coming from real people with legitimate claims.

“The vast majority of cases we find are people who are entitled to claim for something, claiming for that thing,” he told TechCrunch.

If those people weren’t claiming the benefits before, it may have been because the work of applying was too forbidding — something known in the policy world as administrative burden. Now that AI can lift that burden, it could be an opportunity to remake many of these services in a more AI-friendly way.

It’s a major task, which we mostly haven’t begun to tackle, but Schmitz sees it as reason for optimism.

“A big part of making AI go well is being able to detail out what the good version of things looks like. And anyone who’s ever used ChatGPT to do the tax return knows that there’s a good version here where you’re being helped,” Schmitz says. “This could be the moment to say, ‘we need to rethink pretty much everything about how this process looks.’”

Tech.title: Bending Spoons to buy collaboration tools maker Miro for $1.36B, 90% less than its 2022 valuation
Tech.content:
Bending Spoons is continuing its trend of buying once-sought-after software companies for pennies on the dollar. This time, the Italian company is buying Miro for $1.36 billion in cash (equity value of $1.79 billion), a mighty dip in valuation for the once-hot workplace collaboration startup that was awarded a price tag of $17.5 billion in late 2021.

Founded in 2011 as a whiteboarding tool called RealtimeBoard, Miro found great fortune during the COVID-19 pandemic, when companies moved to remote work en masse and found their employees wanting to replicate the experience of collaborating on a physical whiteboard.

Miro quickly capitalized on that momentum by building a platform that could integrate with more than 250 apps and struck partnerships with Atlassian, Cisco, Microsoft, and Zoom. The company also started letting its users build integrations with common tools and customize the base product to meet their needs. Today, it calls itself an “AI innovation workspace” that offers AI assistants for its whiteboard tools, AI workflows, prototyping tools, and AI connectors that pull context from various platforms like GitHub, Jira, and Slack.

By 2022, Miro had grown from 5 million to about 30 million users within a scant two years, and its paying customer base had expanded by 550% — factors that likely contributed to its immense valuation at the time.

By all indications, the company has continued growing, though not at that blistering pace. Today, Miro has more than 4 million paying users and 100 million total users. Bending Spoons said Miro now has about $600 million in annual recurring revenue, of which 90% comes from businesses and enterprises. The company also has about $435 million in net cash and is profitable.

Still, the 92% dip in Miro’s valuation illustrates just how much software-as-a-service (SaaS) multiples have unwound since its heyday in 2021. By 2022, the dying pandemic tailwinds spurred companies to tighten spending by cutting down on duplicate apps and licenses. Miro, competing with much-better funded rivals such as Canva, Figma, and Microsoft in the workplace collaboration space, likely found itself shoved aside as businesses started preferring suites of various products instead of individual collaboration tools.

Miro, which had about 1,200 employees in 2022, cut jobs twice, laying off 119 staff in February 2023 and reportedly another 275 people in October 2024.

Bending Spoons, however, is probably happy it is able to snap up a company that’s been doing quite well for a smidgen of its former, arguably inflated, value. In that way, Miro is pretty similar to Airtable, which was valued at over $11 billion in the boom days of 2021 but sold to Bending Spoons for $1.28 billion last month.

The Italian serial acquirer of software companies seems to be exploiting a specific change: large, recognizable SaaS companies that were priced in 2021 as if they’d become software giants, but matured into slower-growing but still substantial businesses with decent recurring revenue and established user bases.

Still, it’s curious why Miro’s board and investors agreed to sell at that price now, especially seeing that the company didn’t apparently need the cash. Has confidence in SaaS companies being able to go public or find a comparable exit really plummeted that low?

Tech.title: Maven Robotics wants to steal your robot deployment deal
Tech.content:
In 2024, Maven Robotics was brand new, and they had nothing — “a cartoon of a robot and a team of people,” CEO and co-founder Hamza Derbas told TechCrunch.

Still, they heard a large consumer goods company with logistics needs was in town to meet with four rival robot companies about automation. Derbas talked his way into a meeting with the company and, instead of talking about his views on robots, asked to visit their factories and warehouses.

“We saw how people were working; we zeroed in on flows we could immediately bring value to,” he told TechCrunch. “We showed them that our approach to robotics is different — we’re not trying to solve a single robot problem. We’re trying to autonomously take on the task end to end: It hooks in from one side to a warehouse management system; product goes on trucks on the other side.”

They won the deal, beating out companies with existing robots. After two years of work with that company and a few other partners, Derbas says Maven has as many as eight robots working 16 hours a day, with 99% or higher uptime.

Today, the startup is emerging from stealth after raising $100 million from RoboStrategy, LocalGlobe, Vine Ventures, and XTX Markets Ventures, with plans to build 250 of their third-generation robots and begin design on a fourth-generation platform.

Image Credits:Maven

Their robots sit on wheeled bases, capable of moving 10 miles an hour, with two arms that can lift up to 30 kilograms. Their main job is “mixed palletizing” — wooden pallets carrying boxed goods come from different factories to a distribution center, where the robot creates a new pallet containing a mix of goods to be sent to a store.

“Within 48 hours of them putting the stuff on the shelves, they want to change the mix based on real-time demand. Here’s an order with different mixed [products] going to that retail store; please build it out. It’s all done with human labor today, running around the warehouse picking one of this, one of that.”

At Maven’s Santa Clara facility, the robot moves smoothly about its work in a training area, using vacuum suckers to pick up and arrange the boxes at a reasonable speed. A live video screen shows two robots working in a customer facility while employees walk around them.

Derbas spent his career in automotive engineering, with a focus on EVs, but before Maven he spent nine years working at Apple on the company’s special project group, which he wouldn’t discuss but is widely thought to have been building a self-driving car before it was disbanded in 2024. That was when he started Maven with his brother, Khalid, who serves as the company’s CFO after a career in private equity.

Like other physical AI companies, the firm relies on veterans of self-driving car efforts, which have developed the most sophisticated approaches to training autonomous hardware from real data. That requires data pipelines that return information from operating robots within minutes or hours — “then retrain, evaluate, run ablation studies, figure out what’s the right set of weights, redeploy, and then turn that loop again.”

In a crowded world of robot companies, Maven sets itself apart with its focus on the realities of industrial operation. Jack Pearson, an investor at RoboStrategy who backed the company, says what sets the company apart is its background in industrial systems, rather than a research culture that is optimized for learning or focused on a specific architecture.

Agility, the robotics company going public this fall in a $2.5 billion SPAC deal, might be the most similarly positioned firm in the market, focused on safety and specific industrial workflows. But its robots stand on two legs, something Derbas, while stressing his respect for the company, says “make zero sense for anything they’re doing…they are very complex, unreliable, and add unnecessary cost. ROI is the name of the game here.”

That understanding of the realities of overheated facilities and the needs of the people who operate them has helped them get the startup out the door, but if Maven wants to expand beyond its current workflows, it will figure out some kind of research culture. While palletization might be an $80 billion market, the next set of tasks the company is targeting will require robotic manipulation capabilities that don’t yet exist.

Maven’s next big push is to collect more data and train its robots to be able to handle materials, and then to move toward automation and fabrication. The company will draw on its own systems, tap third-party providers, and has even developed a pair of pincer-like gloves that allow humans to emulate the form factor they want for their grippers. While the company bills itself as a maker of general-purpose robots, its strategy is to go task-by-task toward that goal.



“We’re grounded in solving one customer problem at a time,” Derbas said. “If you focus on solving problems and you pick sizeable problems, each problem is a multibillion-dollar market. If you do that, there’s plenty of data to master these skills.”

That process might be the most viable path to putting robots in the workplace — or an opportunity to get one-shotted by the next powerful physical AI model to roll out of the frontier labs.

“We’re not in the race for models — we’re in the race to solve industrial labor and make this work possible at the scale the world needs,” Derbas told TechCrunch.

Tech.title: Google signs its biggest rice-methane carbon credit deal with Indian startup Mitti Labs
Tech.content:
Google has agreed to buy 1 million carbon credits from Indian climate-tech startup Mitti Labs through 2030, in what the companies say is the largest publicly announced deal to date for credits generated from cutting methane emissions in rice farming.

The four-year agreement will cover rice farms across the Indian states of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana, reaching about 100,000 hectares at peak delivery, Mitti Labs co-founder Xavier Laguarta said in an interview. Financial terms were not disclosed.

The project will pay farmers to adopt practices that reduce how long rice fields remain flooded, cutting methane released during cultivation while also reducing water use. Mitti Labs says the technique can cut methane emissions by about 50% and irrigation water use by about 40% without reducing crop yields.

The deal comes as Google faces the challenge of reaching its goal of going net-zero emissions by 2030 amid investing heavily in artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Its greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 grew 18% year-over-year to about 14.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, per its environmental report (PDF) released in June.

Mitti Labs began talks with Google about a year ago, Laguarta told TechCrunch, as the tech company explored adding methane-reduction projects to its carbon-credit portfolio. Google was drawn in part to the project’s water savings and Mitti Labs’ ability to operate at scale, he stated.

The startup’s projects have saved more than 500 billion liters of water over the past two years. The Google deal, Laguarta said, would allow Mitti Labs to expand further, giving it the scale needed to work with large corporate buyers.

Mitti Labs’ Measurement Chamber at a Rice Farm Image Credits:Mitti Labs

“Having Google, one of the most sophisticated buyers in the market with rigorous due diligence processes, is obviously a good signal for us,” Laguarta said, adding that the deal would allow Mitti to scale significantly.

Google’s evaluation included scrutiny of Mitti Labs’ monitoring technology and visits to farms before the companies signed the agreement, Laguarta said. Founded in 2023, the New York- and Bengaluru-based startup has built a GeoAI platform that combines satellite radar imagery with field measurements to remotely track crop growth, soil moisture, and flooding across smallholder farms.

The platform uses synthetic aperture radar imagery from commercial and public satellites, with resolutions ranging from 50 centimeters to 10 meters. Mitti also uses proprietary data collected in the field to train its AI models, Laguarta said.

The credits sold to Google can be issued under either Gold Standard or Isometric, two carbon-credit certification bodies, Laguarta said. He added that the projects undergo independent third-party verification as part of the certification process before credits are issued.

In addition to Google, Mitti Labs works with customers including carbon marketplace Cool Effect, rice producer Ebro Foods, and agricultural company Syngenta. Laguarta told TechCrunch that the Google agreement is Mitti Labs’ largest offtake deal to date.

Mitti Labs currently works with more than 100,000 farmers and aims to have millions of farmers by 2030. The Google deal, Laguarta said, would help the startup move toward that goal by allowing it to expand its projects.

A majority of the revenue from the startup’s projects goes to farming communities, Laguarta noted. He declined to disclose how much farmers participating in the Google project would receive, however.

While the Google project is limited to India, Mitti Labs plans to launch operations in the Philippines later this year and expand into Indonesia and other Southeast Asian markets in 2027.

Laguarta sees room for the market to grow as more companies look to agricultural projects to tackle methane emissions. About 150 million farmers grow rice across India, Southeast Asia, and China, he told TechCrunch.

The deal with Mitti Labs is not Google’s first carbon-removal investment in India. In January 2025, the Mountain View, California-headquartered company partnered with Gurugram-based Varaha to buy 100,000 tons of carbon credits. That was Google’s first large-scale purchase of carbon removal credits in the country and the largest involving biomass-produced biochar.

Google is also turning to clean-energy projects in India to address its supply-chain emissions. The company has signed an agreement tied to a 150-megawatt solar project in Rajasthan, taking its contracted solar capacity with ReNew in the state to 300 megawatts.

Tech.title: Which iPhone 18 Model Should You Buy?
Tech.content:
With a fresh folding form factor, the new iPhone Duo is Apple’s most radical redesign in years. It lands alongside the more familiar-looking iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. There’s no regular iPhone 18, or at least, not yet. Rumors suggest we may see a more affordable base model, perhaps flanked by an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air, in spring 2027.

The two new Pro iPhones are available to preorder on September 12 and ship on September 18. You can preorder the iPhone Duo from October 16, ahead of a full release on October 23. But which iPhone 18 model is right for you? I’ll break down the differences and what these phones have in common, so you can choose with confidence. For options beyond the iPhone 18 lineup, read our Best iPhones guide.

Why You Might Not Need to Upgrade

Before you drop all those hard-earned dollars, remember that you probably don’t need the latest iPhone. If you have an older iPhone, Apple does a good job of updating the software (the iPhone 11 Pro is still supported), and for hardware issues, your iPhone might be repairable; maybe it needs a battery replacement or these troubleshooting tips. Don’t feel like you have to spring for Apple’s shiny new thing.

Sadly, Apple raised iPhone Pro prices this year, so both models are $100 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro series.

If you’re set on upgrading, consider raising funds by selling your old iPhone. Just be sure to back up your iPhone, and factory reset it before you sell or give it away. Once the new device arrives, we have tips on how to set up your new iPhone and what settings to change to get the most out of it.

Which iPhone 18 Is Right for You?

The Similarities

We’ll start by looking at what’s the same across the iPhone 18 models this year.

The Processor

All three new iPhones have Apple’s A20 Pro chip inside, and, you guessed it, this is Apple’s most powerful chip ever. Now, iPhones are already the most capable phones for raw compute power, but the A20 Pro promises a significant jump in performance (around 20 percent faster and 30 percent more efficient than the last generation). It also packs a new neural engine to power on-device AI and a new thermal design with a larger vapor chamber to keep things cool. For the iPhone Duo, the A20 Pro has a display engine to ensure smooth transitions between two screens. While Apple doesn’t list the RAM, every model is rumored to have 12 GB.

The Display

While they come in different sizes and the Duo has two, every iPhone features an OLED screen that Apple calls a Super Retina XDR display. They also have ProMotion technology, otherwise known as a 120-Hz refresh rate. These adaptive refresh rates can drop as low as 1 Hz when there's little activity on the screen, enabling features like the always-on display without draining the battery too much.

The displays are protected by the scratch-resistant and antireflective Ceramic Shield 2, the same as last year’s iPhone 17 range. And they can go from 1 nit up to 3,000 nits of brightness. Only the iPhone Duo has a custom nano-texture finish on the interior screen, giving it a matte look that’s designed to reduce glare and crease visibility.

The Usual Specs

All the phones have an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance, meaning they can survive a short dunk in fresh water. They all come in four storage options (256 GB, 512 GB, 1 TB, or 2 TB), support Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (MagSafe), USB-C 3.2, Dual SIM, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). It also has Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, Emergency SOS via Satellite, and Crash Detection.

The Differences

To help you better understand which model to buy, here's precisely where they diverge.

Tech.title: Best Robot Lawn Mowers (2026): 12+ Models Tested Over 3 Years
Tech.content:
Other Robot Mowers I Tested and Liked

Photograph: Simon Hill

Photograph: Simon Hill

Video: Simon Hill Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Roborock Rockmow Z120 Lidar Shop Now

Roborock Rockmow X120H Lidar for $3,200: Better known for its robot vacuums, Roborock also makes robot mowers, and the X120H Lidar is its flagship model (discounted to a far more reasonable $2,000 at the time of writing). I actually tested the UK model, the identical Z120 Lidar (£2,299). This mower employs Lidar and AI vision, so it can cut without satellite connections, with no RTK antenna required. It also supports 4G and comes with a 3-year data plan. It is Four Wheel Drive (4WD) and has ingenious front wheels that pivot and turn independently to navigate tight areas smoothly, with minimal churning of your lawn. There’s a single disc underneath with six cutting blades and a reasonably wide, 9.5-inch (24 cm) cutting width. It supports a 0.8 to 2.7-inch (20 to 70 mm) cutting height, can cover up to around 21,500 square feet, and, most impressively, can handle an 80 percent (up to 39-degree) slope. A full charge gives you 110 minutes of mowing time, and it takes around 50 minutes to charge.

After some minor setup hassles (battery error), the Rockmow Z120 has impressed me. It looks to be the most capable mower I have tested yet for navigating uneven terrain. Apparently, it can automatically create maps, but it defaulted to the manual mode for me, prompting me to remote control it around the borders of my lawn. Edge mowing is the big disappointment, with the mower regularly leaving a strip on one edge of my lawn. I’m not keen on the optional PreciEdge Module (£150) that promises to reduce edges to 3 cm. I haven’t tested it, but feel it should be included in a mower this expensive. Why is it optional? Who doesn’t want their edges properly cut? It avoided most obstacles just fine, but was occasionally oversensitive, avoiding plants swaying over the border edge. The Rain Protection mode is a little too sensitive, preventing the mower from starting several hours after rain, so I had to override it. It also lacks a Spot Mode, though it is so heavy I would not want to carry it between lawn areas. I think this design, with the rotating wheels, has real potential if Roborock can improve the AI/software. Unfortunately, it's not currently available in the US right now, but hopefully be back in stock soon since it was released just this past summer.

Eufy Robot Lawn Mower E15 for $1,300: This is another wire-free mower that uses a camera system to automatically map lawns and avoid obstacles. It’s very similar to my top pick and also has a super handy Spot Mode that lets you drop and mow on unmapped areas. But even after a big price drop from its original RRP, it’s still more expensive than the TerraMow, and it’s not as good at cutting edges. It can cover up to 0.2 acres (8,700 square feet), cut from 1 to 3 inches, and handle up to 18-degree slopes. It is also fairly quiet and has GPS tracking, but you must have Wi-Fi coverage in your backyard, or you'll need a 4G data subscription. I found the setup lengthy due to a firmware download, but the mapping and the first cut were decent. Object avoidance is very good. The E15 can only run during the day and doesn't cope very well with inclines. I also found it frequently failed to cut the edges of the lawn and doesn't perform well if the grass is damp. The more affordable Eufy C15 (£999) is very similar, but designed for smaller lawns (up to 5,300 square feet) and only available in the UK and Europe right now.

It kept my back lawn neat without issues, but my front lawn has a dip and ill-defined border that it struggled with. That said, every time it looked as though it might get stuck, it managed to maneuver out of trouble. There’s a dial to adjust mowing height for the C15, whereas you can do it in the app with the E15. Both come with a covered charging base, which often costs extra with rivals. If you’re interested, watch out for a sale event (I’ve seen the E15 drop below $1,000, which makes it far more tempting).

Segway Navimow X430 for $2,249: My backyard is both a Wi-Fi and 5G dead zone. Before manually mowing the yard I save all my podcasts and music to offline mode, and I let my fiancee know she’ll need to deploy a carrier pigeon if she needs to get my attention. So, it was a relief to see just how quickly the navigation system of the Navimow X430 recognized the unit across the treacherous triple lot that surrounds my house. It connected within seconds of beginning the initial setup and 20 minutes later, the robot mower was on its way using the handy auto-mapping function. As it turns out, I didn't need the three beers I'd brought with me when I embarked upon this process, assuming it would be on par with the weeks-long headache it took to get the Mammotion Luba 2 connected and operational last summer.

It did an above-average job on its first pass despite the endless flurry of compost piles, stray bushes, fencing and detritus from half-finished gardening projects that litter my half-acre lawn, though I opted for manual mapping to take advantage of its aptitude at hugging the wobbly brick borders of some raised beds with relative ease. The sites claims that it can handle “tall, thick and dense grass," which I had the perfect scenario to test. After a two weeks of dealing with an endless cycle of torrential downpours and blistering heat, I was left with few open windows for a good mow before my patchy, crabby grass got too unwieldy for the Navimow’s 4-inch height maximum. I watched with disappointment as it casually drove over some stray blades that went to seed without making any impact whatsoever. Despite that, the Navimow X430 has impressed me with its ease-of-use. We'll update our impressions here with additional testing, but so far so good.—Pete Cottell

Photograph: Simon Hill

Sunseeker X7 Gen 2 Wireless Robot Lawn Mower for $2,700: If you have a large, challenging lawn, this could be a mower worth considering. It combines built-in NET-RTK, GPS, and AI vision, has floating dual disc blades for uneven terrain, and can work at night thanks to an Indirect Time of Flight camera. It is also all-wheel drive (AWD) and can handle 70 percent slopes up to 35 degrees. It can cover more than 32,000 square feet. I love the wide 14-inch cutting width, the relatively quiet operation (it never went over 60 decibels but was usually even quieter), even though I’d advise against mowing at night because of the risk to wildlife. Sadly, the automatic mapping was mediocre, and there’s no Spot Mode for a drop-and-mow. This Gen 2 mower brings a raft of improvements over the original, including night vision, faster processing, enhanced durability and traction, a built-in screen, and onboard RTK without a separate antenna. But only the original Sunseeker X7 ($2,700) is available to buy on Amazon. You currently have to go through a dealer to get the Gen 2.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Husqvarna Aspire R6V for £999: While the reliable Husqvarna 410XE Nera was my top pick for a long time, you can get more affordable mowers now, without the hassle of RTK antennas. The Husqvarna Aspire R6V is just such a mower. It uses a combination of GPS and AI vision with a camera on the front. It was easy to set up and map the lawn in the app, but you will need a good Wi-Fi signal across your yard for it to work effectively. I was a little disappointed in the sensitive obstacle avoidance, as it left large uncut strips around the edges of my lawn. I was able to reduce the verge a little with some tinkering, but it was still larger than the recommendations above. Note: This model is currently not available in the US.

Anthbot Genie 3000 for $900: This often-discounted mower was my budget pick for a while, but mowers have moved on, so you can get better performance without the satellite antenna now. It offers auto-mapping, but the remote-control option works better. The mower cut my lawn effectively, but even after repeated map updates, it left an uncut verge. The obstacle avoidance works well, and it cuts in neat lines. It had no issues returning to charge or following a schedule. The voice that says it has connected or started mowing began to annoy me, but thankfully, it can be turned off. There were some glitches with rain alerts that prevented it from mowing, even long after the rain had stopped. I also experienced some flaky connection issues with the GPS, and it occasionally got stuck. While there is support for multiple areas, the mower often struggled picking up a signal in my front yard. Ultimately, this is still a decent mower when discounted, provided you have a modest-sized, straightforward lawn.

Mova Lidax 2000 for $1,199: With a sleek design and a mixture of 360-degree lidar for 3D mapping and a camera with AI vision, this mower proved very effective. Setup was straightforward, and there’s no need for wires or an antenna, though I did have to adjust the map manually. You can set multiple areas, and its navigation is generally very good. It mowed in neat lines, successfully avoided thin posts for the badminton net and other obstacles, and completed an excellent edge pass at the end. With some of the closest edge mowing I’ve seen, I was all set to recommend this mower, but then it got stuck. A couple of times, it seemed to be stuck, then managed to free itself, but an uneven problem spot proved to be its nemesis, and it chewed up a patch of grass trying to get free. Eventually, I had to make that spot a no-go zone. This mower is still worth considering, particularly if you see it on sale; just be prepared to tweak the map. The 2000 covers up to half an acre. If you have a quarter of an acre or less, the Mova Lidax 1000 ($1,299) is much cheaper but has the same features.

Avoid These Mowers

Stiga A6V Photograph: Simon Hill

Stiga A6V: I like that this mower only needs the charging station and has no need for an antenna. The buggy setup was my first red flag, as a firmware update failed and had to be repeated. Once up and running, I found the mower always left a big verge, even after adjustment. The AI vision camera is very slow to react to obstacles and not very good at navigating around them. It hit the ball several times in my test, and I had to hit the stop button as it got too close to my cat. It lacks useful features like automapping and spot-mow, and there are better options for the money above. The yellow finish is a bit garish for my tastes too.

EcoFlow Blade Photograph: Simon Hill

EcoFlow Blade: While it was easy to set up and cut my lawn nicely without the need for any boundary wire, the EcoFlow Blade sometimes struggled with GPS navigation and ended up stuck in a flower bed. It also left an untouched strip around the edge of my lawn. The object avoidance was solid, and it can be automated in the app, though it occasionally failed to start a scheduled cut for me. EcoFlow seems to have discontinued this model, though it is still on sale in Europe. Probably best to avoid.

Yardcare E400 Photograph: Simon Hill

Yardcare E400: Curious about the budget end of the robot mower market, I agreed to try the Yardcare E400, but this mower was an unmitigated disaster from start to finish. It’s a boundary wire model, so you must run wire around the area you want mowed. Yardcare suggests it can cover up to 4,300 square feet and cut grass between 0.8 and 2.4 inches. The problem is that it gets stuck frequently and struggles to even get on and off its charging station reliably. After trying multiple fixes to no avail and going through customer support, I had to conclude that this model has a serious design flaw.

How Do Robot Lawn Mowers Work? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Perhaps counterintuitively, the setup instructions for your robot lawn mower will likely tell you to start by cutting the grass. Robot mowers mostly can’t deal with long grass. Unlike traditional mowers, these robots don’t collect grass cuttings; they mulch instead, and they are designed to cut frequently, keeping your lawn short and simply leaving the cuttings on the ground, which can also improve lawn health. Most robot mowers are designed to run two or three times a week during the growing season (from late spring to early fall). They have rechargeable batteries onboard and can last from half an hour to several hours on a full charge. They return to the charging base and recharge automatically when their power runs low. Most mowers have simple controls, a small display, and an emergency stop button. You can generally start and stop mowing, set schedules, and create or edit mapped areas using the onboard controls or the companion mobile app, very much like a robot vacuum. What Features Should I Look For in a Robot Mower? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron There are many factors to consider in choosing a robot mower, and the best choice for you often depends on your yard. Lawn Size and Shape Robot lawn mowers are generally rated to cover a specific square footage, with wider coverage requiring models with larger batteries. Alongside yard size, you should consider the shape and topography of your lawn, as most robot mowers will struggle with steep inclines. While you can often map out separate areas so your robot mower can mow front and back lawns, for example, it will generally need you to lift and carry it between those areas. If you have an uneven garden or steep slopes, look for a four-wheel-drive (4WD) or all-wheel-drive (AWD) mower and check the manufacturer's rating for inclines. Navigation Type There are a few types of navigation that robot mowers employ. We’ve tested five different approaches, though some mowers combine multiple technologies for better performance. Satellite : Often employing something called Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) Global Positioning System (GPS), these mowers need a satellite signal to navigate and will have a receiver that must be placed in the open with a clear line of sight to the sky. Satellite navigation mowers are not suitable for areas with tall trees or buildings.

Satellite navigation mowers are not suitable for areas with tall trees or buildings. Light Detection and Ranging (lidar) : This technology sends out rapid laser pulses to 3D map the terrain (it is also used by self-driving cars). It enables mowers to cut grass under thick tree canopies or near tall buildings where GPS signals usually fail.

It enables mowers to cut grass under thick tree canopies or near tall buildings where GPS signals usually fail. Cameras : Cameras and onboard AI are used for obstacle detection and avoidance. AI vision can automatically map areas and cut the grass while avoiding obstacles it encounters, much like how most robot vacuums navigate a home to clean the floors.
