AI vision can automatically map areas and cut the grass while avoiding obstacles it encounters, much like how most robot vacuums navigate a home to clean the floors. Wire boundary : These mowers require you to install a perimeter wire as a boundary around your lawn that marks out the border the mower should not cross. It's a messy job that can be tricky.

: These mowers require you to install a perimeter wire as a boundary around your lawn that marks out the border the mower should not cross. It's a messy job that can be tricky. Remote control: You mow your lawn from the comfort of your home using a remote controller or an app on your phone. Some only work via remote control, while others can also cut automatically. Power and Charging Robot mowers generally come with large charging docks, and you’ll need to earmark a suitable spot for yours. They usually have extensive weatherproof cabling, but you will have to find a route to an outdoor socket. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth To connect to your mower and schedule a mow, update the firmware, or remote control it where supported, you need a decent Wi-Fi signal or a Bluetooth connection. It’s best to set up your mower’s charging station within range of your Wi-Fi network. Some mowers also need a strong Wi-Fi signal to operate effectively, so you might consider adding an outdoor mesh router. If you want to connect your phone via Bluetooth, you will have to get quite close. How Noisy Are Robot Mowers? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Most robot mowers are far quieter than their traditional counterparts. You can expect them to operate at around 55 decibels, though they may go as high as 75 decibels. We only tested battery-powered mowers, but expect gas mowers to be louder. While the operation is often quiet, I did find that several mowers made annoying beeping sounds when backing up or had a loud recorded voice during setup or upon receiving a command. Do Robot Mowers Work in Any Weather? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Robot mowers and their charging stations usually have IP ratings and can cope with rain, but you should pack up and bring your mower indoors during the winter months. Many robot mowers have some kind of rain sensor and will pause mowing when it gets too wet. Some mowers may need to be paused manually. The wheels can churn up your lawn and get caked in mud if mowers continue to labor in the rain, especially with larger and heavier models. How Well Do Robot Mowers Cut? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Mowers of different sizes will have varying cutting widths, denoting the width of the strip they can cut on each pass. Most also have floating cutting decks that enable you to choose the length of grass you want (typically 1 to 3 inches). Many robot mowers seem to struggle with cutting around the edges of a lawn, especially if there’s a wall or fence that prevents them from getting close enough. It’s common to find an uncut verge around the edge of your lawn, so you might need to occasionally get the string trimmer out. Every robot mower I’ve tested has also struggled to cut the area around the charging station, so I recommend placing the unit on a deck or pavement if possible. Can I Install a Robot Mower Myself? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron ​Yes, most robot mowers can be installed by anyone, but you might want to set aside an afternoon to work out any snags. Finding the best spot for the receiver for a satellite mower can be tricky. The mapping process can also take a while; usually, the mower will prompt you to remote-control it around the border you want to set. After the first mow, you should review its performance and make tweaks to ensure it’s covering the entire area you want to cut. Can Robot Mowers Mow at Night? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Some models are capable of mowing at night in the dark using headlights, Lidar, and Time of Flight sensors, alongside their usual navigation capabilities. This can be convenient and also removes the risk for pets or children playing on the lawn during the day. However, there is a risk of injuring nocturnal wildlife, like hedgehogs in the UK and Europe. Mowers are also more likely to make mistakes and get stuck in the dark. It may be better to schedule mowing for dawn or dusk. How I Test Robot Lawn Mowers AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron I test each robot lawn mower for at least a month, on at least two different lawn areas, assessing the ease of setup, the mapping process, automatic scheduling (where available), navigation, obstacle avoidance, and the quality of the final cut, looking for length, uniformity, and any missed patches. Where applicable, I try extra features, tweak settings in the app, and check how the mower handles different weather conditions. I also keep an eye on battery performance and charging time to ensure it aligns with the manufacturer's claims.

Tech.title: Charlie Kirk Was Shot a Year Ago. The Conspiracy Theories Are More Rampant Than Ever
Tech.content:
In the days after the assassination of conservative activist and Turning Point cofounder Charlie Kirk, the online reaction was a mess. Graphic videos of the shooting were everywhere within minutes of his death, far-right figures called for violence and vengeance, and right-wing lawmakers and influencers called for the cancellation—and worse—of anyone celebrating. Then, the conspiracy theories began.

It’s been one year since Kirk’s death, and conspiracy theories about the shooting have persisted, supercharged by social media algorithms and right-wing influencers like Candace Owens, who has used her huge following to push baseless allegations about the incident.

Experts believe these conspiracy theories will continue for a long time to come. “There’s no reason to believe conspiracy theories about Kirk’s murder will lose steam anytime soon,” Jared Holt, senior researcher at Open Measures, tells WIRED. “If anything, I expect them to escalate further as the criminal trial against Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing Kirk, plays out over the next year or so. The trial is bound to draw major media attention and offer conspiracy theorists a source of new material to work from.”

In the immediate aftermath of Kirk’s death, some conspiracy theorists claimed the assassination was a false flag operation designed to deflect attention away from President Donald Trump’s connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Others claimed the entire thing was staged. There was the AI-powered gun theory, the claim that the shooter was a Kirk supporter, and even claims that Kirk was still alive.

But ultimately, the baseless claim that persisted is that someone close to Kirk, or operating on behalf of Israel, was responsible for his death, that Robinson was simply a patsy, and what really killed Kirk was an exploding microphone. This is the narrative that has been central to Owens’ monthslong conspiracy theory campaign. Her Kirk content has racked up hundreds of millions of views.

Owens’ success is fueled in large part by the way that social media platforms today encourage their users to post content. “X and YouTube are rife with speculation about Kirk’s death, where it is both still possible to recruit new audiences and monetize them,” Joan Donovan, assistant professor of journalism and emerging media studies at Boston University, tells WIRED.

Tech.title: Best Bluetooth Speaker (2026): JBL, Sonos, Marshall, and More
Tech.content:
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.

What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.

The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.

Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.

Honorable Mentions

Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.

Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.

Tech.title: ‘Killmonger Locs’ Are Everywhere in Video Games. This Artist Is Sick of It
Tech.content:
When the life-simulation game Paralives was released in early access, Danielle Udogaranya’s hand ached at the thought of making new Black hairstyles for it.

It wasn't because she didn't want to create for the game. Udogaranya, better known as Ebonix, has spent over a decade creating custom content for life-simming games with the goal of helping people see themselves on digital screens. Her hesitation stemmed from the physical toll it takes to craft the perfect digital coil, braid, and kink—painstakingly long hours and tedious precision.

“I thought to myself, why am I still having to do this?” Udogaranya, a technical artist who has a degree in psychology, tells WIRED.

Fans of games like The Sims spend time flipping through her sites, downloading custom hair packs inspired by real-life styles not otherwise available in-game. As of now, the Ebonix Patreon has over 115,000 members, and hundreds of both free and paid content items.

The reason behind the demand for custom content in life-simming games is both simple and disappointing: Natural Black hairstyles have been historically underrepresented, and the technology used to make them has been slow to improve.

“With new games coming out now, I'm still seeing the issues, and I'm still seeing the ‘Killmonger locs.’ God forbid we get more than three options,” Udogaranya says, in reference to the stiff, short-dreaded style featured by Michael B. Jordan’s character in Black Panther that became a go-to for many games as well as some other films. Similar examples can be seen in old and new franchises alike, including Tekken 8, Spider-Man 2, Apex Legends, Horizon Zero Dawn, and more. The reason for this Black hair default? Textured hairstyles in games have been reliant on code that was not made for them.

Tech.title: Everything New You Can Do With Siri AI
Tech.content:
Siri made its debut on the iPhone in 2011, five years ahead of Google Assistant and 11 years before ChatGPT would open up to the public. Despite the head start, Apple's voice AI has been comprehensively overtaken in recent years, and made to look rather primitive compared to the many generative AI rivals it’s now up against.

With the launch of iOS 27, Apple and Siri are fighting back. There's a new name—Siri AI—and a host of new capabilities that are coming to your iPhone.

These are the new features that you'll be able to make use of once iOS 27 appears on your handset, if you're running the iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max or later (including, of course, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo). Only these latest phones have the necessary on-board silicon to meet the higher AI processing demands.

Get More Personal Context

You'll notice when Siri AI arrives that it spends some time indexing everything on your iPhone. That's so it can dig deep into your texts, emails, calendars, and whatever else you have stored on your phone (everything is kept on-device though—nothing gets sent back to Apple).

It means you can ask natural questions about text conversations, email interactions, and appointments—"What day is my work appraisal happening?" for example, or "Where did I say I'd meet Mom?"—and get informed, personalized answers back, based on what's already stored in your apps.

This works for photos and videos as well. Open up the Photos app and you're able to ask Siri AI to show you all the pictures of your pet, or the images you took on your last vacation, or all the photos of trees you've collected, via simple, conversational prompts.

Ask About Anything on the Screen

Siri AI knows what you're looking at while you're using your iPhone—perhaps even better than you do. Whereas before you would've had to take a screenshot and give it to Siri to look at, now you can just ask.

So if you're on the web in Safari, you can say "Hey Siri" and then get it to summarize the text onscreen or identify a landmark in an image in an online article. You can ask what certain options mean in Settings, or look up more details about a game you're thinking about downloading from the App Store.

The same sort of visual processing is available through the iOS Camera app too: Just switch to Siri mode using the selector by the shutter button, and ask Siri AI about anything that's in view (nutritional information about an item on a menu, for instance).

Siri AI can see what you see. Courtesy of David Nield

Write and Edit Text Anywhere

The old Siri could generate text for you, but it offloaded the job to an integrated ChatGPT plug-in. With Siri AI, no third-party help is needed, and you can use it for things like text messages and emails.

Just call up Siri AI by saying "Hey Siri" or tapping on the Write with Siri link, then tell it what you want to say or describe the edits you'd like it to make. You can instruct it to make your messages sound more or less formal, to expand or shorten sections of text, or to turn quick notes into full paragraphs and sentences.

Tech.title: 9 Windows Laptops That Give MacBooks a Run for Their Money
Tech.content:
You'll want to read our extensive guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop, but for the basics, decide what category of laptop you need. Most people should buy a 13-inch or 14-inch laptop, and spending around $750 to $1,000 is a good place to start. At this price, you should expect good battery life, a decent screen, solid performance for basic tasks, and a comfortable keyboard and touchpad. You should also expect at least 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Anything more than that gets into premium territory where you're paying for higher specs, more performance, or extra features. If you want a discrete GPU for gaming or creative workflows, you'll need to spend more.

A laptop like the Dell 14 Plus is a great example of what you can get in this price range. You can even find laptops with OLED panels and up to one terabyte of storage, depending on how good the discounts are. I would consider anything under $750 a cheap laptop, and it will come with significant compromises, especially in panel and touchpad quality. Fortunately, laptops that use the Qualcomm Snapdragon X chip get great battery life, even when they fall under $750, such as the HP OmniBook 5 14.

Here's a list of important specs to consider:

CPU: Thanks to the huge variety of good chip options, it's never been trickier to buy a laptop. For thin-and-light laptops, I would recommend one of the following chips:

Qualcomm Snapdragon X, Snapdragon X Plus, or Snapdragon X Elite

Qualcomm Snapdragon X2, Snapdragon X2 Plus, or Snapdragon X2 Elite

Intel Core Ultra 225 V or Core Ultra 7 258V

Intel Core 5 320, Core Ultra 7 365, or Core Ultra X7 358H

There are many variations of these chips, so you'll undoubtedly run across other strings of numbers, especially on the Intel front. But the above is a good place to start. There’s lots more to say in the world of gaming laptops or content creation devices, so make sure to read our full guide to How to Buy a Gaming Laptop.

GPU: As of now, Intel's Panther Lake X7 or X9 chips have the most powerful integrated graphics. You'll find them in laptops like the Dell XPS 14, which can replicate discrete GPU-level performance like the RTX 4050. Unlike many laptops with discrete GPUs, though, Panther Lake X chips offer great battery life, making them better Windows alternatives to the MacBook Pro.

For discrete options, you'll want one of the latest Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs, such as the RTX 5060. The biggest leap in performance is between the RTX 5070 and the RTX 5070 Ti, which increases VRAM to 12 GB.

RAM (or memory): Stick with at least 16 GB if you can. Since the Copilot+ designation was introduced in 2024, it has become the new standard. You'll even find laptops as cheap as $600 that have 16 GB of memory. Gamers and content creators should upgrade to 32 GB if possible, though the ongoing memory shortage makes this more expensive. There's been a new surge in 8 GB options, such as the Dell XPS 13, but these should be reserved for only light usage.

Storage: Similar to memory, many laptops have moved to 512 GB as the new standard, and you'll find lots of affordable laptops with that as the base configuration. Upgrading to 1 or 2 terabytes, where possible, will make your life that much easier, especially since many laptops don't offer expandable storage.

Display: Laptops are usually categorized by screen size, with 13-inch, 14-inch, and 16-inch being the most common. Consider size, resolution, refresh rate, and panel type.

Portability: Aside from display size, chassis thickness and weight are the main factors, determining how portable a laptop is to travel with. Other dimensions are important too, but more often than not, that is determined by the screen size.

Ports: Many laptops are limited to USB-C and a headphone jack these days, with some exceptions that include USB-A or HDMI. Make sure your laptop has what you need, or you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station to add ports or increase external display support.

Tech.title: Book Excerpt: Emily St. John Mandel’s ‘Exit Party’ Imagines a Future Where a Spy Could Disappear
Tech.content:
True diligence is following the improbable path. I read the sentence in a detective novel in childhood, when I was 8 or 9 years old, and then the phrase stayed with me forever after.

For a long time I wrote True Diligence in stylized curly letters on the inside page of every notebook, or sometimes on the front cover. I had notebooks for writing down clues, because even at 9 I wanted to work for the Internal Intelligence Service. What child doesn’t secretly wish to be a spy?

We were terrified and fascinated by Service in equal measure. Service was dark cars moving down the block, men and women in forgettable clothing stopping our parents on the street for brief random interrogations. Service was the force that made people disappear—when I was in the first grade, my friend from across the street climbed into the back of a black car with her parents, and their apartment stood empty for a year before other people moved in—but also Service carried a kind of dark glamour, an aura of power that called to us.

We played Ghosts and Agents all the time, my friends and I, but eventually they drifted off into other interests and I still wanted to be a spy, so after high school I applied successfully to the Service Academy in Los Angeles. I was talented and moved through school quickly, and afterward I was posted to Fillmore, a pretty town about 80 kilometers north of LA. My parents came to visit me there in my first year.

“This is lovely, Ibari,” my mother said, when she stepped off the train. The town made a good first impression. The central station was beautiful, one of those Southern California structures with no serious boundary between indoors and out, a tiled platform that turned into a waiting area with benches, then archways opening out to the street.

My parents had been on the train since Ohio, and they looked worn and dazed, blinking in the relentless sunlight. I was only in my mid-twenties at that point, which is to say I hadn’t thought much about the reality of aging parents, and their haziness was a glimpse into a future where I was the adult and they were confused. I didn’t like it.

“Not a cloud in the sky,” my father said.

“Do we need a taxi?” my mother asked. “I wouldn’t mind walking a bit, stretching my legs.”

“My house is close,” I said. “We can easily walk there if you’d like.”

“Downtown residency permit?” my father asked, and whistled softly.

“What can I say,” I said. “I’ve been well-behaved.”

I’ve spent a long time thinking about the nature of life in a surveillance state, which is perhaps obvious given my work, but there are observations I’ve made that I share with no one, and one of them has to do with the way in a place like this, reality splits into two.

Courtesy of Alfred A. Knopf Buy This Book At: Amazon

Bookshop.org

This will seem a bit obvious­—there’s your actual job, which is Service, and then there’s your cover, which is what you tell everyone you do—­but for a long period of my life, at the beginning of my career, there was truth in both versions.

At the Service Academy I’d been trained in espionage and investigation, obviously, in relevant law, in the ins and outs of running down leads, interrogation, documentation, maintaining relationships with confidential informants, etc., but also I’d earned a master’s in urban planning, and this was my cover. As far as my parents and everyone else in my life was concerned, I was an up-­and-­coming academic with a tenure-­track job at the local college. My parents didn’t know I was Service, because no one in my life knew I was Service.

Here was the branching, as I thought of it, the point where one reality split off into another: It was actually true that I was a junior professor in an urban planning department. I’d applied for and earned that position, or so I told myself—­if strings were pulled behind the scenes, that was well above my pay grade—and I took that job seriously. With that being the case, was it really just cover? It was a real job, a real life. When I introduced myself as a college instructor in urban planning, it wasn’t a lie. There was an expansiveness about it. It was like getting to live two lives at once.

Tech.title: Apple Watch Series 12 Hands-On: Familiar Design, Different Everywhere Else
Tech.content:
The Apple Watch Series 12 has arrived, and like clockwork, Apple unveiled its latest flagship smartwatch at its September launch event alongside the Apple Watch Ultra 4, new iPhone 18 models and the long-awaited foldable iPhone Duo. I got to test out the new Series 12 in the demo room and see its new features up close.

Apple may have kept the familiar Apple Watch design for another year, but it has seemingly changed everything else inside. The most important upgrades are the hardware that powers its new features: a new S11 processor and reengineered health sensors. Combined, they allow for higher heart rate accuracy, deeper recovery insights and a new AI-powered Audio Intelligence feature that can transcribe and save important conversations.

But perhaps the biggest surprise is what didn’t change: the price. While Apple raised prices on its iPhone 18 Pro lineup, the Series 12 still starts at $399, while the Ultra 4 starts at $799.

More processing power for Siri AI

Apple had ground to make up on processing power this year after using the S10 chip for two generations. The new S11 chip makes up for some lost time, with a faster GPU, CPU and neural engine.

One place that extra processing power could come in handy is WatchOS 27, which brings the new Siri AI to the Apple Watch. I’ve already been testing Siri AI in beta on the Ultra 3, and it’s miles ahead of traditional Siri. It can answer more complex and contextual questions, reference information in Apple’s native apps and generally avoid the frustrating “here’s what I found on the web” response that made traditional Siri feel especially limited on the wrist.

But I’ve also noticed some lag. Some of that could be because the software is still in beta, but I’m curious to see whether the new S11 chip speeds up those interactions on the Series 12.

The new processor could also help with battery life. Apple rates the Series 12 for the same 24 hours as the previous generation, but it’s now taking heart rate samples more frequently than before for increased accuracy and uses a separate always-one processor within the S11 chip for these types of tasks.

For context, the Series 11 lasted about 28 hours during my real-world testing, so I’ll be looking to see whether those gains translate outside Apple’s controlled testing.

Apple/CNET

Audio Intelligence feature recaps older conversations

One of the most interesting new AI-powered features on the watch is what Apple calls Audio Intelligence. It’s essentially the ability for your watch to listen in on conversations, to either transcribe the last 15 seconds of a missed conversation with live Rewind — like revisiting the specials at a restaurant if you zoned out while the waiter was talking — or give you a high-level summaries of longer conversations and meetings with Siri Recap.

You can set up this feature manually or enable it to turn on at a specific time. Apple also says none of the conversations are stored and that even what is processed in the cloud to surface on your other Apple devices can’t be accessed by the company (or anyone else).

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Apple gets serious about recovery

Compared with the sensor array on my Series 11, the back of the Series 12 looks almost flower-like, with 32 electrodes that look like the petals of a daisy instead of the ring array with two electrodes on the older model. That gives the electrodes more surface area to capture better ECG readings. Apple also rearranged the green and infrared LEDs from the optical sensor into a smaller, circular cluster in the middle of the petals and reduced the size of the dots.

The new sensors enable more frequent heart rate and heart rate variability (or HRV) readings to (among other things) power a new Readiness score that tells you how your body is recovering.

Rather than looking at individual metrics in isolation, the app combines biometric signals associated with sleep, activity and other vitals to help you decide whether your body is ready for a hard workout or could be better off taking it easy.

This is similar to the existing Vitals app, which shows when overnight health metrics fall outside your typical range, and an addition to Training Load, which tracks how much strain you’re putting on your body.

And while recovery metrics aren’t new to wearables, Apple’s is different in that it reacts in real time and can change throughout the day depending on whether you’re draining or fueling your body. It’s also not locked behind a paywall and doesn’t require an additional subscription to unlock, just seven days (and nights) of use.

Revamped health app and other health features

Apple also announced a redesigned Health app that will combine AI insights and biometrics to give you daily summaries and personalized health recommendations similar to what other wearables such as Fitbit Air, Whoop and Oura give you, but also behind a paywall.

It also has a more comprehensive health test you can take on the app related to VO2 max and mobility using the cameras on the phone. It feeds all this data, along with optional blood panels, into a longevity tab that assesses different health categories.

WatchOS 27 will also bring more health features that aren’t exclusive to the Series 12, including workout updates and new perimenopause insights for women. Workout Buddy, Apple’s hype person in your ear during workouts, will also work in Spanish and without an iPhone nearby.

Familiar design, new paint job

If you were hoping for a dramatically different Apple Watch, this isn’t the year. The Series 12 keeps the familiar rectangular, all-screen display like its predecessor, but Apple is giving it a refresh with new colors, case finishes and bands.

The Series 12 comes in black, silver, light gold and a new bronze aluminum finish. Apple is also bringing back a ceramic case option for the Series 12, a material we haven’t seen on its flagship watch since the Series 5 in 2019, as well as a new gold titanium Hermes edition and new band options across the board.

Apple Watch Series 12: Price and availability

The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399 for the 42mm aluminum Wi-Fi model, and is available for preorder now.

Is the Apple Watch Series 12 worth the upgrade?

The Series 12 may look the same, but it has enough upgrades under the hood to warrant an upgrade, especially if you’re coming from an older model such as the Series 8 or below that won’t support some of the AI capabilities such as Siri AI.

The biggest issue right now is that a lot of the best features — including Siri AI, the revamped Health app and Audio Intelligence — won’t be available to test until later this year, so I can’t make a recommendation until these key features have been put to the test.

Tech.title: Want Some Movie Suggestions? You Should Call This Tubi Hotline
Tech.content:
Once upon a time in the ‘80s and ‘90s, hotlines were a thing. You could dial a 1-900 or 1-800 number for entertainment, advice or to chat with strangers. I won’t help you age yourself by reminiscing about whether you called Nintendo’s tip line or Freddy Krueger (who wanted us all to know he was just a phone call away), but I do want to let you know Tubi is bringing that vibe back with TubiFone.

The free streaming service is one of my favorite platforms for finding classic movies and TV shows (and lots of other content, too), and now it wants to help you pick something to watch with its recommendation hotline. It’s matching your energy. How? By calling 1-833-605-TUBI and sharing what kind of mood you’re in. The hotline is part of the streamer’s new “Find Any Feeling for Free” campaign.

I dialed TubiFone myself, and the hotline delivers a lineup of movies after you make your selection based on how you’re feeling. For each of the five recommendations, a prerecorded voice recites the film’s description and cast members, followed by its title. When I clicked the option for “Adventurous,” here’s what I got:

To Live and Die in LA Men in Black The Mummy The Thomas Crown Affair Where the Wild Things Are

This is a different kind of hotline bling — one that offers movie recs. Tubi

It’s up to you whether to rely solely on an algorithm or your device’s search function to sift through Tubi’s extensive library, or make a quick phone call for some film recommendations. The service has other ways you can find content to watch, too, including its Scenes feature, its ChatGPT app and dedicated content hubs.

Tech.title: NASA and IBM Launch Open-Source AI Model for Future Moon Explorations
Tech.content:
The NASA‑IBM Lunar Foundation Model is one of the first of its kind: a publicly available AI model created to support exploration of the moon under NASA’s Artemis program.

Launched on Thursday and now available on the collaborative, open-source AI platform Hugging Face, the model was trained on decades of lunar observation data selected by IBM and NASA researchers to provide insights to advance human presence on the moon, according to a press release.

IBM and NASA have worked together for over 60 years, since they first collaborated to put the first man on the moon.

A new phase for moon exploration

In the past, scientists had to manually examine maps and images collected by different instruments that had been analyzing the moon for decades. Or they used low-resolution machine learning models designed only for a specific task.

This infographic shows how the NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model helps analyze widespread lunar imagery and data. IBM

The NASA‑IBM Lunar Foundation Model not only saves researchers time by identifying data patterns at scale and across different instruments but, according to the press release, also outperforms widely used methods by up to 23% in identifying the moon’s key geographic features. This includes craters, volcanic formations and potential ice deposits, all of which provide crucial information for future Artemis moon explorations.

Shining light on the first lunar dataset of its kind

In addition to the foundation AI model, IBM and NASA scientists also built what they’re calling the first open-source lunar dataset of its kind, bringing together tens of thousands of maps and images collected by nine instruments across four moon missions.

The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model uses multiple lunar data inputs to identify areas on the moon that may contain ice. IBM

Campbell Watson, senior research manager at IBM Research, told CNET in an email that by making the model and the dataset publicly available, IBM and NASA want to provide the global scientific community with a shared foundation that researchers can adapt and apply to new questions about the moon.

“This work builds on decades of publicly released lunar data collected across multiple missions, so open-sourcing the model continues that tradition of broad scientific access and collaboration,” Watson said.

The NASA‑IBM Lunar Foundation Model isn’t the only one of NASA and IBM’s open-source AI models on Hugging Face. It also hosts the Prithvi family of models for weather, climate and earth observation.

The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model can analyze lunar imagery to automatically identify craters on the moon. IBM

Researchers can build on the NASA‑IBM model to make new discoveries, rather than creating an AI model from scratch each time.

Tech.title: Sorry, Apple, but the iPhone Duo Isn’t the Smart Display I’m Waiting For
Tech.content:
Apple’s “Surprise and shine” on Wednesday featured plenty of callouts to AI, with Apple envisioning its iPhone and the new foldable iPhone Duo as “personal hubs” where artificial intelligence is everywhere, especially the new Siri AI. But one major announcement was notably missing, and it’s especially frustrating for smart home fans.

Throughout 2026, I’ve heard reports from publications citing Apple insiders that the delayed Apple smart home push was finally — no, really this time — coming during the Apple fall event. Most importantly, the rumors said Apple was ready to unleash a smart home display, similar to Amazon Echo Shows but with a unique, versatile design and updated features like facial recognition. Reports mentioned several installation options, including wall mounting or a pivoting smart display that could let Siri watch different faces in turn.

With Siri AI early access debuting throughout this year, and Apple talking about new Apple Home features like video descriptions for security cameras, the smart display seemed like a done deal for this fall. But no. Apple didn’t show a hint of any Siri home display. I don’t think the Apple Home app got even a second of screen time for this event.

The closest we’ll get to any kind of Apple display is the new iPhone Duo, which can be tented to resemble something sort of like a smart display, showing calendars or an alarm clock, but it’s a far cry from a fully independent device made to take up permanent residence in a kitchen, shelf or bedside table. And while it may be the “largest iPhone display we’ve ever designed,” according to Apple, at $1,999, the Duo is exponentially more expensive than today’s smart displays.

Ginormous pricing aside, the foldable Duo isn’t big enough to take over my favorite roles for a smart display, like serving as a second TV screen while you’re busy, and its speakers certainly can’t compare with the room-filling options most home displays come with these days. Siri AI also doesn’t appear set up to display conversations, food orders and video at a command like Alexa Plus can — although that remains to be tested.



Why didn’t we see Apple’s home display device?

Apple faces home-screen competition from Amazon and others, which could be one reason it’s delaying plans here. Amazon

My first thought is that the iPhone Duo already took enough work to prep for this event, and Siri AI (available in beta when OS 27 drops on Monday) may not be quite ready for a home screen the way Alexa Plus is. With the Duo playing so many different roles, Apple may be watching its performance and popularity carefully before deciding if and how to move into smart displays. Ditto for Siri AI, which, as I mentioned, may not be ready for the many integrations other AI voice assistants currently offer.

Since RAMageddon and other trends are pushing device prices higher and higher right now, Apple may also be leery of releasing a new device at a price that almost surely wouldn’t compete with top-rated competitor models. Remember, that was one complaint people had about the original Apple HomePod smart speaker, which launched at $349, way above the smart speakers of the day, and eventually led to the more reasonably priced HomePod mini.

Apple’s reaping some advantages by waiting so long to get into the AI game, but those delays also invite risk. A smart space occupied by Echo Shows, Nest Hubs and smart calendars for years could be challenging to enter, which may be another reason Apple is weighing its options here.

But Apple may also be saving its home display for a different reveal. We are expecting more news about the iPad mini, potentially in October. I don’t think this is likely, especially since a standalone display would be a new category for Apple, and it would prefer to announce that with more fanfare.

As for me, I can’t wait for an Apple smart display to finally — if ever — launch. Not only are these some of my favorite devices to test, but I think Apple could make its display refreshing and useful, including connections to Apple TV shows, an easy FaceTime experience and easy handoffs when switching from iPhone or iPad to a more central display. But time will, once again, have to tell on those specifics.

Tech.title: I Tested 2 Popular Vitamix Blenders and Prefer the One That’s $120 Less
Tech.content:
CNET’s key takeaways

If you want a great Vitamix blender, you don’t have to spend $500 for a great model. Go for the VX1 instead and save yourself $120.

The VX1 has self-cleaning and pulse modes, a sleek, modern design and doesn’t compromise on power.

The VX1 is a larger blender at 64 ounces. If you don’t need that much blending space, opt for a personal blender, such as the $130 Ninja BlendBoss, instead.

Certain brands have become synonymous with the products they create. Think Kleenex, Sharpie, Band-Aid and even Vitamix. That notoriety can make it easier to know which brands to turn to for quality tissues, permanent markers, adhesive bandages or blenders. But choosing becomes tricky when you realize these brands offer multiple versions of their most popular products. So which model should you buy?

In the case of Vitamix, when testing the VX1 and 5200, two of its most popular blenders, for CNET’s best blenders list, I learned that more expensive doesn’t always mean better. Here’s why.

The Best Blenders: Picks for Smoothies, Dips, Soup and More See It

My experience with the Vitamix VX1

Launched as a replacement for the discontinued and beloved Explorian, the VX1 is now one of Vitamix’s most affordable blenders at $380. It’s also CNET’s pick for the best overall blender, since it excelled during our hands-on testing.

Vitamix VX1 vs. 5200

Both the 5200 and VX1 have a 64-ounce capacity, cord storage underneath and 10 speeds, but neither is dishwasher-safe. However, the VX1 has a few extra features, including a pulse mode, a self-cleaning program and 0.2 more horsepower. It also has a slightly smaller footprint than the 5200.

The VX1 (right) measures 9.5×7.8×19.6 inches, compared to the 5200’s 20.5×8.75×7.25 inches. Anna Gragert/CNET

During testing, the 1440-watt VX1 outperformed 10 other models at blending raw almonds into almond butter, taking only 1 minute and 13 seconds. It also excelled at turning chickpeas into hummus in less than a minute.

As for the 1380-watt 5200, it took 1 minute and 51 seconds to blend almond butter and 1 minute and 41 seconds to blend hummus. It also took 12 seconds longer than the VX1 to blend a green smoothie.

Where the 5200 impressed

Although I preferred the VX1’s operation, the 5200 still performed well in two specific tests: blending cubed ice and butternut squash soup. It blended the former in 24 seconds to create snow-like ice, leaving just two medium cubes, while the VX1 took 26 seconds and left several large cubes. When blending the soup, the 5200 required only 12 seconds, which was five seconds less than the VX1.

The 5200 was also a smidge quieter than the VX1 when mixing a green smoothie on high speed, with a max of 93 A-weighted decibels. The VX1 was 95.1 dBA on high. Despite these wins, I don’t think the 5200 justifies such a steep price increase.

While it doesn’t have a pulse mode, the 5200 does have a “high” speed switch, which is nice if you often blend challenging ingredients that require more power and don’t want to fiddle with a speed dial.

I prefer the more modern look of the VX1. Anna Gragert/CNET

The one I’d keep on my countertop

Numbers aside, I prefer the VX1 over the 5200 in terms of design. It has a more modern look and is visually less angular and bulky. I also like that there are three different ways to safely stop blending: an on/off switch under the base, a start/pause switch on its front and a standby mode on the speed dial.

3.5 feet of cord storage. Not too shabby. Anna Gragert/CNET

Vitamix’s 5200 costs $500, $120 more than the $380 VX1. While both models have a limited warranty, you get seven years with the 5200, two years more than the VX1’s five-year warranty.

Overall, based on my testing, I don’t think you need to spend the extra money to get a great Vitamix blender. If you’re stuck choosing between the 5200 and VX1, I’d go with the VX1 and rest assured you won’t miss out on anything.

Tech.title: I Tried the iPhone 18 Pro’s New Deluxe Camera and Shot Photos With Starbursts
Tech.content:
While the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are among Apple’s newest phones, they are the ones that don’t fold. Thankfully, a handful of upgrades, like a fancy new camera tool, will make photographers rejoice!

I tried the iPhone 18 Pro in a packed demo area in the Steve Jobs Theater at Apple Park right after the company’s “Surprise and shine” event. Admittedly, it wasn’t the ideal environment for photographic testing. But I was later able to take some photos and videos using the new variable aperture, in a calmer setting that showed off its potential. I now understand what the “shine” in the event’s name referred to.

Think of a camera’s aperture like your eyelids. When your eyes are wide open, they let in more light. Under the bright sun, you squint to reduce the glare and see better. A variable aperture does the same for a camera lens. There are tiny blades that open and close to let more light onto the image sensor, or to reduce exposure in a bright scene.



Most phone cameras have a fixed aperture that can’t be adjusted. But the iPhone 18 Pro acts more like a dedicated camera, letting you stop it down for sharper images or, in dark environments, open the aperture wide to capture a brighter scene.

I was even able to achieve starbursts, thanks to the physical aperture blades. If there’s a bright light source in your shot, like string lights, you can stop the aperture down to add light peaks. The effect is caused by the way the aperture blades meet.

In terms of how it works, there’s an auto setting that lets the phone pick the best aperture. But you can also set it manually, choosing between four f-stops, which determine how wide the aperture’s opening is set.

The iPhone 18 Pro isn’t the first phone with a mechanical aperture. I remember shooting photos in 2018 with the Galaxy S9, which had a dual-aperture camera. Xiaomi’s 14 Ultra had a stepless aperture that let you stop anywhere between f/1.63 and f/4.0. The iPhone 18 Pro has fours stops: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0.

While I think professional photographers, filmmakers and other creative types will enjoy it most, a variable aperture isn’t enough of a reason for most people to buy an iPhone 18 Pro, especially if you’re just posting pics on social media. Just get the iPhone 17, especially since the iPhone 18 Pro now starts at $1,199 and the 18 Pro Max at $1,299, a $100 more than the 17 Pro and Pro Max from last year.

So what else did I think from my hands-on time with the new Apple phones?

The burgundy color looks magnificent in-person. It has a rich and sophisticated charm, forgoing the iPhone 17 Pro’s bold construction vest orange.

The iPhone 18 Pro in silver (left), burgundy, glacier and black.

The Dynamic Island is slimmer, thanks to a wildly clever implementation of putting the FaceTime camera under the display. We’re still not at a full circle for the Dynamic Island, but it’s now closer in size to an ibuprofen tablet than the 17 Pro’s longer, slender oval.



The batteries on both Pro models are larger, with the SIM card tray models of the iPhone 18 Pro at 4,056 mAh and the 18 Pro Max at 5,391 mAh, according to Apple’s site in Ireland. (Thanks, EU, for Apple requiring energy labels!). While US models are only eSIM, Apple fills the space normally used by a SIM card tray with more battery. By contrast, SIM card tray versions of the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max have 3,988 mAh and 4,823 mAh, respectively.

It will be curious to see how those increased capacities offset power-hungry Siri AI features and operating that variable aperture. The 18 Pro and Pro Max are powered by a new A20 Pro chip, which Apple says brings efficiency gains to offset battery drain.

I look forward to testing the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, once I can get them. You can preorder the new Pro iPhones starting Saturday, Sept. 12 and they’ll be in stores starting Friday, Sept. 18.

Tech.title: The iPhone Air 2 Wasn’t Announced. Here’s Why That’s Bad for Apple Buyers
Tech.content:
We got a host of new iPhones at Wednesday’s Apple Surprise and Shine event. But there were some noticeable absences: base iPhone 18 models, as Apple focused purely on premium devices, and a second iteration of its lightweight iPhone Air.

At just 5.6mm thick and weighing only 165 grams, last year’s $999 iPhone 17 Air gave buyers a middle-ground option between the base iPhone 17 and the iPhone 17 Pro models, and for a pretty reasonable price.

While sales of the iPhone Air were reportedly disappointing, it was arguably a first step toward launching the iPhone Duo — a demonstration that a slim, lightweight phone could be just as durable and high-functioning as a fully specced-out one. It came with just one rear 48-megapixel wide-angle camera, a smaller battery and a single speaker.

The Air’s pared-back features and slim profile would have been pivotal to designing Apple’s new folding phone, since foldables must be both slim and make similar compromises on specs — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 only has two rear lenses, compared with the three that come on other Galaxy models, and the iPhone Duo likewise has just two rear cameras.

We were hoping Apple would release another version of the Air with improved cameras and battery life, especially since that middle ground still exists. Some people just want a phone that’s slightly better than the base iPhone, and many people want a capable phone without having to spend upward of $1,199 — the cheapest phone Apple announced on Wednesday as it took the wraps off premium handsets like the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max See at Apple

Many people also don’t want a phone that folds. CNET’s survey of more than 2,600 adults last month found that 75% were not interested in a foldable iPhone and that most would want to spend less than $1,000 if they did get one. But the Duo costs between $1,999 and $3,199 — far exceeding the iPhone Air’s original $999 price tag.

Apple also raised the prices on its iPhone 17 lineup on Wednesday as it announced its new high-end handsets, leaving the middle ground with fewer options, even in previously available models. The iPhone 17 Air now starts at $1,099, with the price increases coming amid RAMageddon, the global memory shortage caused by the spike in AI tools. Apple continues to whittle down options for more budget-conscious consumers in a difficult economy.

We’re still holding out hope that the iPhone 18 Air has been pushed back until a rumored spring launch, where it could be unveiled alongside an iPhone 18 base model and a potential iPhone 18E, the budget follow-up to this year’s iPhone 17E.

IDC Worldwide Device Trackers Senior Research Director Nabila Popal likewise believes Apple is strategically withholding the second iPhone Air until next year to bundle with the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18E — launching a trio of more affordable smartphones to contrast with the premium trio of the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and Duo that were just announced.

“It allows Apple to spread its shipments more evenly throughout the year and simultaneously allow the spotlight on the premium models this fall — especially the new iPhone foldable,” Popal said. “Apple is spreading its portfolio to a wider consumer demographic and giving consumers more choice.”

But for now, the lack of lower-end models means anyone wanting to upgrade their phone to a brand-new Apple handset will be stuck choosing between an $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro and up to an eye-watering $3,199 for a 2TB iPhone Duo.

Tech.title: I Got My Hands on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s First Foldable Phone. Here’s What Stands Out
Tech.content:
It’s finally here: Apple on Wednesday unveiled its first foldable iPhone, called the iPhone Duo. It’ll start at $1,999 for 256GB in the US. Preorders for the iPhone Duo begin on Oct. 16, ahead of an Oct. 23 release.

Apple debuted the new device during its fall event in Cupertino, California, along with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. It appears the company will save the baseline iPhone 18 for a later reveal, likely in spring 2027.

Similar to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo is designed to be better suited for consuming all kinds of media. If you’re watching a YouTube video or movie, the inside display gives you plenty of room. Rotate it to portrait, and you can endlessly scroll through vertical videos or read an e-book. The compact cover screen can be handy for quickly sending a message or checking notifications. It’s essentially designed to function as a compact iPhone that can double as an iPad Mini when needed.

I spent some time with the iPhone Duo at Apple Park, and here are a few features that stand out to me.

iPhone Duo design and build

The iPhone Duo is compact, with a passport-size design. It has a 7.6-inch display on the inside and a 5.4-inch outer display. It fits squarely in my palm, with dimensions similar to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, which has a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.5-inch cover display.

Apple says the Duo is the thinnest iPhone ever when open, measuring 5.2mm. It’s 11.3mm thick when closed. A titanium frame keeps it lightweight at 254 grams.

One of the key differences in feel between Apple’s and Samsung’s phones is that the iPhone Duo has a matte, nano-textured finish on the inner display, which reduces the phone’s crease while also curbing reflections. It has a satisfying feel and really makes the crease virtually disappear when the screen is on. I find it even harder to notice than the Z Fold 8’s, which also has an anti-reflective display.

What crease?? Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

While the Z Fold 8 has sharper corners, the iPhone Duo takes on more rounded edges. Which look you prefer comes down to preference. For now, I’m partial to the Z Fold 8’s more square-like design that makes it appear slightly more polished , but it’s possible the Duo’s style will grow on me.

There’s another distinguishing trait on the iPhone Duo. When opening the phone, the content transitions from the cover screen to the main display almost immediately. On the other hand, when I prop the Z Fold 8 open, content shifts from the cover to the main display when it’s about halfway open. It’s a neat element that can help the Duo feel more refined; I’m just not sure if it’ll make a significant difference in the user experience. I’ll need more time with the phone to decide.

The Duo supports multitasking with up to two apps. The Z Fold 8, in comparison, supports up to three apps (though things get a little crowded, so I tend to stick to two).

Interestingly, the Duo’s volume buttons are at the top of the phone when holding it in landscape. That prevents them from being cluttered amid the lock and Camera Control buttons, but it might take some time to get used to the placement. On the other hand, it’ll be easier to adjust the volume when the phone is rotated to portrait.

The Duo’s volume controls sit at the top of the phone. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The Duo’s cover is made with Apple’s Ceramic Shield 2, while Ceramic Shield protects the back. Perhaps one of the Duo’s most impressive traits is the IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, putting it on par with the durable Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Apple says a titanium plate helps to improve the Duo’s durability.

The iPhone Duo’s hinge is made of more than 100 components, according to Apple, making for a smooth open and close. The unfolding mechanism did give off a silky, premium feel as I repeatedly unfurled and shut the display.

The iPhone Duo can be propped half-open to easily watch movies and access controls. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Apple’s foldable comes in two colors, dubbed star white and night sky, which is a navy hue. It’ll be compatible with the Apple Pencil, which separates it from the Z Fold 8, which sadly doesn’t support Samsung’s S Pen.

To unlock, the Duo supports Touch ID, rather than Face ID. That’s a bit of a letdown, especially at such a high price. But I tend to use fingerprint unlock on the Z Fold 8 anyway, so perhaps it won’t be much of an adjustment for everyone.

Like the iPhone 18 Pro models, the Duo is powered by the A20 Pro chip.

iPhone Duo cameras

There are only two rear cameras. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo has a 48-megapixel main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera. Like the Z Fold 8, there’s no telephoto camera. I didn’t mind the lack of a telephoto lens on Samsung’s foldable, so I’m curious if I’ll feel the same once I take Apple’s new foldable out into the world to snap some photos.

The iPhone Duo supports 4K video at 120 frames per second in Dolby Vision, as well as 4K time-lapse video in Dolby Vision HDR.

Dual Capture in FaceTime lets you use the front and rear cameras simultaneously. When taking photos, you can turn on Duo Preview on the cover screen when the phone is unfolded, so your subject can see how the shot will look as you snap with the rear cameras. A feature called Kid Cue displays Peanuts animations on the cover screen to help draw kids’ eyes to the camera. This is similar to Made You Look on Pixel’s foldables.

Duo Preview in action. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

iPhone Duo battery life

Apple says the iPhone Duo will give you up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner display, and 44 hours when using the outer screen. When using both equally, the company says you’ll be able to go 24 hours before needing to charge.

Considering how often I use both the cover and inside displays on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, I have a feeling my battery life would lean more toward that 24-hour mark. But we’ll have to see how the phone holds up in CNET’s battery tests.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

A new foldable competitor

With the iPhone Duo, Apple enters an increasingly competitive foldable phone market, with key players including Samsung, Google and Motorola, as well as Chinese brands like Honor, Oppo and Huawei. Now, it’s Apple’s turn to further shape the space – and likely nudge it forward.

Analysts predict the iPhone Duo could give foldables, which remain a niche smartphone category, a significant boost. IDC forecasts that global foldable shipments will grow by more than 12% this year, with Apple’s entry driving much of that growth. The research firm also expects Apple to ship more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027, giving the company nearly 40% global market share by the end of next year.

“The iPhone Duo is the event’s strategic flagship and a direct test of whether Apple can use design, ecosystem integration and premium positioning to reshape a segment that has so far remained selective,” said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president of devices at IDC.
